paragraphs: The paper investigates combining neural learning with speech-science knowledge to recognize speech across speakers. That knowledge informs several parts of the system: preprocessing, input and output coding, supervision, and architectural constraints. The approach makes domain knowledge part of the design through which the network learns.

To handle speech over time, the authors combine delays with copies of hidden and output activations supplied at the input. They also use Back-Propagation for Sequences, a learning algorithm for networks with local self-loops. These mechanisms let the system incorporate temporal information, which matters because speech recognition depends on how acoustic evidence develops across a sequence.

The strategy is demonstrated in several experiments. The highlighted result concerns distinguishing nasal speech sounds, where applying a hypothesis from speech theory dramatically improves generalization. This finding supports the value of combining learned processing with task-specific knowledge in the reported setting. The evidence links the improvement to a particular speech-theory intervention, rather than claiming that every use of domain knowledge necessarily helps.
summary.tldr: Speech-science knowledge and temporal neural processing are combined, with a reported large generalization improvement on nasal-sound discrimination.

title: Speaker Independent Speech Recognition with Neural Networks and Speech Knowledge

paragraphs: This paper introduces a non-recurrent network for learning sequential tasks by combining higher-order connections with incremental growth. The network adds new units when more complex interactions are needed. These units dynamically modify connection weights, allowing previous inputs to influence later processing through changes in those weights.

The temporal mechanism operates across successive steps: new units use information from the previous step to modify weights at the next one. This lets the network learn temporal relationships without feedback connections, which the authors describe as greatly simplifying training. In principle, adding an unlimited number of units allows the model to reach arbitrarily far into the past.

Experiments using the Reber grammar show speedups of two orders of magnitude over recurrent networks. The result supports the usefulness of the proposed architecture on that sequential learning task. The distinction between theoretical capacity and demonstrated performance matters here: arbitrarily distant history is supported by unlimited growth in principle, while the reported speed advantage comes from the specific grammar experiments.
summary.tldr: An incrementally growing network carries temporal information through changing weights and achieves large speedups on Reber grammar learning.

title: Learning Sequential Tasks by Incrementally Adding Higher Orders

abstract: Dynamic programming provides a methodology to develop planners and controllers for nonlinear systems. However, general dynamic programming is computationally intractable. We have developed procedures that allow more complex planning and control problems to be solved. We use second order local trajectory optimization to generate locally optimal plans and local models of the value function and its derivatives. We maintain global consistency of the local models of the value function, guaranteeing that our locally optimal plans are actually globally optimal, up to the resolution of our search procedures. paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational difficulty of dynamic programming for nonlinear planning and control. A value function represents the future consequences of actions, making it useful for choosing what to do now. Computing such functions generally is intractable, so the authors seek to use fast local optimization within a broader global procedure.

Their method uses second-order trajectory optimization to produce locally optimal plans together with local models of the value function and its derivatives. These pieces describe how future cost behaves around particular plans. The crucial additional step is maintaining global consistency among the local value-function models, allowing separate local computations to contribute to a coherent overall solution.

The authors state that this consistency guarantees global optimality of the resulting plans up to the resolution of their search procedures. That resolution qualification defines the precision of the guarantee. The approach shows how optimizers that provide local answers can accelerate construction or learning of a globally optimal value function, enabling more complex planning and control problems to be addressed.
summary.tldr: Globally consistent local value models let fast trajectory optimizers support dynamic programming with optimality limited by search resolution.

title: Using Local Trajectory Optimizers to Speed Up Global Optimization in Dynamic Programming

abstract: This paper enhances the Q-Iearning algorithm for optimal asset alloca(cid:173) tion proposed in (Neuneier, 1996 [6]). The new formulation simplifies the approach by using only one value-function for many assets and al(cid:173) lows model-free policy-iteration. After testing the new algorithm on real data, the possibility of risk management within the framework of Markov decision problems is analyzed. The proposed methods allows the construction of a multi-period portfolio management system which takes into account transaction costs, the risk preferences of the investor, and several constraints on the allocation.

The new formulation simplifies the approach by using only one value-function for many assets and al(cid:173) lows model-free policy-iteration. After testing the new algorithm on real data, the possibility of risk management within the framework of Markov decision problems is analyzed. The proposed methods allows the construction of a multi-period portfolio management system which takes into account transaction costs, the risk preferences of the investor, and several constraints on the allocation.

paragraphs: Portfolio allocation is a sequence of decisions: an allocation chosen now affects the choices and costs encountered later. This paper revises a Q-learning approach to that problem. Its main simplification is to use one value function across many assets, providing a shared formulation for evaluating allocation decisions.

The revised approach also supports model-free policy iteration, meaning that the decision policy can be improved without requiring an explicit model of the environment. The authors test the algorithm on real data and then examine how risk management can be expressed within a Markov decision problem. This brings investment preferences into the same sequential framework as allocation choices.

The proposed methods support a portfolio-management system operating across multiple periods while accounting for transaction costs, investor risk preferences, and allocation constraints. These considerations matter because a sequence of attractive allocations may still be undesirable when switching costs or restrictions are included. The stated contribution is a simpler learning formulation and a framework for incorporating those practical decision requirements.
summary.tldr: A revised Q-learning formulation uses one value function for multiple assets and supports portfolio decisions with costs, risk preferences, and constraints.

title: Enhancing Q-Learning for Optimal Asset Allocation

abstract: A key question in vision is how to represent our knowledge of previously encountered objects to classify new ones. The answer depends on how we determine the similarity of two objects. Similarity tells us how relevant each previously seen object is in determining the category to which a new object belongs. Here a dichotomy emerges. Complex notions of similarity appear necessary for cognitive models and applications, while simple notions of similarity form a tractable basis for current computational approaches to classification. We explore the nature of this dichotomy and why it calls for new approaches to well-studied problems in learning. We begin this process by demonstrating new computational methods for supervised learning that can handle complex notions of similarity. (1) We discuss how to implement parametric met.hods that represent a class by its mean when using non-metric similarity functions; and (2) We review non-parametric methods that we have developed using nearest neighbor classification in non-metric spaces. Point (2) , and some of the background of our work have been described in more detail in [8].

paragraphs: The paper examines how object classification depends on the meaning of similarity. A similarity function determines which previously encountered objects should inform the classification of a new one. The authors identify a tension: complex similarities appear necessary for cognitive models and applications, while simpler similarities make established computational approaches easier to use.

Their response is to develop supervised learning methods that accommodate non-metric similarities. One direction concerns parametric classifiers that summarize a category by its mean. The paper discusses how to implement this style of representation when the similarity function does not provide the usual metric setting. This extends a familiar way of representing classes to a broader kind of comparison.

The second direction concerns non-parametric classification through nearest neighbors in non-metric spaces. The paper reviews methods the authors developed for this purpose, with some of that work described more fully elsewhere. The contribution is to show computational ways forward for richer similarity functions. It treats the choice of similarity as a fundamental part of the learning problem, with consequences for both class summaries and example-based decisions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and reviews classification methods that can use complex, non-metric notions of object similarity.

title: Classification in Non-Metric Spaces

abstract: In this work, we explore homeostasis in a silicon integrate-and-fire neu(cid:173) ron. The neuron adapts its firing rate over long time periods on the order of seconds or minutes so that it returns to its spontaneous firing rate after a lasting perturbation. Homeostasis is implemented via two schemes. One scheme looks at the presynaptic activity and adapts the synaptic weight depending on the presynaptic spiking rate. The second scheme adapts the synaptic "threshold" depending on the neuron's activity. The threshold is lowered if the neuron's activity decreases over a long time and is increased for prolonged increase in postsynaptic activity. Both these mechanisms for adaptation use floating-gate technology. The re(cid:173) sults shown here are measured from a chip fabricated in a 2-J.lm CMOS process.

paragraphs: The paper implements homeostasis in a silicon integrate-and-fire neuron. Here, homeostasis means adjusting activity over seconds or minutes so that the neuron returns to its spontaneous firing rate after a sustained perturbation. The focus is on slow adaptation of the neuron's behavior, allowing it to recover a baseline level of activity despite a lasting change.

Two mechanisms provide this adaptation. One monitors presynaptic activity and changes the synaptic weight according to the incoming spike rate. The other changes a synaptic threshold according to the neuron's own activity. Prolonged decreases in activity lower the threshold, while prolonged increases raise it, providing an adjustment that opposes the sustained change in firing.

Both mechanisms use floating-gate technology, and the reported results come from measurements of a chip fabricated in a 2-micrometer CMOS process. This makes the contribution a physical implementation of adaptive neural regulation. The two schemes demonstrate ways to base that regulation on either incoming activity or the output activity of the silicon neuron itself.
summary.tldr: A silicon neuron uses floating-gate adaptations of synaptic weight or threshold to recover its baseline firing rate after sustained perturbations.

title: Homeostasis in a Silicon Integrate and Fire Neuron

abstract: Experimental data show that biological synapses behave quite differently from the symbolic synapses in common artificial neural network models. Biological synapses are dynamic, i.e., their "weight" changes on a short time scale by several hundred percent in dependence of the past input to the synapse. In this article we explore the consequences that these synaptic dynamics entail for the computational power of feedforward neural networks. We show that gradient descent suffices to approximate a given (quadratic) filter by a rather small neural system with dynamic synapses. We also compare our network model to artificial neural net(cid:173) works designed for time series processing. Our numerical results are complemented by theoretical analysis which show that even with just a single hidden layer such networks can approximate a surprisingly large large class of nonlinear filters: all filters that can be characterized by Volterra series. This result is robust with regard to various changes in the model for synaptic dynamics.

paragraphs: Biological synapses change their effective strength over short timescales in response to their recent inputs. This paper investigates what those dynamics contribute to computation in feedforward neural networks. Because a synapse's current response depends on past activity, the connection itself supplies a way for input history to influence the network's output.

The authors show that gradient descent is sufficient to approximate a given quadratic filter using a relatively small neural system with dynamic synapses. They also compare this network model with artificial neural networks designed for time-series processing. The construction links a biologically motivated synaptic mechanism to a concrete task involving transformations of signals over time.

The theoretical analysis establishes a broader approximation result: even a single hidden layer can approximate all nonlinear filters describable by Volterra series. That identifies a large specified class of temporal computations, rather than claiming coverage of every possible filter. The result remains valid under various changes to the synaptic-dynamics model, indicating that this computational capability is robust across the variations considered.
summary.tldr: Feedforward networks with dynamic synapses can learn temporal filters and, with one hidden layer, approximate all filters characterized by Volterra series.

title: Processing of Time Series by Neural Circuits with Biologically Realistic Synaptic Dynamics

abstract: We provide a natural gradient method that represents the steepest descent direction based on the underlying structure of the param(cid:173) eter space. Although gradient methods cannot make large changes in the values of the parameters, we show that the natural gradi(cid:173) ent is moving toward choosing a greedy optimal action rather than just a better action. These greedy optimal actions are those that would be chosen under one improvement step of policy iteration with approximate, compatible value functions, as defined by Sut(cid:173) ton et al. [9]. We then show drastic performance improvements in simple MDPs and in the more challenging MDP of Tetris.

paragraphs: The paper develops a natural gradient method for improving a policy, the rule a learning agent uses to choose actions. Its update direction reflects the underlying structure of the parameter space. This makes the meaning of steepest improvement depend on that structure, rather than only on the numerical coordinates used to describe the policy.

The authors connect this direction to policy iteration. Although gradient methods make limited changes to parameter values, they show that the natural gradient moves toward the greedy actions associated with one policy-improvement step. This relationship uses approximate value functions satisfying a compatibility requirement. The claim concerns the direction of improvement under that formulation, rather than an immediate jump to a globally optimal policy.

Experiments show drastic performance improvements in simple Markov decision processes and in Tetris, a more challenging decision problem. Together, the theoretical connection and experiments explain why the update can be useful: a local parameter change can point toward a stronger policy-improvement target than merely favoring a somewhat better action.
summary.tldr: A natural policy gradient follows the structure of policy parameter space toward a policy-iteration improvement target, with large reported performance gains.

title: A Natural Policy Gradient

abstract: We develop a tree-based reparameterization framework that pro(cid:173) vides a new conceptual view of a large class of iterative algorithms for computing approximate marginals in graphs with cycles. It includes belief propagation (BP), which can be reformulated as a very local form of reparameterization. More generally, we consider algorithms that perform exact computations over spanning trees of the full graph. On the practical side, we find that such tree reparameterization (TRP) algorithms have convergence properties superior to BP. The reparameterization perspective also provides a number of theoretical insights into approximate inference, in(cid:173) cluding a new characterization of fixed points; and an invariance intrinsic to TRP /BP. These two properties enable us to analyze and bound the error between the TRP /BP approximations and the actual marginals. While our results arise naturally from the TRP perspective, most of them apply in an algorithm-independent manner to any local minimum of the Bethe free energy. Our re(cid:173) sults also have natural extensions to more structured approxima(cid:173) tions [e.g. , 1, 2].

paragraphs: Computing marginal probabilities in graphs containing cycles often requires approximation. This paper introduces a tree-based reparameterization view of iterative inference algorithms. Belief propagation fits within the framework as a very local reparameterization method, while broader algorithms perform exact computations on spanning trees of the full graph.

The authors find that these tree reparameterization algorithms have better convergence properties than belief propagation in practice. The framework also supplies theoretical insights: a new characterization of fixed points and an invariance shared by tree reparameterization and belief propagation. These properties allow analysis and bounds on the discrepancy between approximate and actual marginals.

Much of the analysis extends beyond the particular algorithm used to obtain an approximation. Most results apply to any local minimum of the Bethe free energy, and the authors describe natural extensions to more structured approximations. The contribution is therefore both computational and explanatory: tree-based updates offer practical convergence advantages, while reparameterization provides tools for understanding the solutions and errors of a broader family of inference procedures.
summary.tldr: Tree-based reparameterization unifies approximate-inference algorithms, improves convergence empirically, and enables analysis of fixed points and marginal errors.

title: Tree-based reparameterization for approximate inference on loopy graphs

abstract: Clustering aims at extracting hidden structure in dataset. While the prob- lem of ﬁnding compact clusters has been widely studied in the litera- ture, extracting arbitrarily formed elongated structures is considered a much harder problem. In this paper we present a novel clustering algo- rithm which tackles the problem by a two step procedure: ﬁrst the data are transformed in such a way that elongated structures become compact ones. In a second step, these new objects are clustered by optimizing a compactness-based criterion. The advantages of the method over related approaches are threefold: (i) robustness properties of compactness-based criteria naturally transfer to the problem of extracting elongated struc- tures, leading to a model which is highly robust against outlier objects; (ii) the transformed distances induce a Mercer kernel which allows us to formulate a polynomial approximation scheme to the generally NP- hard clustering problem; (iii) the new method does not contain free kernel parameters in contrast to methods like spectral clustering or mean-shift clustering.

paragraphs: The paper tackles clusters that form long or irregular shapes. Such structures are difficult for methods whose objective favors compact groups. The proposed solution changes the representation first: it transforms the data so that elongated structures become compact, then groups the transformed objects using a compactness-based criterion.

This separation lets the method apply properties of compact clustering to a different geometric problem. The authors state that robustness to outliers transfers through the transformation, producing a method that is highly resistant to outlying objects. The transformation therefore serves both to reveal the desired structures and to make an established type of clustering objective useful for them.

The transformed distances also define a Mercer kernel, which supports a polynomial approximation scheme for the generally NP-hard clustering problem. This is an approximation result, not a claim that exact clustering becomes easy. A further stated advantage is the absence of free kernel parameters, removing that particular source of tuning present in methods such as spectral clustering and mean-shift clustering.
summary.tldr: A connectivity-based transformation makes elongated clusters compact, supporting robust clustering and a polynomial approximation scheme.

title: Clustering with the Connectivity Kernel

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of untangling hidden graphs from a set of noisy detections of undirected edges. We present a model of the generation of the observed graph that includes degree-based structure priors on the hidden graphs. Exact inference in the model is intractable; we present an e–cient approximate inference algo- rithm to compute edge appearance posteriors. We evaluate our model and algorithm on a biological graph inference problem. 1 Introduction and motivation The inference of hidden graphs from noisy edge appearance data is an important problem with obvious practical application. For example, biologists are currently building networks of all the physical protein-protein interactions (PPI) that occur in particular organisms. The importance of this enterprise is commensurate with its scale: a completed network would be as valuable as a completed genome sequence, and because each organism contains thousands of diﬁerent types of proteins, there are millions of possible types of interactions. However, scalable experimental meth- ods for detecting interactions are noisy, generating many false detections. Motivated by this application, we formulate the general problem of inferring hidden graphs as probabilistic inference in a graphical model, and we introduce an e–cient algorithm that approximates the posterior probability that an edge is present. In our model, a set of hidden, constituent graphs are combined to generate the ob- served graph. Each hidden graph is independently sampled from a prior on graph structure. The combination mechanism acts independently on each edge but can be either stochastic or deterministic. Figure 1 shows an example of our generative model. Typically one of the hidden graphs represents the graph of interest (the true graph), the others represent diﬁerent types of observation noise. Independent edge noise may also be added by the combination mechanism. We use probabilistic in- ference to compute a likely decomposition of the observed graph into its constituent parts. This process is deemed \untangling". We use the term \denoising" to refer to the special case where the edge noise is independent. In denoising there is a single hidden graph, the true graph, and all edge noise in the observed graph is due

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover hidden networks from noisy detections of undirected edges. Its motivating example is biological interaction data, where observed connections can include false detections. The task is to infer which edges belong to the underlying graph rather than simply accept the observed network as accurate.

The generative model combines several hidden graphs to produce the observed graph. Each hidden graph has a structural prior based on node degrees, or how many connections nodes have. One hidden graph can represent the network of interest while others represent different noise sources. The combination acts separately on each edge and may be deterministic or stochastic.

The authors call recovery of these constituent graphs untangling; denoising is the special case involving one true graph and independent edge noise. Exact inference is intractable, so they develop an efficient approximation to posterior edge probabilities. These probabilities express uncertainty about whether individual connections exist. The model and algorithm are evaluated on a biological graph inference problem.
summary.tldr: Degree-based graph priors and approximate inference estimate which observed edges belong to hidden networks rather than noise.

title: Denoising and Untangling Graphs Using Degree Priors

abstract: The correction of bias in magnetic resonance images is an important problem in medical image processing. Most previous approaches have used a maximum likelihood method to increase the likelihood of the pix- els in a single image by adaptively estimating a correction to the unknown image bias field. The pixel likelihoods are defined either in terms of a pre-existing tissue model, or non-parametrically in terms of the image's own pixel values. In both cases, the specific location of a pixel in the im- age is not used to calculate the likelihoods. We suggest a new approach in which we simultaneously eliminate the bias from a set of images of the same anatomy, but from different patients. We use the statistics from the same location across different images, rather than within an image, to eliminate bias fields from all of the images simultaneously. The method builds a "multi-resolution" non-parametric tissue model conditioned on image location while eliminating the bias fields associated with the orig- inal image set. We present experiments on both synthetic and real MR data sets, and present comparisons with other methods.

We present experiments on both synthetic and real MR data sets, and present comparisons with other methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses removal of bias fields from magnetic resonance images. It describes earlier approaches that estimate a correction using pixel likelihoods within a single image, based either on an existing tissue model or on that image's pixel values. In those approaches, the likelihood calculation does not use the pixel's specific location.

The proposed method instead corrects a collection of images of the same anatomy from different patients. It uses statistics gathered at the same location across images, making anatomical position part of the evidence for correction. The images are processed jointly, so estimating their bias fields and learning the shared tissue statistics are connected parts of the task.

During correction, the method builds a nonparametric tissue model conditioned on image location at multiple resolutions. This gives the model a way to express location-dependent tissue statistics while estimating the bias associated with each original image. Experiments use both synthetic and real MR datasets and include comparisons with other methods. The contribution centers on this joint, location-aware formulation.
summary.tldr: The method jointly removes MRI bias fields using location-specific statistics across images from different patients.

title: Joint MRI Bias Removal Using Entropy Minimization Across Images

abstract: Confidence-weighted (CW) learning [6], an online learning method for linear classifiers, maintains a Gaussian distributions over weight vectors, with a covariance matrix that represents uncertainty about weights and correlations. Confidence constraints ensure that a weight vector drawn from the hypothesis distribution correctly classifies examples with a specified probability. Within this framework, we derive a new convex form of the constraint and analyze it in the mistake bound model. Empirical evaluation with both synthetic and text data shows our version of CW learning achieves lower cumulative and out-of-sample errors than commonly used first-order and second-order online methods.

The covariance describes both uncertainty in individual weights and relationships between them, giving the learning procedure richer information than a single estimate.

The framework imposes confidence constraints: a weight vector drawn from that distribution should classify an example correctly with a specified probability. The paper derives a new convex version of this constraint. It also analyzes the resulting method using mistake bounds, connecting the formulation to theoretical control of errors during online learning.

Experiments on synthetic and text data show lower cumulative errors and lower errors on unseen data than commonly used first-order and second-order online methods. These findings support the new formulation in the evaluated settings. The paper's contribution combines a convex confidence requirement, theoretical analysis, and empirical evidence that tracking uncertainty can translate into effective online classification.
summary.tldr: A convex confidence constraint yields an online classifier with mistake-bound analysis and improved errors in synthetic and text experiments.

title: Exact Convex Confidence-Weighted Learning

abstract: The coding of information by neural populations depends critically on the statistical dependencies between neuronal responses. However, there is no simple model that combines the observations that (1) marginal distributions over single-neuron spike counts are often approximately Poisson; and (2) joint distributions over the responses of multiple neurons are often strongly dependent. Here, we show that both marginal and joint properties of neural responses can be captured using Poisson copula models. Copulas are joint distributions that allow random variables with arbitrary marginals to be combined while incorporating arbitrary dependencies between them. Different copulas capture different kinds of dependencies, allowing for a richer and more detailed description of dependencies than traditional summary statistics, such as correlation coefficients. We explore a variety of Poisson copula models for joint neural response distributions, and derive an efficient maximum likelihood procedure for estimating them. We apply these models to neuronal data collected in and macaque motor cortex, and quantify the improvement in coding accuracy afforded by incorporating the dependency structure between pairs of neurons.

paragraphs: Understanding a population of neurons requires describing both individual responses and how those responses depend on one another. Single-neuron spike counts are often approximately Poisson distributed, while the joint activity of several neurons can exhibit strong dependence. The paper proposes Poisson copula models to represent these two properties together.

A copula separates the specification of individual response distributions from the structure linking them. This allows the model to retain Poisson distributions for individual spike counts while varying the kind of dependence between neurons. Different copulas describe different patterns of joint activity, providing more detail than a single correlation coefficient.

The authors explore several such models and derive an efficient maximum-likelihood procedure for estimating them from observations. They apply the approach to neuronal recordings, including macaque motor cortex, and quantify the improvement in coding accuracy obtained by incorporating dependencies between pairs of neurons. The contribution is therefore both representational and practical: a richer description of joint responses comes with an estimation method and a measured connection to coding accuracy.
summary.tldr: Poisson copula models capture individual spike-count distributions and richer neural dependencies, whose inclusion improves coding accuracy in the analyzed recordings.

title: Characterizing neural dependencies with copula models

abstract: ``How is information decoded in the brain?'' is one of the most difficult and important questions in neuroscience. Whether neural correlation is important or not in decoding neural activities is of special interest. We have developed a general framework for investigating how far the decoding process in the brain can be simplified. First, we hierarchically construct simplified probabilistic models of neural responses that ignore more than $K$th-order correlations by using a maximum entropy principle. Then, we compute how much information is lost when information is decoded using the simplified models, i.e., ``mismatched decoders''. We introduce an information theoretically correct quantity for evaluating the information obtained by mismatched decoders. We applied our proposed framework to spike data for vertebrate retina. We used 100-ms natural movies as stimuli and computed the information contained in neural activities about these movies. We found that the information loss is negligibly small in population activities of ganglion cells even if all orders of correlation are ignored in decoding. We also found that if we assume stationarity for long durations in the information analysis of dynamically changing stimuli like natural movies, pseudo correlations seem to carry a large portion of the information.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much detail a decoder needs about relationships among neurons to recover information from their activity. It constructs a hierarchy of simplified response models using maximum entropy. Each model retains correlations only up to a chosen order, making it possible to systematically compare more detailed descriptions with simpler ones.

The central step is to measure the information recovered when decoding uses one of these simplified models. Such a decoder is mismatched because its assumed response distribution differs from the fuller description. The authors introduce an information-theoretically appropriate measure of its performance, connecting simplification directly to information loss.

Applied to vertebrate retinal responses to 100-millisecond natural movies, the framework finds negligible information loss in the studied ganglion-cell populations even when decoding ignores all correlations. This finding concerns those recordings and stimuli. The analysis also identifies a consequential assumption: treating responses to changing stimuli as stationary over long periods can create apparent correlations that seem to carry substantial information.
summary.tldr: A framework measures information lost by simplifying neural decoders and finds negligible loss from ignoring correlations in the studied retinal populations.

title: A general framework for investigating how far the decoding process in the brain can be simplified

abstract: How does one extract unknown but stereotypical events that are linearly superimposed within a signal with variable latencies and variable amplitudes? One could think of using template matching or matching pursuit to find the arbitrarily shifted linear components. However, traditional matching approaches require that the templates be known a priori. To overcome this restriction we use instead semi Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (semi-NMF) that we extend to allow for time shifts when matching the templates to the signal. The algorithm estimates templates directly from the data along with their non-negative amplitudes. The resulting method can be thought of as an adaptive template matching procedure. We demonstrate the procedure on the task of extracting spikes from single channel extracellular recordings. On these data the algorithm essentially performs spike detection and unsupervised spike clustering. Results on simulated data and extracellular recordings indicate that the method performs well for signal-to-noise ratios of 6dB or higher and that spike templates are recovered accurately provided they are sufficiently different.

paragraphs: The paper addresses signals made from overlapping, recurring events whose shapes are initially unknown. Each event can occur at a different time and with a different strength. Traditional template matching can locate shifted copies of known patterns, but that requirement creates a problem when the patterns themselves must be discovered.

The authors extend semi non-negative matrix factorization to accommodate time shifts. Their algorithm jointly estimates event templates and their non-negative amplitudes directly from the signal. This makes template matching adaptive: the method learns what to look for while also finding where those patterns occur and how strongly they contribute.

The demonstration uses single-channel extracellular neural recordings, where the method effectively combines spike detection with unsupervised spike clustering. Tests on simulated signals and recorded data indicate good performance at signal-to-noise ratios of 6 dB or above. Accurate template recovery also depends on the spike shapes being sufficiently different. These findings support learning and locating recurring events together under the stated signal conditions.
summary.tldr: A time-shift-aware factorization learns unknown spike templates while detecting and grouping their occurrences in neural recordings.

title: Adaptive Template Matching with Shift-Invariant Semi-NMF

abstract: Fast retrieval methods are increasingly critical for many large-scale analysis tasks, and there have been several recent methods that attempt to learn hash functions for fast and accurate nearest neighbor searches. In this paper, we develop an algorithm for learning hash functions based on explicitly minimizing the reconstruction error between the original distances and the Hamming distances of the corresponding binary embeddings. We develop a scalable coordinate-descent algorithm for our proposed hashing objective that is able to efficiently learn hash functions in a variety of settings. Unlike existing methods such as semantic hashing and spectral hashing, our method is easily kernelized and does not require restrictive assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data. We present results over several domains to demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

In this paper, we develop an algorithm for learning hash functions based on explicitly minimizing the reconstruction error between the original distances and the Hamming distances of the corresponding binary embeddings. We develop a scalable coordinate-descent algorithm for our proposed hashing objective that is able to efficiently learn hash functions in a variety of settings. Unlike existing methods such as semantic hashing and spectral hashing, our method is easily kernelized and does not require restrictive assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data. We present results over several domains to demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: Fast nearest-neighbor retrieval depends on comparing many items efficiently while retaining meaningful similarity information. This paper learns hash functions that map data into binary codes. Its central objective is to make distances between those codes reproduce distances in the original representation, so that the compressed representation remains useful for finding nearby items.

The training criterion explicitly minimizes reconstruction error between original distances and Hamming distances, which count differing bits between binary codes. The authors develop a scalable coordinate-descent algorithm for optimizing this objective. Learning therefore directly addresses the discrepancy between the similarity information available before encoding and the distances used after encoding.

The method can be kernelized and does not require restrictive assumptions about the underlying data distribution, features the authors contrast with semantic and spectral hashing. Results across several domains show performance exceeding existing state-of-the-art techniques in the reported evaluations. The findings support distance reconstruction as an effective objective for learning binary representations for retrieval.
summary.tldr: Learning binary hash codes to reconstruct original distances yields scalable nearest-neighbor representations with strong results across several domains.

title: Learning to Hash with Binary Reconstructive Embeddings

abstract: We present a novel probabilistic model for distributions over sets of structures -- for example, sets of sequences, trees, or graphs. The critical characteristic of our model is a preference for diversity: sets containing dissimilar structures are more likely. Our model is a marriage of structured probabilistic models, like Markov random fields and context free grammars, with determinantal point processes, which arise in quantum physics as models of particles with repulsive interactions. We extend the determinantal point process model to handle an exponentially-sized set of particles (structures) via a natural factorization of the model into parts. We show how this factorization leads to tractable algorithms for exact inference, including computing marginals, computing conditional probabilities, and sampling. Our algorithms exploit a novel polynomially-sized dual representation of determinantal point processes, and use message passing over a special semiring to compute relevant quantities. We illustrate the advantages of the model on tracking and articulated pose estimation problems.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a probabilistic model for selecting sets of structured objects, such as sequences, trees, or graphs. Its defining preference is diversity: a set containing dissimilar structures receives greater probability. The goal is therefore to model collections whose members complement one another, taking relationships among selected structures into account.

The approach combines structured probabilistic models with determinantal point processes, which represent repulsive interactions. A major challenge is that the number of possible structures can be exponential. The authors address this by factoring each structure into parts, allowing the model to work with the structure of the candidate space instead of explicitly enumerating every candidate.

This factorization supports tractable exact computation of marginals and conditional probabilities, as well as sampling. The algorithms use a polynomial-size dual representation of determinantal point processes and message passing with a specially defined semiring. Applications to tracking and articulated pose estimation illustrate the advantages. The contribution makes diversity-aware distributions computationally accessible for structured candidate spaces that would otherwise be too large to list.
summary.tldr: Structured determinantal point processes support diversity-aware selection from exponentially large structured spaces through factorization and tractable exact inference.

title: Structured Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: In multi-instance learning, there are two kinds of prediction failure, i.e., false negative and false positive. Current research mainly focus on avoding the former. We attempt to utilize the geometric distribution of instances inside positive bags to avoid both the former and the latter. Based on kernel principal component analysis, we define a projection constraint for each positive bag to classify its constituent instances far away from the separating hyperplane while place positive instances and negative instances at opposite sides. We apply the Constrained Concave-Convex Procedure to solve the resulted problem. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach offers improved generalization performance.

We apply the Constrained Concave-Convex Procedure to solve the resulted problem. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach offers improved generalization performance.

paragraphs: Multi-instance learning makes predictions using bags containing multiple instances. This paper addresses two ways those predictions can fail: missing positives and incorrectly declaring positives. The authors argue that existing research has concentrated mainly on the first problem. They investigate whether the geometric arrangement of instances within positive bags can help address both kinds of error.

Their method uses kernel principal component analysis to define a projection constraint for each positive bag. The constraint aims to place its constituent instances far from the separating hyperplane, while keeping positive and negative instances on opposite sides. The arrangement of points inside a bag therefore directly influences how the classification boundary is learned.

The resulting optimization problem is solved using the Constrained Concave-Convex Procedure. Empirical results show improved generalization performance for the proposed approach. The methodological contribution is to make the internal geometry of positive bags part of training, with the explicit goal of avoiding false positives as well as false negatives.
summary.tldr: Geometric constraints within positive bags help a multi-instance learner address both false positives and false negatives.

title: Avoiding False Positive in Multi-Instance Learning

abstract: Topic models are learned via a statistical model of variation within document collections, but designed to extract meaningful semantic structure. Desirable traits include the ability to incorporate annotations or metadata associated with documents; the discovery of correlated patterns of topic usage; and the avoidance of parametric assumptions, such as manual specification of the number of topics. We propose a doubly correlated nonparametric topic (DCNT) model, the first model to simultaneously capture all three of these properties. The DCNT models metadata via a flexible, Gaussian regression on arbitrary input features; correlations via a scalable square-root covariance representation; and nonparametric selection from an unbounded series of potential topics via a stick-breaking construction. We validate the semantic structure and predictive performance of the DCNT using a corpus of NIPS documents annotated by various metadata.

paragraphs: Topic models aim to extract meaningful semantic structure from document collections. This paper combines three desirable capabilities: incorporating document metadata, representing correlations in topic usage, and allowing the number of topics to emerge without being fixed manually. The authors present their doubly correlated nonparametric topic model as the first to combine all three.

Each capability has a corresponding modeling component. Flexible Gaussian regression connects arbitrary input features to the model. A square-root covariance representation captures correlations in a scalable form. A stick-breaking construction permits selection from an unbounded sequence of potential topics, avoiding a manually specified finite topic count.

The authors evaluate semantic structure and predictive performance using a collection of NIPS documents annotated with metadata. The stated validation addresses both the model's intended interpretive role and its predictions. Its main contribution is the combined representation: document information, correlated topic use, and an adaptable topic inventory are handled within the same statistical model.
summary.tldr: The DCNT model combines document metadata, correlated topic usage, and an unbounded potential topic inventory in one framework.

title: The Doubly Correlated Nonparametric Topic Model

abstract: Recovering hidden structure from complex and noisy non-linear data is one of the most fundamental problems in machine learning and statistical inference. While such data is often high-dimensional, it is of interest to approximate it with a low-dimensional or even one-dimensional space, since many important aspects of data are often intrinsically low-dimensional. Furthermore, there are many scenarios where the underlying structure is graph-like, e.g, river/road networks or various trajectories. In this paper, we develop a framework to extract, as well as to simplify, a one-dimensional "skeleton" from unorganized data using the Reeb graph. Our algorithm is very simple, does not require complex optimizations and can be easily applied to unorganized high-dimensional data such as point clouds or proximity graphs. It can also represent arbitrary graph structures in the data. We also give theoretical results to justify our method. We provide a number of experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of our algorithm, including comparisons to existing methods, such as principal curves. We believe that the simplicity and practicality of our algorithm will help to promote skeleton graphs as a data analysis tool for a broad range of applications.

paragraphs: Complex, noisy data can contain a much simpler underlying shape. In some cases that shape resembles a network, such as a road system or a collection of trajectories. This paper develops a framework for extracting a one-dimensional graph skeleton from unorganized data, making such structure available as a compact object for analysis.

The framework uses Reeb graphs to both extract and simplify the skeleton. The proposed algorithm can work with high-dimensional point clouds or proximity graphs, does not require complex optimization, and can represent arbitrary graph structures. That flexibility matters when the desired summary has a graph structure that a single curve cannot adequately express.

The authors give theoretical results supporting the method and demonstrate it through experiments, including comparisons with principal curves. These experiments support its effectiveness and generality in the tested settings. The broader contribution is a simple, practical route from unorganized observations to a graph summary, bringing skeleton extraction and simplification together within one framework.
summary.tldr: A Reeb-graph framework extracts and simplifies graph-shaped skeletons from unorganized high-dimensional data without complex optimization.

title: Data Skeletonization via Reeb Graphs

abstract: Most state-of-the-art techniques for multi-class image segmentation and labeling use conditional random ﬁelds deﬁned over pixels or image regions. While region- level models often feature dense pairwise connectivity, pixel-level models are con- siderably larger and have only permitted sparse graph structures. In this paper, we consider fully connected CRF models deﬁned on the complete set of pixels in an image. The resulting graphs have billions of edges, making traditional inference algorithms impractical. Our main contribution is a highly efﬁcient approximate inference algorithm for fully connected CRF models in which the pairwise edge potentials are deﬁned by a linear combination of Gaussian kernels. Our experi- ments demonstrate that dense connectivity at the pixel level substantially improves segmentation and labeling accuracy.

paragraphs: Image segmentation assigns categories to pixels, and conditional random fields can express relationships among those assignments. Pixel-level models are large enough that earlier approaches generally used sparse connections. This paper considers the much denser alternative of connecting every pixel to every other pixel, creating graphs with billions of edges.

The central contribution is an efficient approximate inference algorithm for a particular family of these fully connected models. Their pairwise interaction terms must be expressible as linear combinations of Gaussian kernels. That structure makes the dense model computationally usable despite the impracticality of applying traditional inference algorithms to such a large collection of edges.

The experiments show substantial improvements in segmentation and labeling accuracy from dense pixel-level connectivity. The result matters because it makes richer relationships between pixel labels accessible without first reducing the image to a smaller set of regions. The scope remains specific: the algorithm performs approximate inference and relies on the stated Gaussian-kernel form of the pairwise interactions.
summary.tldr: Efficient approximate inference makes fully connected pixel CRFs with Gaussian-kernel interactions practical and improves segmentation in experiments.

title: Efficient Inference in Fully Connected CRFs with Gaussian Edge Potentials

abstract: Structured sparse estimation has become an important technique in many areas of data analysis. Unfortunately, these estimators normally create computational difficulties that entail sophisticated algorithms. Our first contribution is to uncover a rich class of structured sparse regularizers whose polar operator can be evaluated efficiently. With such an operator, a simple conditional gradient method can then be developed that, when combined with smoothing and local optimization, significantly reduces training time vs. the state of the art. We also demonstrate a new reduction of polar to proximal maps that enables more efficient latent fused lasso.

paragraphs: Structured sparse estimation encourages a model to use relatively few components while respecting additional organization. Such regularization is useful in data analysis, but the resulting optimization problems often demand sophisticated algorithms. This paper looks for a computational route that makes a broad class of these estimators easier to train.

The authors identify a rich class of structured sparse regularizers whose polar operators can be computed efficiently. That operator supplies a key operation for a simple conditional gradient method. Combined with smoothing and local optimization, the resulting approach significantly reduces training time compared with the state of the art, according to the reported findings.

The paper also establishes a reduction from polar computations to proximal maps and uses it to enable more efficient latent fused lasso. This provides another connection between the regularizer's mathematical structure and an available optimization operation. The broader contribution is to identify efficiently computable building blocks that can support simpler training methods for otherwise computationally demanding structured estimators.
summary.tldr: Efficient polar operators enable faster conditional gradient methods for structured sparsity, with a further reduction benefiting latent fused lasso.

title: Polar Operators for Structured Sparse Estimation

abstract: We describe a seriation algorithm for ranking a set of n items given pairwise comparisons between these items. Intuitively, the algorithm assigns similar rankings to items that compare similarly with all others. It does so by constructing a similarity matrix from pairwise comparisons, using seriation methods to reorder this matrix and construct a ranking. We first show that this spectral seriation algorithm recovers the true ranking when all pairwise comparisons are observed and consistent with a total order. We then show that ranking reconstruction is still exact even when some pairwise comparisons are corrupted or missing, and that seriation based spectral ranking is more robust to noise than other scoring methods. An additional benefit of the seriation formulation is that it allows us to solve semi-supervised ranking problems. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that seriation based spectral ranking achieves competitive and in some cases superior performance compared to classical ranking methods.

Intuitively, the algorithm assigns similar rankings to items that compare similarly with all others. It does so by constructing a similarity matrix from pairwise comparisons, using seriation methods to reorder this matrix and construct a ranking. We first show that this spectral seriation algorithm recovers the true ranking when all pairwise comparisons are observed and consistent with a total order. We then show that ranking reconstruction is still exact even when some pairwise comparisons are corrupted or missing, and that seriation based spectral ranking is more robust to noise than other scoring methods. An additional benefit of the seriation formulation is that it allows us to solve semi-supervised ranking problems. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that seriation based spectral ranking achieves competitive and in some cases superior performance compared to classical ranking methods.

paragraphs: SerialRank constructs a ranking from pairwise comparisons by asking which items behave similarly against the rest. Items with similar comparison patterns are assigned similar positions. The algorithm builds a similarity matrix from the comparisons, then uses spectral seriation to reorder that matrix and obtain a ranking.

The authors prove exact recovery when every pairwise comparison is observed and all comparisons agree with a total order. They also show that exact reconstruction remains possible with some missing or corrupted comparisons. This extends the recovery result beyond fully clean data without asserting recovery under arbitrary amounts or patterns of corruption.

The paper reports greater robustness to noise than other scoring methods and explains that the seriation formulation also accommodates semi-supervised ranking problems. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show competitive performance, with superiority in some cases, relative to classical ranking methods. The contribution is a ranking strategy that uses the structure of entire comparison patterns, supported by exact-recovery results and empirical evidence under imperfect observations.
summary.tldr: SerialRank orders items through similarities in their pairwise comparison patterns, with exact-recovery results and competitive empirical robustness.

title: SerialRank: Spectral Ranking using Seriation

abstract: Markov Logic Networks (MLNs) are weighted first-order logic templates for generating large (ground) Markov networks. Lifted inference algorithms for them bring the power of logical inference to probabilistic inference. These algorithms operate as much as possible at the compact first-order level, grounding or propositionalizing the MLN only as necessary. As a result, lifted inference algorithms can be much more scalable than propositional algorithms that operate directly on the much larger ground network. Unfortunately, existing lifted inference algorithms suffer from two interrelated problems, which severely affects their scalability in practice. First, for most real-world MLNs having complex structure, they are unable to exploit symmetries and end up grounding most atoms (the grounding problem). Second, they suffer from the evidence problem, which arises because evidence breaks symmetries, severely diminishing the power of lifted inference. In this paper, we address both problems by presenting a scalable, lifted importance sampling-based approach that never grounds the full MLN. Specifically, we show how to scale up the two main steps in importance sampling: sampling from the proposal distribution and weight computation. Scalable sampling is achieved by using an informed, easy-to-sample proposal distribution derived from a compressed MLN-representation. Fast weight computation is achieved by only visiting a small subset of the sampled groundings of each formula instead of all of its possible groundings. We show that our new algorithm yields an asymptotically unbiased estimate. Our experiments on several MLNs clearly demonstrate the promise of our approach.
originalAbstract: Markov Logic Networks (MLNs) are weighted first-order logic templates for generating large (ground) Markov networks. Lifted inference algorithms for them bring the power of logical inference to probabilistic inference. These algorithms operate as much as possible at the compact first-order level, grounding or propositionalizing the MLN only as necessary. As a result, lifted inference algorithms can be much more scalable than propositional algorithms that operate directly on the much larger ground network. Unfortunately, existing lifted inference algorithms suffer from two interrelated problems, which severely affects their scalability in practice. First, for most real-world MLNs having complex structure, they are unable to exploit symmetries and end up grounding most atoms (the grounding problem). Second, they suffer from the evidence problem, which arises because evidence breaks symmetries, severely diminishing the power of lifted inference. In this paper, we address both problems by presenting a scalable, lifted importance sampling-based approach that never grounds the full MLN. Specifically, we show how to scale up the two main steps in importance sampling: sampling from the proposal distribution and weight computation. Scalable sampling is achieved by using an informed, easy-to-sample proposal distribution derived from a compressed MLN-representation. Fast weight computation is achieved by only visiting a small subset of the sampled groundings of each formula instead of all of its possible groundings. We show that our new algorithm yields an asymptotically unbiased estimate. Our experiments on several MLNs clearly demonstrate the promise of our approach.

Lifted inference tries to work with those templates without expanding every instance. Complex structure and observed evidence can break the symmetries that make this possible, forcing existing methods to ground much of the network and reducing their scalability.

This paper proposes lifted importance sampling that never grounds the entire network. It addresses both expensive parts of importance sampling: generating samples and computing their weights. An informed proposal distribution comes from a compressed network representation and is easy to sample. Weight computation visits only a small subset of sampled groundings for each formula instead of all possible groundings.

The authors show that the resulting estimate is asymptotically unbiased. This qualification concerns its limiting behavior, rather than guaranteeing an unbiased answer from any finite run. Experiments on several Markov logic networks demonstrate promise for the approach. The contribution is a coordinated way to reduce the cost of both sampling and weighting while maintaining a formal asymptotic property.
summary.tldr: Compressed proposals and selective weight computation enable asymptotically unbiased importance sampling without fully grounding a Markov logic network.

title: Scaling-up Importance Sampling for Markov Logic Networks

abstract: We examine the number of controlled experiments required to discover a causal graph. Hauser and Buhlmann showed that the number of experiments required is logarithmic in the cardinality of maximum undirected clique in the essential graph. Their lower bounds, however, assume that the experiment designer cannot use randomization in selecting the experiments. We show that significant improvements are possible with the aid of randomization – in an adversarial (worst-case) setting, the designer can then recover the causal graph using at most O(log log n) experiments in expectation. This bound cannot be improved; we show it is tight for some causal graphs. We then show that in a non-adversarial (average-case) setting, even larger improvements are possible: if the causal graph is chosen uniformly at random under a Erdös-Rényi model then the expected number of experiments to discover the causal graph is constant. Finally, we present computer simulations to complement our theoretic results. Our work exploits a structural characterization of essential graphs by Andersson et al. Their characterization is based upon a set of orientation forcing operations. Our results show a distinction between which forcing operations are most important in worst-case and average-case settings.

The distinction matters because the earlier lower bounds discussed in the paper assume that experiment selection cannot use randomization.

summary.tldr: Randomized experiment selection reduces expected causal-discovery experiment counts, with tight worst-case bounds and constant expectations under an Erdős–Rényi model.

title: Randomized Experimental Design for Causal Graph Discovery

abstract: Trace regression models have received considerable attention in the context of matrix completion, quantum state tomography, and compressed sensing. Estimation of the underlying matrix from regularization-based approaches promoting low-rankedness, notably nuclear norm regularization, have enjoyed great popularity. In this paper, we argue that such regularization may no longer be necessary if the underlying matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite (spd) and the design satisfies certain conditions. In this situation, simple least squares estimation subject to an spd constraint may perform as well as regularization-based approaches with a proper choice of regularization parameter, which entails knowledge of the noise level and/or tuning. By contrast, constrained least squaresestimation comes without any tuning parameter and may hence be preferred due to its simplicity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate an unknown matrix in trace regression, a setting relevant to matrix completion, quantum state tomography, and compressed sensing. Popular approaches use regularization to encourage a low-rank estimate. Nuclear norm regularization is one such approach, adding a preference for low rank to the estimation procedure.

The authors argue that this extra regularization may be unnecessary when the unknown matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite and the measurement design satisfies certain conditions. They consider least squares estimation constrained to matrices with that structure. The central idea is that this structural constraint, together with suitable design conditions, may suffice to obtain performance comparable to regularized estimation.

The comparison is with regularization methods whose tuning parameter has been properly chosen. Choosing that parameter entails knowledge of the noise level and/or tuning, whereas the constrained least squares approach has no tuning parameter. Its appeal is therefore practical simplicity with potentially comparable performance under the stated conditions. The claim remains conditional on the matrix structure and design; it does not establish that regularization is unnecessary throughout trace regression.
summary.tldr: Under suitable design conditions, least squares constrained to symmetric positive semidefinite matrices may match properly tuned regularized methods without a tuning parameter.

title: Regularization-Free Estimation in Trace Regression with Symmetric Positive Semidefinite Matrices

abstract: Due to the computational difficulty of performing MMSE (minimum mean squared error) inference, maximum a posteriori (MAP) is often used as a surrogate. However, the accuracy of MAP is suboptimal for high dimensional inference, where the number of model parameters is of the same order as the number of samples. In this work we demonstrate how MMSE performance is asymptotically achievable via optimization with an appropriately selected convex penalty and regularization function which are a smoothed version of the widely applied MAP algorithm. Our findings provide a new derivation and interpretation for recent optimal M-estimators discovered by El Karoui, et. al. PNAS 2013 as well as extending to non-additive noise models. We demonstrate the performance of these optimal M-estimators with numerical simulations. Overall, at the heart of our work is the revelation of a remarkable equivalence between two seemingly very different computational problems: namely that of high dimensional Bayesian integration, and high dimensional convex optimization. In essence we show that the former computationally difficult integral may be computed by solving the latter, simpler optimization problem.

These choices form a smoothed version of the commonly used maximum a posteriori approach. Numerical simulations demonstrate the estimators' performance. The central significance is computational: under the paper's framework, a carefully designed convex optimization problem can reach the asymptotic accuracy associated with a more demanding Bayesian calculation.
summary.tldr: Appropriately designed convex estimators can asymptotically attain Bayes-optimal mean squared error in the high-dimensional setting studied.

title: An equivalence between high dimensional Bayes optimal inference and M-estimation

abstract: Decision tree (and its extensions such as Gradient Boosting Decision Trees and Random Forest) is a widely used machine learning algorithm, due to its practical effectiveness and model interpretability. With the emergence of big data, there is an increasing need to parallelize the training process of decision tree. However, most existing attempts along this line suffer from high communication costs. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, called \emph{Parallel Voting Decision Tree (PV-Tree)}, to tackle this challenge. After partitioning the training data onto a number of (e.g., $M$) machines, this algorithm performs both local voting and global voting in each iteration. For local voting, the top-$k$ attributes are selected from each machine according to its local data. Then, the indices of these top attributes are aggregated by a server, and the globally top-$2k$ attributes are determined by a majority voting among these local candidates. Finally, the full-grained histograms of the globally top-$2k$ attributes are collected from local machines in order to identify the best (most informative) attribute and its split point. PV-Tree can achieve a very low communication cost (independent of the total number of attributes) and thus can scale out very well. Furthermore, theoretical analysis shows that this algorithm can learn a near optimal decision tree, since it can find the best attribute with a large probability. Our experiments on real-world datasets show that PV-Tree significantly outperforms the existing parallel decision tree algorithms in the tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Training decision trees across several machines can become expensive because the machines must exchange information about candidate splits. PV-Tree addresses this communication problem by using votes to narrow the set of attributes worth examining in detail. The training data are partitioned across machines, each of which evaluates attributes using its own portion of the data.

In each iteration, every machine selects its top k attributes and sends their indices to a server. The server uses majority voting to choose the globally top 2k candidates. Only then do the machines transmit detailed histograms for those candidates, allowing the algorithm to select an informative attribute and its split point.

This staged exchange makes communication cost independent of the total number of attributes. The theoretical analysis shows that the best attribute can be found with high probability, supporting a near-optimal decision tree. Experiments on real datasets report a substantially better accuracy–efficiency tradeoff than existing parallel tree algorithms.
summary.tldr: PV-Tree reduces distributed decision-tree communication by voting on candidate attributes before exchanging detailed split information.

title: A Communication-Efficient Parallel Algorithm for Decision Tree

abstract: We investigate active learning with access to two distinct oracles: LABEL (which is standard) and SEARCH (which is not). The SEARCH oracle models the situation where a human searches a database to seed or counterexample an existing solution. SEARCH is stronger than LABEL while being natural to implement in many situations. We show that an algorithm using both oracles can provide exponentially large problem-dependent improvements over LABEL alone.
originalAbstract: We investigate active learning with access to two distinct oracles: LABEL (which is standard) and SEARCH (which is not). The SEARCH oracle models the situation where a human searches a database to seed or counterexample an existing solution. SEARCH is stronger than LABEL while being natural to implement in many situations. We show that an algorithm using both oracles can provide exponentially large problem-dependent improvements over LABEL alone.

paragraphs: Active learning usually gives a learner access to a labeling oracle: it can ask for the label of an example. This paper considers a second kind of assistance, called SEARCH. SEARCH represents a human looking through a database to find an example that can seed a solution or serve as a counterexample to an existing one.

The distinction concerns what the human is asked to contribute. Labeling supplies information about an example already selected for a query. Searching can identify a relevant example in response to the current solution. The authors treat SEARCH as a stronger oracle and argue that this form of assistance is natural to implement in many situations.

The main result shows that an algorithm using both LABEL and SEARCH can obtain exponentially large improvements over using LABEL alone. These gains depend on the problem; they are not claimed for every active learning setting. The finding makes the design of human assistance itself consequential: changing the available query types can substantially change what a learner can achieve.
summary.tldr: Combining labeling with human search for useful examples can yield exponentially large, problem-dependent improvements in active learning.

title: Search Improves Label for Active Learning

abstract: The problem of estimating a random vector x from noisy linear measurements y=Ax+w with unknown parameters on the distributions of x and w, which must also be learned, arises in a wide range of statistical learning and linear inverse problems. We show that a computationally simple iterative message-passing algorithm can provably obtain asymptotically consistent estimates in a certain high-dimensional large-system limit (LSL) under very general parameterizations. Previous message passing techniques have required i.i.d. sub-Gaussian A matrices and often fail when the matrix is ill-conditioned. The proposed algorithm, called adaptive vector approximate message passing (Adaptive VAMP) with auto-tuning, applies to all right-rotationally random A. Importantly, this class includes matrices with arbitrarily bad conditioning. We show that the parameter estimates and mean squared error (MSE) of x in each iteration converge to deterministic limits that can be precisely predicted by a simple set of state evolution (SE) equations. In addition, a simple testable condition is provided in which the MSE matches the Bayes-optimal value predicted by the replica method. The paper thus provides a computationally simple method with provable guarantees of optimality and consistency over a large class of linear inverse problems.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems seek an unknown vector x from measurements y = Ax + w. The task becomes harder when parameters describing both x and the noise w are also unknown. This paper introduces Adaptive VAMP with auto-tuning, a simple iterative message-passing method that learns those parameters while estimating the vector.

The theory applies to right-rotationally random measurement matrices, a class that includes arbitrarily ill-conditioned matrices. This extends beyond the independent sub-Gaussian matrices required by earlier message-passing approaches. In a specified high-dimensional large-system limit, the algorithm gives asymptotically consistent parameter estimates under very general parameterizations.

The authors also show that each iteration's parameter estimates and mean squared error converge to deterministic values described by state-evolution equations. A testable additional condition ensures that the error matches the Bayes-optimal value predicted by the replica method. These qualifications matter: the guarantees concern the stated matrix class and asymptotic regime, with optimal error requiring the additional condition. Within that scope, the method offers both estimation guarantees and predictable dynamics.
summary.tldr: Adaptive VAMP learns unknown distribution parameters and estimates signals with asymptotic guarantees for right-rotationally random matrices, including arbitrarily ill-conditioned ones.

title: Rigorous Dynamics and Consistent Estimation in Arbitrarily Conditioned Linear Systems

abstract: We explore deep reinforcement learning methods for multi-agent domains. We begin by analyzing the difficulty of traditional algorithms in the multi-agent case: Q-learning is challenged by an inherent non-stationarity of the environment, while policy gradient suffers from a variance that increases as the number of agents grows. We then present an adaptation of actor-critic methods that considers action policies of other agents and is able to successfully learn policies that require complex multi-agent coordination. Additionally, we introduce a training regimen utilizing an ensemble of policies for each agent that leads to more robust multi-agent policies. We show the strength of our approach compared to existing methods in cooperative as well as competitive scenarios, where agent populations are able to discover various physical and informational coordination strategies.
