We then present an adaptation of actor-critic methods that considers action policies of other agents and is able to successfully learn policies that require complex multi-agent coordination. Additionally, we introduce a training regimen utilizing an ensemble of policies for each agent that leads to more robust multi-agent policies. We show the strength of our approach compared to existing methods in cooperative as well as competitive scenarios, where agent populations are able to discover various physical and informational coordination strategies.

paragraphs: Learning becomes difficult when several reinforcement-learning agents act and adapt together. The paper identifies two obstacles for familiar methods: Q-learning faces an environment whose behavior changes as other agents change, while policy-gradient estimates become more variable as the number of agents grows. These problems complicate learning coordinated behavior from interaction.

The authors adapt actor-critic methods to take other agents' action policies into account. This approach successfully learns policies requiring complex coordination among multiple agents. They also introduce a training regimen that uses an ensemble of policies for each agent, and report that this produces more robust multi-agent policies.

Evaluations cover cooperative and competitive scenarios and demonstrate the approach's strength relative to existing methods. The agent populations discover multiple strategies involving physical and informational coordination. These findings support explicitly accounting for other agents during learning and using policy ensembles to improve robustness. The contribution addresses both the instability of learning alongside other learners and the practical challenge of developing coordinated behavior across different kinds of multi-agent interaction.
summary.tldr: An actor-critic approach that accounts for other agents' policies learns coordination in cooperative and competitive settings.

title: Multi-Agent Actor-Critic for Mixed Cooperative-Competitive Environments

abstract: There is rapidly growing interest in using Bayesian optimization to tune model and inference hyperparameters for machine learning algorithms that take a long time to run. For example, Spearmint is a popular software package for selecting the optimal number of layers and learning rate in neural networks. But given that there is uncertainty about which hyperparameters give the best predictive performance, and given that fitting a model for each choice of hyperparameters is costly, it is arguably wasteful to "throw away" all but the best result, as per Bayesian optimization. A related issue is the danger of overfitting the validation data when optimizing many hyperparameters. In this paper, we consider an alternative approach that uses more samples from the hyperparameter selection procedure to average over the uncertainty in model hyperparameters. The resulting approach, empirical Bayes for hyperparameter averaging (EB-Hyp) predicts held-out data better than Bayesian optimization in two experiments on latent Dirichlet allocation and deep latent Gaussian models. EB-Hyp suggests a simpler approach to evaluating and deploying machine learning algorithms that does not require a separate validation data set and hyperparameter selection procedure.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning can require many expensive model fits, yet a selection procedure may ultimately retain only its best configuration. This paper asks whether the other fitted results can contribute to prediction. Its motivation is that uncertainty remains about which settings are best, and repeatedly optimizing against validation data also creates a risk of overfitting that data.

The proposed method, empirical Bayes for hyperparameter averaging, uses more samples from the hyperparameter selection process to average over uncertainty. Instead of committing all predictive weight to one selected setting, it incorporates information from multiple settings. This makes the results of the search useful beyond identifying a single winner.

In two experiments involving latent Dirichlet allocation and deep latent Gaussian models, the method predicts held-out data better than Bayesian optimization. The authors also suggest that this approach could simplify evaluation and deployment by removing the need for a separate validation dataset and hyperparameter selection procedure. That broader simplification is presented as a possibility motivated by the method and its experimental results.
summary.tldr: Empirical Bayes hyperparameter averaging reuses multiple tuning results and improves held-out prediction in two reported experiments.

title: An Empirical Bayes Approach to Optimizing Machine Learning Algorithms

abstract: It is well known that weight initialization in deep networks can have a dramatic impact on learning speed. For example, ensuring the mean squared singular value of a network's input-output Jacobian is O(1) is essential for avoiding exponentially vanishing or exploding gradients. Moreover, in deep linear networks, ensuring that all singular values of the Jacobian are concentrated near 1 can yield a dramatic additional speed-up in learning; this is a property known as dynamical isometry. However, it is unclear how to achieve dynamical isometry in nonlinear deep networks. We address this question by employing powerful tools from free probability theory to analytically compute the {\it entire} singular value distribution of a deep network's input-output Jacobian. We explore the dependence of the singular value distribution on the depth of the network, the weight initialization, and the choice of nonlinearity. Intriguingly, we find that ReLU networks are incapable of dynamical isometry. On the other hand, sigmoidal networks can achieve isometry, but only with orthogonal weight initialization. Moreover, we demonstrate empirically that deep nonlinear networks achieving dynamical isometry learn orders of magnitude faster than networks that do not. Indeed, we show that properly-initialized deep sigmoidal networks consistently outperform deep ReLU networks. Overall, our analysis reveals that controlling the entire distribution of Jacobian singular values is an important design consideration in deep learning.

Keeping the average squared singular value of the input–output Jacobian at order one helps avoid exponentially shrinking or growing gradients. This paper studies a stronger property, dynamical isometry, in which the singular values concentrate near one, preserving signal magnitudes across directions.

Using free probability theory, the authors calculate the full singular-value distribution and examine its dependence on depth, initialization, and activation function. Their analysis finds that ReLU networks cannot achieve dynamical isometry in the setting studied. Sigmoidal networks can achieve it, but orthogonal weight initialization is required.

Properly initialized deep sigmoidal networks also consistently outperform deep ReLU networks in the reported comparisons. The paper's design lesson is to consider the full distribution of signal amplification, beyond its average, when initializing deep networks. Its theoretical and empirical results connect that distribution to learning speed.
summary.tldr: The paper links dynamical isometry to faster learning and shows how orthogonal initialization enables it in deep sigmoidal networks.

title: Resurrecting the sigmoid in deep learning through dynamical isometry: theory and practice

abstract: Despite being virtually ubiquitous, sequence-to-sequence models are challenged by their lack of diversity and inability to be externally controlled. In this paper, we speculate that a fundamental shortcoming of sequence generation models is that the decoding is done strictly from left-to-right, meaning that outputs values generated earlier have a profound effect on those generated later. To address this issue, we propose a novel middle-out decoder architecture that begins from an initial middle-word and simultaneously expands the sequence in both directions. To facilitate information flow and maintain consistent decoding, we introduce a dual self-attention mechanism that allows us to model complex dependencies between the outputs. We illustrate the performance of our model on the task of video captioning, as well as a synthetic sequence de-noising task. Our middle-out decoder achieves significant improvements on de-noising and competitive performance in the task of video captioning, while quantifiably improving the caption diversity. Furthermore, we perform a qualitative analysis that demonstrates our ability to effectively control the generation process of our decoder.

paragraphs: Sequence generators commonly produce outputs from left to right, giving early choices a strong influence on everything that follows. This paper suggests that this ordering may contribute to limited diversity and difficulty controlling generation. It proposes a decoder that starts with a middle word and expands the sequence in both directions simultaneously.

To coordinate the two growing parts, the architecture includes a dual self-attention mechanism. This mechanism supports information flow and models dependencies among outputs, helping the bidirectional generation process remain consistent. The initial middle word also provides a point around which the output is constructed, making the generation order central to the proposed approach.

The authors evaluate the decoder on synthetic sequence denoising and video captioning. They report significant denoising improvements, competitive captioning performance, and measurable gains in caption diversity. Qualitative analysis also demonstrates control over generation. These findings support the usefulness of middle-out decoding in the evaluated settings, while the claim that left-to-right ordering is a fundamental shortcoming remains the paper's motivating hypothesis.
summary.tldr: A decoder that expands from a middle word improves denoising and caption diversity while enabling qualitative control over generation.

title: Middle-Out Decoding

abstract: Quantum Graphical Models (QGMs) generalize classical graphical models by adopting the formalism for reasoning about uncertainty from quantum mechanics. Unlike classical graphical models, QGMs represent uncertainty with density matrices in complex Hilbert spaces. Hilbert space embeddings (HSEs) also generalize Bayesian inference in Hilbert spaces. We investigate the link between QGMs and HSEs and show that the sum rule and Bayes rule for QGMs are equivalent to the kernel sum rule in HSEs and a special case of Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression, respectively. We show that these operations can be kernelized, and use these insights to propose a Hilbert Space Embedding of Hidden Quantum Markov Models (HSE-HQMM) to model dynamics. We present experimental results showing that HSE-HQMMs are competitive with state-of-the-art models like LSTMs and PSRNNs on several datasets, while also providing a nonparametric method for maintaining a probability distribution over continuous-valued features.
originalAbstract: Quantum Graphical Models (QGMs) generalize classical graphical models by adopting the formalism for reasoning about uncertainty from quantum mechanics. Unlike classical graphical models, QGMs represent uncertainty with density matrices in complex Hilbert spaces. Hilbert space embeddings (HSEs) also generalize Bayesian inference in Hilbert spaces. We investigate the link between QGMs and HSEs and show that the sum rule and Bayes rule for QGMs are equivalent to the kernel sum rule in HSEs and a special case of Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression, respectively. We show that these operations can be kernelized, and use these insights to propose a Hilbert Space Embedding of Hidden Quantum Markov Models (HSE-HQMM) to model dynamics. We present experimental results showing that HSE-HQMMs are competitive with state-of-the-art models like LSTMs and PSRNNs on several datasets, while also providing a nonparametric method for maintaining a probability distribution over continuous-valued features.

This paper investigates how these two frameworks connect, focusing on the operations used to combine and update uncertain information.

They also connect the quantum-model Bayes rule to a particular case of Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression. abstract: Algorithms for clustering points in metric spaces is a long-studied area of research. Clustering has seen a multitude of work both theoretically, in understanding the approximation guarantees possible for many objective functions such as k-median and k-means clustering, and experimentally, in finding the fastest algorithms and seeding procedures for Lloyd's algorithm. The performance of a given clustering algorithm depends on the specific application at hand, and this may not be known up front. For example, a "typical instance" may vary depending on the application, and different clustering heuristics perform differently depending on the instance. In this paper, we define an infinite family of algorithms generalizing Lloyd's algorithm, with one parameter controlling the the initialization procedure, and another parameter controlling the local search procedure. This family of algorithms includes the celebrated k-means++ algorithm, as well as the classic farthest-first traversal algorithm. We design efficient learning algorithms which receive samples from an application-specific distribution over clustering instances and learn a near-optimal clustering algorithm from the class. We show the best parameters vary significantly across datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR, and mixtures of Gaussians. Our learned algorithms never perform worse than k-means++, and on some datasets we see significant improvements.

This paper treats the choice of clustering algorithm as something that can itself be learned. Training examples are clustering instances sampled from a distribution associated with a particular application.

The authors construct an infinite family of algorithms extending Lloyd's algorithm. One parameter controls initialization, while another controls the local search procedure. The family includes k-means++ and farthest-first traversal. The learned algorithms do not perform worse than k-means++ in the reported evaluation and improve significantly on some datasets. These findings support adapting both initialization and search to an application's instances instead of assuming that one parameter choice is best everywhere.
summary.tldr: The paper learns application-specific clustering algorithms by tuning initialization and local search within a family extending Lloyd's algorithm.

title: Data-Driven Clustering via Parameterized Lloyd's Families

abstract: A major difficulty in studying the neural mechanisms underlying olfactory perception is the lack of obvious structure in the relationship between odorants and the neural activity patterns they elicit. Here we use odor-evoked responses in piriform cortex to identify a latent manifold specifying latent distance relationships between olfactory stimuli. Our approach is based on the Gaussian process latent variable model, and seeks to map odorants to points in a low-dimensional embedding space, where distances between points in the embedding space relate to the similarity of population responses they elicit. The model is specified by an explicit continuous mapping from a latent embedding space to the space of high-dimensional neural population firing rates via nonlinear tuning curves, each parametrized by a Gaussian process. Population responses are then generated by the addition of correlated, odor-dependent Gaussian noise. We fit this model to large-scale calcium fluorescence imaging measurements of population activity in layers 2 and 3 of mouse piriform cortex following the presentation of a diverse set of odorants. The model identifies a low-dimensional embedding of each odor, and a smooth tuning curve over the latent embedding space that accurately captures each neuron's response to different odorants. The model captures both signal and noise correlations across more than 500 neurons. We validate the model using a cross-validation analysis known as co-smoothing to show that the model can accurately predict the responses of a population of held-out neurons to test odorants.

title: Learning a latent manifold of odor representations from neural responses in piriform cortex

abstract: In this paper we address the problem of Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) that is currently the computational bottleneck in a large number of machine learning applications. While being similar to the nearest neighbor search (NNS), the MIPS problem was shown to be more challenging, as the inner product is not a proper metric function. We propose to solve the MIPS problem with the usage of similarity graphs, i.e., graphs where each vertex is connected to the vertices that are the most similar in terms of some similarity function. Originally, the framework of similarity graphs was proposed for metric spaces and in this paper we naturally extend it to the non-metric MIPS scenario. We demonstrate that, unlike existing approaches, similarity graphs do not require any data transformation to reduce MIPS to the NNS problem and should be used for the original data. Moreover, we explain why such a reduction is detrimental for similarity graphs. By an extensive comparison to the existing approaches, we show that the proposed method is a game-changer in terms of the runtime/accuracy trade-off for the MIPS problem.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search asks which stored vectors have the largest inner product with a query. It resembles nearest-neighbor search, but inner products do not form a proper metric. This difference complicates the use of methods designed around metric distances, even though fast retrieval is important in many machine-learning applications.

The paper extends similarity graphs to this non-metric setting. Such graphs connect each vertex to vertices judged most similar under a chosen function. The proposed method works directly with the original data, without transforming maximum inner product search into a nearest-neighbor problem. The authors also explain why that transformation is detrimental when using similarity graphs.

An extensive experimental comparison reports a major improvement in the trade-off between runtime and accuracy over existing approaches. The significance is not only faster search in the evaluated comparisons, but also the suitability of using the original similarity relationship when constructing the graph. The work demonstrates that a framework originally proposed for metric spaces can be extended effectively to this non-metric retrieval problem.
summary.tldr: Similarity graphs applied directly to original vectors substantially improve the reported runtime–accuracy trade-off for maximum inner product search.

title: Non-metric Similarity Graphs for Maximum Inner Product Search

abstract: Over the past few years, Batch-Normalization has been commonly used in deep networks, allowing faster training and high performance for a wide variety of applications. However, the reasons behind its merits remained unanswered, with several shortcomings that hindered its use for certain tasks. In this work, we present a novel view on the purpose and function of normalization methods and weight-decay, as tools to decouple weights' norm from the underlying optimized objective. This property highlights the connection between practices such as normalization, weight decay and learning-rate adjustments. We suggest several alternatives to the widely used $L^2$ batch-norm, using normalization in $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ spaces that can substantially improve numerical stability in low-precision implementations as well as provide computational and memory benefits. We demonstrate that such methods enable the first batch-norm alternative to work for half-precision implementations. Finally, we suggest a modification to weight-normalization, which improves its performance on large-scale tasks.

paragraphs: Batch normalization is widely used to improve neural-network training, but its benefits and shortcomings motivate a closer look at what normalization actually does. This paper interprets normalization and weight decay as ways to separate the magnitude of weights from the objective being optimized. That perspective connects normalization choices with weight decay and learning-rate adjustments.

The authors propose alternatives to conventional L2 batch normalization using L1 and L-infinity normalization. Changing the norm changes the numerical operations involved in normalization. The proposed alternatives can substantially improve numerical stability in low-precision implementations while also offering computational and memory benefits, making the choice relevant to how training is implemented.

The paper demonstrates methods that enable what it describes as the first batch-normalization alternative to work in half precision. It also modifies weight normalization and reports improved performance on large-scale tasks. Together, these contributions combine an interpretation of weight magnitude during optimization with concrete normalization designs, showing how mathematical choices about scale can influence both training behavior and implementation efficiency.
summary.tldr: A weight-scale perspective motivates alternative normalization schemes with low-precision stability, efficiency, and performance benefits.

title: Norm matters: efficient and accurate normalization schemes in deep networks

abstract: In this paper we address the graph matching problem. Following the recent works of \cite{zaslavskiy2009path,Vestner2017} we analyze and generalize the idea of concave relaxations. We introduce the concepts of \emph{conditionally concave} and \emph{probably conditionally concave} energies on polytopes and show that they encapsulate many instances of the graph matching problem, including matching Euclidean graphs and graphs on surfaces. We further prove that local minima of probably conditionally concave energies on general matching polytopes (\eg, doubly stochastic) are with high probability extreme points of the matching polytope (\eg, permutations).
originalAbstract: In this paper we address the graph matching problem. Following the recent works of \cite{zaslavskiy2009path,Vestner2017} we analyze and generalize the idea of concave relaxations. We introduce the concepts of \emph{conditionally concave} and \emph{probably conditionally concave} energies on polytopes and show that they encapsulate many instances of the graph matching problem, including matching Euclidean graphs and graphs on surfaces. We further prove that local minima of probably conditionally concave energies on general matching polytopes (\eg, doubly stochastic) are with high probability extreme points of the matching polytope (\eg, permutations).

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between the elements of two graphs. A relaxation represents candidate matches in a continuous feasible region, called a polytope, rather than restricting the search immediately to discrete assignments. This paper analyzes and generalizes concave relaxations, focusing on when their solutions retain the structure of actual matches.

The authors introduce conditionally concave and probably conditionally concave energies on polytopes. These concepts describe objective functions relevant to a range of graph matching instances, including Euclidean graphs and graphs defined on surfaces. The framework lets the analysis address multiple matching settings through properties of the objective and feasible region.

The main result is that local minima of probably conditionally concave energies are, with high probability, extreme points of the matching polytope. For a doubly stochastic matching polytope, those extreme points correspond to permutations. This matters because a continuous relaxation can then have local minima that already represent discrete matches. The conclusion concerns the form of local minima with high probability; it does not assert that every such minimum is globally optimal.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies graph-matching relaxations whose local minima correspond to extreme-point matches with high probability.

title: (Probably) Concave Graph Matching

abstract: Normalizing flows can be used to construct high quality generative probabilistic models, but training and sample generation require repeated evaluation of Jacobian determinants and function inverses. To make such computations feasible, current approaches employ highly constrained architectures that produce diagonal, triangular, or low rank Jacobian matrices. As an alternative, we investigate a set of novel normalizing flows based on the circular and symmetric convolutions. We show that these transforms admit efficient Jacobian determinant computation and inverse mapping (deconvolution) in O(N log N) time. Additionally, element-wise multiplication, widely used in normalizing flow architectures, can be combined with these transforms to increase modeling flexibility. We further propose an analytic approach to designing nonlinear elementwise bijectors that induce special properties in the intermediate layers, by implicitly introducing specific regularizers in the loss. We show that these transforms allow more effective normalizing flow models to be developed for generative image models.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows build probabilistic generative models using invertible transformations. Training and sampling repeatedly require inverses and Jacobian determinants, so the computational cost of these operations shapes which architectures are practical. This paper investigates convolutional transformations as an alternative to architectures constrained to diagonal, triangular, or low-rank Jacobian structures.

The proposed flows use circular and symmetric convolutions. For these transforms, both determinant evaluation and inverse mapping through deconvolution can be performed in O(N log N) time. The authors also show that elementwise multiplication can be combined with these operations to increase modeling flexibility while building on the proposed transform family.

These transformations can induce desired properties in intermediate layers by implicitly introducing particular regularizers into the loss. The authors show that the resulting components support more effective generative image models. The broader contribution is an expanded set of flow transformations whose inverse and determinant calculations remain efficient, allowing computational tractability and modeling flexibility to be considered together.
summary.tldr: Circular and symmetric convolutions provide flexible normalizing-flow components with efficient inverse and Jacobian determinant computations.

title: Invertible Convolutional Flow

abstract: Recent advances in 3D deep learning have shown that it is possible to train highly effective deep models for 3D shape generation, directly from 2D images. This is particularly interesting since the availability of 3D models is still limited compared to the massive amount of accessible 2D images, which is invaluable for training. The representation of 3D surfaces itself is a key factor for the quality and resolution of the 3D output. While explicit representations, such as point clouds and voxels, can span a wide range of shape variations, their resolutions are often limited. Mesh-based representations are more efficient but are limited by their ability to handle varying topologies. Implicit surfaces, however, can robustly handle complex shapes, topologies, and also provide flexible resolution control. We address the fundamental problem of learning implicit surfaces for shape inference without the need of 3D supervision. Despite their advantages, it remains nontrivial to (1) formulate a differentiable connection between implicit surfaces and their 2D renderings, which is needed for image-based supervision; and (2) ensure precise geometric properties and control, such as local smoothness. In particular, sampling implicit surfaces densely is also known to be a computationally demanding and very slow operation. To this end, we propose a novel ray-based field probing technique for efficient image-to-field supervision, as well as a general geometric regularizer for implicit surfaces, which provides natural shape priors in unconstrained regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the task of single-view image-based 3D shape digitization and show how we outperform state-of-the-art techniques both quantitatively and qualitatively.

The contribution joins an efficient image-based learning connection with geometric regularization, making the representation's flexibility usable in the stated reconstruction setting.
summary.tldr: Ray-based field probing and geometric regularization enable implicit 3D surface learning from images without 3D supervision.

title: Learning to Infer Implicit Surfaces without 3D Supervision

abstract: We study least squares linear regression over $N$ uncorrelated Gaussian features that are selected in order of decreasing variance. When the number of selected features $p$ is at most the sample size $n$, the estimator under consideration coincides with the principal component regression estimator; when $p>n$, the estimator is the least $\ell_2$ norm solution over the selected features. We give an average-case analysis of the out-of-sample prediction error as $p,n,N \to \infty$ with $p/N \to \alpha$ and $n/N \to \beta$, for some constants $\alpha \in [0,1]$ and $\beta \in (0,1)$. In this average-case setting, the prediction error exhibits a ``double descent'' shape as a function of $p$. We also establish conditions under which the minimum risk is achieved in the interpolating ($p>n$) regime.

paragraphs: The paper examines how prediction error changes as a regression model uses more features. It assumes uncorrelated Gaussian features selected from highest to lowest variance. When the selected feature count does not exceed the number of observations, the estimator coincides with principal component regression. Beyond that point, it uses the solution with the smallest Euclidean norm.

The analysis considers average prediction error on new data as the total feature count, selected feature count, and sample size all grow. The proportions of selected features and observations relative to the total feature count approach fixed constants. This gives a defined large-scale setting for comparing models on both sides of the point where features outnumber observations.

Within this setting, the prediction error follows a double descent shape as the number of selected features changes. The authors also establish conditions under which the lowest risk occurs in the interpolating regime, where selected features exceed observations. The result shows that this regime can be optimal under the analyzed conditions, rather than asserting that it is always preferable.
summary.tldr: An average-case analysis of Gaussian-feature regression finds double descent and conditions where using more features than observations minimizes prediction risk.

title: On the number of variables to use in principal component regression

abstract: This paper studies the universal approximation property of deep neural networks for representing probability distributions. Given a target distribution $\pi$ and a source distribution $p_z$ both defined on $\mathbb{R}^d$, we prove under some assumptions that there exists a deep neural network $g:\mathbb{R}^d\gt \mathbb{R}$ with ReLU activation such that the push-forward measure $(\nabla g)_\# p_z$ of $p_z$ under the map $\nabla g$ is arbitrarily close to the target measure $\pi$. The closeness are measured by three classes of integral probability metrics between probability distributions: $1$-Wasserstein distance, maximum mean distance (MMD) and kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD). We prove upper bounds for the size (width and depth) of the deep neural network in terms of the dimension $d$ and the approximation error $\varepsilon$ with respect to the three discrepancies. In particular, the size of neural network can grow exponentially in $d$ when $1$-Wasserstein distance is used as the discrepancy, whereas for both MMD and KSD the size of neural network only depends on $d$ at most polynomially. Our proof relies on convergence estimates of empirical measures under aforementioned discrepancies and semi-discrete optimal transport.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a neural network can transform samples from one probability distribution into samples approximating another. It considers source and target distributions in the same d-dimensional space. Under assumptions, the authors prove that a suitable deep network can represent a transformation whose resulting distribution is arbitrarily close to the target.

The construction uses a scalar-valued network with ReLU activations, then takes its gradient to obtain the transformation applied to source samples. The authors measure the resulting distribution’s accuracy in three ways: Wasserstein-1 distance, maximum mean distance, and kernelized Stein discrepancy. They also bound the network width and depth needed for a requested approximation error.

The choice of discrepancy substantially changes these size bounds. The bound can grow exponentially with dimension for Wasserstein-1, whereas its dimensional dependence is at most polynomial for the other two discrepancies. The proof combines empirical-distribution convergence estimates with semi-discrete optimal transport. The result establishes representational capacity under the stated assumptions, with different complexity guarantees depending on how distributional agreement is measured.
summary.tldr: Under assumptions, gradients of deep ReLU networks can approximate target distributions, with network-size bounds that depend strongly on the chosen discrepancy.

title: A Universal Approximation Theorem of Deep Neural Networks for Expressing Probability Distributions

abstract: Random projections or sketching are widely used in many algorithmic and learning contexts. Here we study the performance of iterative Hessian sketch for least-squares problems. By leveraging and extending recent results from random matrix theory on the limiting spectrum of matrices randomly projected with the subsampled randomized Hadamard transform, and truncated Haar matrices, we can study and compare the resulting algorithms to a level of precision that has not been possible before. Our technical contributions include a novel formula for the second moment of the inverse of projected matrices. We also find simple closed-form expressions for asymptotically optimal step-sizes and convergence rates. These show that the convergence rate for Haar and randomized Hadamard matrices are identical, and asymptotically improve upon Gaussian random projections. These techniques may be applied to other algorithms that employ randomized dimension reduction.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching reduces the dimensionality of computations used in optimization. This paper studies iterative Hessian sketch methods for least-squares problems, asking how the choice of random projection affects convergence. It focuses on subsampled randomized Hadamard transforms and truncated Haar matrices, using random matrix theory to compare them with greater precision.

The analysis extends results about the limiting spectrum of projected matrices and derives a new formula for the second moment of their inverses. These mathematical tools yield simple expressions for asymptotically optimal step sizes and convergence rates. They connect the statistical structure of the projection to concrete choices made by the iterative algorithm.

The resulting rates are identical for Haar and randomized Hadamard projections, and asymptotically better than those for Gaussian projections. The asymptotic qualification matters: the result describes the limiting analysis rather than asserting the same ordering for every finite problem. The authors also suggest that these techniques may support analysis of other algorithms using randomized dimensionality reduction.
summary.tldr: Random matrix analysis yields asymptotically optimal sketching steps and shows matching Haar and Hadamard convergence rates that improve on Gaussian projections.

title: Optimal Iterative Sketching Methods with the Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform

abstract: This paper studies the problem of learning with augmented classes (LAC), where augmented classes unobserved in the training data might emerge in the testing phase. Previous studies generally attempt to discover augmented classes by exploiting geometric properties, achieving inspiring empirical performance yet lacking theoretical understandings particularly on the generalization ability. In this paper we show that, by using unlabeled training data to approximate the potential distribution of augmented classes, an unbiased risk estimator of the testing distribution can be established for the LAC problem under mild assumptions, which paves a way to develop a sound approach with theoretical guarantees. Moreover, the proposed approach can adapt to complex changing environments where augmented classes may appear and the prior of known classes may change simultaneously. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: A classifier may encounter categories during testing that were absent from its labeled training examples. The paper studies this setting as learning with augmented classes. Earlier approaches used geometric patterns to discover these categories, with encouraging empirical results, but the authors identify a gap in theoretical understanding of how well such methods generalize.

Their approach uses unlabeled training data to approximate the distribution that the additional classes might follow. Under assumptions described as mild, this information makes it possible to construct an unbiased estimator of risk on the testing distribution. Here, unbiasedness concerns estimating the testing risk correctly on average; it does not mean that the resulting classifier makes no mistakes.

title: An Unbiased Risk Estimator for Learning with Augmented Classes

abstract: This work proposes a novel analysis of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for non-convex and smooth optimization. Our analysis sheds light on the impact of the probability distribution of the gradient noise on the convergence rate of the norm of the gradient. In the case of sub-Gaussian and centered noise, we prove that, with probability $1-\delta$, the number of iterations to reach a precision $\varepsilon$ for the squared gradient norm is $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\ln(1/\delta))$. In the case of centered and integrable heavy-tailed noise, we show that, while the expectation of the iterates may be infinite, the squared gradient norm still converges with probability $1-\delta$ in $O(\varepsilon^{-p}\delta^{-q})$ iterations, where $p,q > 2$. This result shows that heavy-tailed noise on the gradient slows down the convergence of SGD without preventing it, proving that SGD is robust to gradient noise with unbounded variance, a setting of interest for Deep Learning. In addition, it indicates that choosing a step size proportional to $T^{-1/b}$ where $b$ is the tail-parameter of the noise and $T$ is the number of iterations leads to the best convergence rates. Both results are simple corollaries of a unified analysis using the novel concept of biased expectations, a simple and intuitive mathematical tool to obtain concentration inequalities. Using this concept, we propose a new quantity to measure the amount of noise added to the gradient, and discuss its value in multiple scenarios.

The analysis therefore concerns reaching approximate stationary behavior, and studies how quickly that happens with high probability under different kinds of noise.

title: Robustness Analysis of Non-Convex Stochastic Gradient Descent using Biased Expectations

abstract: As a fundamental issue in lifelong learning, catastrophic forgetting is directly caused by inaccessible historical data; accordingly, if the data (information) were memorized perfectly, no forgetting should be expected. Motivated by that, we propose a GAN memory for lifelong learning, which is capable of remembering a stream of datasets via generative processes, with \emph{no} forgetting. Our GAN memory is based on recognizing that one can modulate the ``style'' of a GAN model to form perceptually-distant targeted generation. Accordingly, we propose to do sequential style modulations atop a well-behaved base GAN model, to form sequential targeted generative models, while simultaneously benefiting from the transferred base knowledge. The GAN memory -- that is motivated by lifelong learning -- is therefore itself manifested by a form of lifelong learning, via forward transfer and modulation of information from prior tasks. Experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing approaches and its effectiveness in alleviating catastrophic forgetting for lifelong classification problems. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/MiaoyunZhao/GANmemory_LifelongLearning}.

paragraphs: Continual learning becomes difficult when earlier datasets are no longer accessible. This paper approaches that problem by retaining information through a generative memory: a system that can produce data associated with datasets encountered over time. Its motivation is that perfectly retained data information would remove the corresponding cause of forgetting.

The proposed GAN memory builds on a well-behaved base GAN. The authors observe that changing its style can produce perceptually distant target distributions, and use sequential style modulations to form generators for successive datasets. This process also transfers knowledge from the base model, so learning later generative targets can benefit from information already available.

The paper describes the resulting memory as retaining a stream of datasets without forgetting. Its classification experiments support the more specific downstream claim that the approach alleviates catastrophic forgetting, and the reported comparisons favor it over existing approaches. The distinction matters: preserving generative memories supplies information for continual classification, while the stated classification result is an improvement in forgetting behavior.
summary.tldr: Sequential style modulation creates a GAN memory described as retaining past datasets without forgetting and empirically alleviates forgetting in continual classification.

title: GAN Memory with No Forgetting

abstract: We investigate whether Differentially Private SGD offers better privacy in practice than what is guaranteed by its state-of-the-art analysis. We do so via novel data poisoning attacks, which we show correspond to realistic privacy attacks. While previous work (Ma et al., arXiv 2019) proposed this connection between differential privacy and data poisoning as a defense against data poisoning, our use as a tool for understanding the privacy of a specific mechanism is new. More generally, our work takes a quantitative, empirical approach to understanding the privacy afforded by specific implementations of differentially private algorithms that we believe has the potential to complement and influence analytical work on differential privacy.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent comes with mathematical privacy guarantees, but those guarantees leave an empirical question: does a particular implementation provide substantially more privacy in practice than its analysis promises? This paper investigates that question through attacks designed to measure the privacy behavior of the learning procedure.

The authors develop data poisoning attacks and show that they correspond to realistic privacy attacks. This connection makes deliberate changes to training data useful as an auditing instrument. Earlier work had connected differential privacy and poisoning in the context of defending against poisoned data. Here, the connection is used to investigate the privacy of a particular mechanism.

The contribution is a quantitative, empirical approach to examining implementations of private learning algorithms. It gives analytical privacy work another source of evidence about how mechanisms behave under attack. The authors present this approach as potentially complementary to theoretical analysis; the abstract does not assert a specific numerical gap between guaranteed and observed privacy.
summary.tldr: The paper uses data poisoning attacks as an empirical audit of how much privacy specific implementations of differentially private SGD provide.

title: Auditing Differentially Private Machine Learning: How Private is Private SGD?

abstract: Successful adoption of deep learning (DL) in the wild requires models to be: (1) compact, (2) accurate, and (3) robust to distributional shifts. Unfortunately, efforts towards simultaneously meeting these requirements have mostly been unsuccessful. This raises an important question: Is the inability to create Compact, Accurate, and Robust Deep neural networks (CARDs) fundamental? To answer this question, we perform a large-scale analysis of popular model compression techniques which uncovers several intriguing patterns. Notably, in contrast to traditional pruning approaches (e.g., fine tuning and gradual magnitude pruning), we find that ``lottery ticket-style'' approaches can surprisingly be used to produce CARDs, including binary-weight CARDs. Specifically, we are able to create extremely compact CARDs that, compared to their larger counterparts, have similar test accuracy and matching (or better) robustness---simply by pruning and (optionally) quantizing. Leveraging the compactness of CARDs, we develop a simple domain-adaptive test-time ensembling approach (CARD-Decks) that uses a gating module to dynamically select appropriate CARDs from the CARD-Deck based on their spectral-similarity with test samples. The proposed approach builds a "winning hand'' of CARDs that establishes a new state-of-the-art (on RobustBench) on CIFAR-10-C accuracies (i.e., 96.8% standard and 92.75% robust) and CIFAR-100-C accuracies (80.6% standard and 71.3% robust) with better memory usage than non-compressed baselines (pretrained CARDs and CARD-Decks available at https://github.com/RobustBench/robustbench). Finally, we provide theoretical support for our empirical findings.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a deep network can simultaneously be small, accurate, and robust when its inputs differ from training data. Its large-scale analysis of compression methods finds that lottery ticket-style approaches can produce networks with all three properties. The authors call these Compact, Accurate, and Robust Deep neural networks, or CARDs.

This adaptive ensemble reports state-of-the-art RobustBench results on CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C while using less memory than uncompressed baselines. The paper provides theoretical support alongside these empirical findings, supporting compression as a possible route toward practical robustness.
summary.tldr: Lottery ticket-style compression can preserve accuracy and improve distribution-shift robustness, while compact ensembles further strengthen reported results.

title: A Winning Hand: Compressing Deep Networks Can Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a prevalent optimization technique for large-scale distributed machine learning. While SGD computation can be efficiently divided between multiple machines, communication typically becomes a bottleneck in the distributed setting. Gradient compression methods can be used to alleviate this problem, and a recent line of work shows that SGD augmented with gradient compression converges to an $\varepsilon$-first-order stationary point. In this paper we extend these results to convergence to an $\varepsilon$-second-order stationary point ($\varepsilon$-SOSP), which is to the best of our knowledge the first result of this type. In addition, we show that, when the stochastic gradient is not Lipschitz, compressed SGD with RandomK compressor converges to an $\varepsilon$-SOSP with the same number of iterations as uncompressed SGD [Jin et al.,2021] (JACM), while improving the total communication by a factor of $\tilde \Theta(\sqrt{d} \varepsilon^{-3/4})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the optimization problem. We present additional results for the cases when the compressor is arbitrary and when the stochastic gradient is Lipschitz.

In this paper we extend these results to convergence to an $\varepsilon$-second-order stationary point ($\varepsilon$-SOSP), which is to the best of our knowledge the first result of this type. In addition, we show that, when the stochastic gradient is not Lipschitz, compressed SGD with RandomK compressor converges to an $\varepsilon$-SOSP with the same number of iterations as uncompressed SGD [Jin et al.,2021] (JACM), while improving the total communication by a factor of $\tilde \Theta(\sqrt{d} \varepsilon^{-3/4})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the optimization problem. paragraphs: Distributing stochastic gradient descent across machines can reduce computation time, but exchanging gradients can become a communication bottleneck. Compression reduces that traffic. Earlier guarantees established convergence to points with small gradients, which alone does not rule out saddle points. This paper strengthens the analysis to approximate second-order stationary points, adding a condition on curvature.

The authors prove that compressed SGD can reach this stronger stationarity criterion. They also identify a specific guarantee for the RandomK compressor when the stochastic gradient is not Lipschitz: it matches the iteration count of the uncompressed SGD result used for comparison. At the same time, it improves total communication by a factor scaling as roughly √d ε⁻³⁄⁴, with logarithmic factors suppressed.

Here, d is the problem dimension and ε sets the desired stationarity tolerance. The paper also provides results for arbitrary compressors and for Lipschitz stochastic gradients. Its central significance is that communication savings can coexist with guarantees that address saddle-point behavior; the stated iteration-matching result applies to the specified compressor and gradient setting.
summary.tldr: Compressed SGD can reach approximate second-order stationary points, with a RandomK result matching uncompressed iterations while reducing communication.

title: Escaping Saddle Points with Compressed SGD

abstract: There are two types of deep generative models: explicit and implicit. The former defines an explicit density form that allows likelihood inference; while the latter targets a flexible transformation from random noise to generated samples. While the two classes of generative models have shown great power in many applications, both of them, when used alone, suffer from respective limitations and drawbacks. To take full advantages of both models and enable mutual compensation, we propose a novel joint training framework that bridges an explicit (unnormalized) density estimator and an implicit sample generator via Stein discrepancy. We show that our method 1) induces novel mutual regularization via kernel Sobolev norm penalization and Moreau-Yosida regularization, and 2) stabilizes the training dynamics. Empirically, we demonstrate that proposed method can facilitate the density estimator to more accurately identify data modes and guide the generator to output higher-quality samples, comparing with training a single counterpart. The new approach also shows promising results when the training samples are contaminated or limited.

paragraphs: Generative models can describe data in two different ways: by assigning a density to possible observations, or by transforming random noise into samples. This paper joins an explicit, unnormalized density estimator with an implicit sample generator. The motivation is that their different strengths can help compensate for the drawbacks each has when trained alone.

The proposed framework connects the two models through Stein discrepancy. The authors show that this joint training induces mutual regularization, expressed mathematically through kernel Sobolev norm penalization and Moreau-Yosida regularization. They also show that it stabilizes training dynamics. The connection therefore does more than place two models side by side: it changes how each is trained through its relationship with the other.

Empirically, joint training helps the density estimator identify data modes more accurately and helps the generator produce higher-quality samples compared with training either counterpart alone. The approach also gives promising results with contaminated or limited training data. Those findings support complementary learning between density estimation and sample generation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Joint training through Stein discrepancy lets a density estimator and sample generator regularize each other and improve their empirical results.

title: Bridging Explicit and Implicit Deep Generative Models via Neural Stein Estimators

abstract: We study prior-independent dynamic auction design with production costs for a value-maximizing buyer, a paradigm that is becoming prevalent recently following the development of automatic bidding algorithms in advertising platforms. In contrast to a utility-maximizing buyer, who maximizes the difference between her total value and total payment, a value-maximizing buyer aims to maximize her total value subject to a return on investment (ROI) constraint. Our main result is a dynamic mechanism with regret $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$, where $T$ is the time horizon, against the first-best benchmark, i.e., the maximum amount of revenue the seller can extract assuming all values of the buyer are publicly known.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated auction design with production costs for a buyer whose objective is to maximize total value while satisfying a return-on-investment constraint. That behavior differs from maximizing utility, where the objective is value minus payment. The distinction matters because the auction must account for a buyer pursuing value subject to a spending-related constraint, a model motivated by automated advertising bids.

The authors seek a prior-independent dynamic mechanism. Their performance comparison is especially demanding: the benchmark is the largest revenue a seller could extract if every buyer value were publicly known. Regret measures the mechanism's revenue shortfall relative to this fully informed benchmark over a horizon of T interactions.

The main result is a mechanism with regret bounded by Õ(T^(2/3)), where the notation suppresses logarithmic factors. Because this grows more slowly than T, the guaranteed benchmark shortfall per interaction decreases as the horizon grows. The contribution establishes a quantitative connection between prior-independent auction design and the first-best revenue target in the stated setting with production costs and a value-maximizing buyer.
summary.tldr: A prior-independent dynamic auction achieves Õ(T^(2/3)) regret against fully informed revenue extraction for an ROI-constrained, value-maximizing buyer.

title: Prior-independent Dynamic Auctions for a Value-maximizing Buyer

abstract: Geometric alignment appears in a variety of applications, ranging from domain adaptation, optimal transport, and normalizing flows in machine learning; optical flow and learned augmentation in computer vision and deformable registration within biomedical imaging. A recurring challenge is the alignment of domains whose topology is not the same; a problem that is routinely ignored, potentially introducing bias in downstream analysis. As a first step towards solving such alignment problems, we propose an unsupervised algorithm for the detection of changes in image topology. The model is based on a conditional variational auto-encoder and detects topological changes between two images during the registration step. We account for both topological changes in the image under spatial variation and unexpected transformations. Our approach is validated on two tasks and datasets: detection of topological changes in microscopy images of cells, and unsupervised anomaly detection brain imaging.

paragraphs: Geometric alignment tries to bring corresponding structures in two images into agreement. A recurring difficulty is that the images may differ in topology, so their structural relationship cannot be understood only as spatial displacement. Ignoring such differences can introduce bias into later analysis, making detection of these changes a useful part of registration.

The paper proposes an unsupervised method based on a conditional variational autoencoder. It detects topological differences between images during the registration process, accounting for both topology changes under spatial variation and unexpected transformations. The alignment procedure therefore becomes an opportunity to identify structural changes as well as match image content.

The authors validate the approach on detecting topological changes in microscopy images of cells and on unsupervised anomaly detection in brain imaging. They frame the work as an initial step toward alignment when domains have different topology. Its significance lies in explicitly recognizing a source of mismatch that conventional alignment workflows may overlook, rather than assuming all differences can be resolved through deformation.
summary.tldr: A conditional variational autoencoder detects topological changes during image registration, with validation on cell microscopy and brain-image anomaly detection.

title: Spot the Difference: Detection of Topological Changes via Geometric Alignment

abstract: Differentially Private-SGD (DP-SGD) of Abadi et al. and its variations are the only known algorithms for private training of large scale neural networks. This algorithm requires computation of per-sample gradients norms which is extremely slow and memory intensive in practice. In this paper, we present a new framework to design differentially private optimizers called DP-SGD-JL and DP-Adam-JL. Our approach uses Johnson–Lindenstrauss (JL) projections to quickly approximate the per-sample gradient norms without exactly computing them, thus making the training time and memory requirements of our optimizers closer to that of their non-DP versions. Unlike previous attempts to make DP-SGD faster which work only on a subset of network architectures or use compiler techniques, we propose an algorithmic solution which works for any network in a black-box manner which is the main contribution of this paper. To illustrate this, on IMDb dataset, we train a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to achieve good privacy-vs-accuracy tradeoff, while being significantly faster than DP-SGD and with a similar memory footprint as non-private SGD.

paragraphs: Differentially private neural-network training can be slow and memory intensive because DP-SGD needs the gradient norm for each training example. Computing those individual quantities creates substantial overhead beyond ordinary training. This paper targets that bottleneck with an algorithmic change to the optimizer.

The proposed DP-SGD-JL and DP-Adam-JL methods use Johnson–Lindenstrauss projections to approximate per-example gradient norms quickly, avoiding their exact computation. The resulting framework brings training time and memory requirements closer to those of the corresponding non-private optimizers. Its stated scope is broad: the approach treats networks as black boxes and does not depend on restricting the architecture or applying compiler-specific techniques.

The authors illustrate the framework by training a recurrent neural network on IMDb. They report a good privacy–accuracy tradeoff, significantly faster training than DP-SGD, and memory use similar to non-private SGD. The practical contribution is therefore reducing the computational burden of private training through approximate norm estimation, with the reported demonstration showing that this can work for a recurrent architecture.
summary.tldr: Random projections approximate per-example gradient norms, making differentially private optimization faster and more memory efficient without architecture-specific modifications.

title: Fast and Memory Efficient Differentially Private-SGD via JL Projections

abstract: To understand the relationship between behavior and neural activity, experiments in neuroscience often include an animal performing a repeated behavior such as a motor task. Recent progress in computer vision and deep learning has shown great potential in the automated analysis of behavior by leveraging large and high-quality video datasets. In this paper, we design Disentangled Behavior Embedding (DBE) to learn robust behavioral embeddings from unlabeled, multi-view, high-resolution behavioral videos across different animals and multiple sessions. We further combine DBE with a stochastic temporal model to propose Variational Disentangled Behavior Embedding (VDBE), an end-to-end approach that learns meaningful discrete behavior representations and generates interpretable behavioral videos. Our models learn consistent behavior representations by explicitly disentangling the dynamic behavioral factors (pose) from time-invariant, non-behavioral nuisance factors (context) in a deep autoencoder, and exploit the temporal structures of pose dynamics. Compared to competing approaches, DBE and VDBE enjoy superior performance on downstream tasks such as fine-grained behavioral motif generation and behavior decoding.

paragraphs: Analyzing animal behavior from video can help neuroscience experiments relate actions to neural activity. This paper targets unlabeled, high-resolution videos recorded from multiple views, animals, and sessions. Its central challenge is to learn a consistent representation of behavior while separating it from contextual differences that are not themselves the behavior of interest.

Disentangled Behavior Embedding, or DBE, uses a deep autoencoder to separate changing behavioral factors, represented as pose, from time-invariant nuisance factors, represented as context. It also uses the temporal structure of pose dynamics. This separation makes the representation explicitly distinguish behavioral change from the stable context in which that change is observed.

The authors combine DBE with a stochastic temporal model to create Variational Disentangled Behavior Embedding, or VDBE. This end-to-end method learns meaningful discrete behavior representations and generates interpretable behavioral videos. Both models outperform competing approaches on downstream tasks including fine-grained behavioral motif generation and behavior decoding. The results support using explicit factor separation and temporal structure together when learning behavioral representations across varied recordings.
summary.tldr: DBE and VDBE separate changing pose from stable context to learn useful behavior representations from unlabeled animal videos.

title: Learning Disentangled Behavior Embeddings

abstract: Post-processing in algorithmic fairness is a versatile approach for correcting bias in ML systems that are already used in production. The main appeal of post-processing is that it avoids expensive retraining. In this work, we propose general post-processing algorithms for individual fairness (IF). We consider a setting where the learner only has access to the predictions of the original model and a similarity graph between individuals, guiding the desired fairness constraints. We cast the IF post-processing problem as a graph smoothing problem corresponding to graph Laplacian regularization that preserves the desired "treat similar individuals similarly" interpretation. Our theoretical results demonstrate the connection of the new objective function to a local relaxation of the original individual fairness. Empirically, our post-processing algorithms correct individual biases in large-scale NLP models such as BERT, while preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: Individual fairness asks that similar people receive similar treatment from a machine learning system. This paper studies how to improve that property after a model has already been trained. Post-processing is useful for deployed systems because it can adjust their predictions without the expense of retraining the underlying model.

The proposed algorithms require access only to the original predictions and a graph describing similarity between individuals. The authors formulate the adjustment as graph smoothing using graph Laplacian regularization. In plain terms, relationships in the graph guide which predictions should be encouraged to agree, preserving the intended connection between similarity and treatment.

The theoretical analysis links the new objective to a local relaxation of individual fairness. This specifies how the smoothing objective relates to the fairness principle without equating it with an unrestricted guarantee of the original definition. Experiments on large-scale language models, including BERT, show that the algorithms correct individual biases while preserving accuracy. The results support prediction-level intervention when retraining is undesirable.
summary.tldr: Graph-based post-processing improves individual fairness using only model predictions and similarity relationships, with accuracy preserved in the reported experiments.

title: Post-processing for Individual Fairness

abstract: We present Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimization (CoPPO), an algorithm that extends the original Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to the multi-agent setting. The key idea lies in the coordinated adaptation of step size during the policy update process among multiple agents. We prove the monotonicity of policy improvement when optimizing a theoretically-grounded joint objective, and derive a simplified optimization objective based on a set of approximations. We then interpret that such an objective in CoPPO can achieve dynamic credit assignment among agents, thereby alleviating the high variance issue during the concurrent update of agent policies. Finally, we demonstrate that CoPPO outperforms several strong baselines and is competitive with the latest multi-agent PPO method (i.e. MAPPO) under typical multi-agent settings, including cooperative matrix games and the StarCraft II micromanagement tasks.

paragraphs: Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimization extends PPO to settings where multiple agents learn together. Its central idea is to coordinate how far agents move during policy updates. This makes the adaptation of update step sizes a joint concern when several policies change concurrently.

The authors first construct a theoretically grounded joint objective and prove monotonic policy improvement when optimizing it. They then use approximations to derive a simpler optimization objective. The distinction matters: the improvement theorem concerns the theoretical objective, while the simplified objective is the practical form derived from it. The authors interpret this simplified form as dynamically assigning credit among agents, helping alleviate high variance during simultaneous policy updates.

Experiments include cooperative matrix games and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. CoPPO outperforms several strong baselines and is competitive with MAPPO in these settings. The results support coordinated updates as a useful design for cooperative multi-agent learning, alongside a theoretical account of why optimizing a suitable joint objective can improve policies.
summary.tldr: CoPPO coordinates agents' policy-update sizes, combining a joint improvement analysis with competitive cooperative multi-agent results.

title: Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimization

abstract: Independent component analysis provides a principled framework for unsupervised representation learning, with solid theory on the identifiability of the latent code that generated the data, given only observations of mixtures thereof. Unfortunately, when the mixing is nonlinear, the model is provably nonidentifiable, since statistical independence alone does not sufficiently constrain the problem. Identifiability can be recovered in settings where additional, typically observed variables are included in the generative process. We investigate an alternative path and consider instead including assumptions reflecting the principle of independent causal mechanisms exploited in the field of causality. Specifically, our approach is motivated by thinking of each source as independently influencing the mixing process. This gives rise to a framework which we term independent mechanism analysis. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence that our approach circumvents a number of nonidentifiability issues arising in nonlinear blind source separation.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis aims to recover hidden sources from observed mixtures. Its central question is identifiability: whether the observations and assumptions pin down the underlying representation. When the mixing process is nonlinear, statistical independence of the sources alone is insufficient, so different hidden representations can remain compatible with the observed data.

One way to recover identifiability is to introduce additional variables into the generative setting, typically variables that are observed. This paper investigates a different route by adding assumptions inspired by independent causal mechanisms. The motivation is to treat each source as independently influencing the mixing process, placing structure on how the observations are generated.

The authors call the resulting framework independent mechanism analysis. They provide theoretical and empirical evidence that it avoids a number of nonidentifiability problems in nonlinear blind source separation. The claim concerns particular ambiguities rather than a complete resolution of nonlinear identifiability. Its significance is the proposed source of additional structure: assumptions about the mixing mechanisms can contribute information beyond independence of the hidden sources themselves.
summary.tldr: Independent mechanism analysis uses assumptions about how sources influence nonlinear mixing to address several identifiability problems.

title: Independent mechanism analysis, a new concept?

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning (offline RL), one of the main challenges is to deal with the distributional shift between the learning policy and the given dataset. To address this problem, recent offline RL methods attempt to introduce conservatism bias to encourage learning in high-confidence areas. Model-free approaches directly encode such bias into policy or value function learning using conservative regularizations or special network structures, but their constrained policy search limits the generalization beyond the offline dataset. Model-based approaches learn forward dynamics models with conservatism quantifications and then generate imaginary trajectories to extend the offline datasets. However, due to limited samples in offline datasets, conservatism quantifications often suffer from overgeneralization in out-of-support regions. The unreliable conservative measures will mislead forward model-based imaginations to undesired areas, leading to overaggressive behaviors. To encourage more conservatism, we propose a novel model-based offline RL framework, called Reverse Offline Model-based Imagination (ROMI). We learn a reverse dynamics model in conjunction with a novel reverse policy, which can generate rollouts leading to the target goal states within the offline dataset. These reverse imaginations provide informed data augmentation for model-free policy learning and enable conservative generalization beyond the offline dataset. ROMI can effectively combine with off-the-shelf model-free algorithms to enable model-based generalization with proper conservatism. Empirical results show that our method can generate more conservative behaviors and achieve state-of-the-art performance on offline RL benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from a fixed dataset even when its policy would visit different situations. Conservative methods try to keep learning in trustworthy regions. However, restricting policy search can limit generalization, while forward model-generated trajectories can drift into poorly supported regions when estimates of conservatism are unreliable.

ROMI changes the direction of model-based imagination. It learns reverse dynamics together with a reverse policy, generating rollouts that lead toward target goal states already present in the offline dataset. These imagined trajectories augment the data used by a model-free learner. The approach aims to extend learning beyond recorded experience while grounding generated behavior in destinations supported by the dataset.

The framework can be combined with existing model-free algorithms. The authors report more conservative behavior and state-of-the-art performance on offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks. These empirical findings support reverse imagination as a way to balance generalization with caution. The key contribution is using the direction of generated trajectories to inform that balance, rather than relying only on conservative estimates attached to forward predictions.
summary.tldr: ROMI augments offline reinforcement-learning data with reverse-generated trajectories leading to dataset-supported goals, enabling more conservative generalization.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Reverse Model-based Imagination

abstract: Recently, contrastive learning attracts increasing interests in neural text generation as a new solution to alleviate the exposure bias problem. It introduces a sequence-level training signal which is crucial to generation tasks that always rely on auto-regressive decoding. However, previous methods using contrastive learning in neural text generation usually lead to inferior performance. In this paper, we analyse the underlying reasons and propose a new Contrastive Neural Text generation framework, CoNT. CoNT addresses bottlenecks that prevent contrastive learning from being widely adopted in generation tasks from three aspects -- the construction of contrastive examples, the choice of the contrastive loss, and the strategy in decoding. We validate CoNT on five generation tasks with ten benchmarks, including machine translation, summarization, code comment generation, data-to-text generation and commonsense generation. Experimental results show that CoNT clearly outperforms its baseline on all the ten benchmarks with a convincing margin. Especially, CoNT surpasses previous the most competitive contrastive learning method for text generation, by 1.50 BLEU on machine translation and 1.77 ROUGE-1 on summarization, respectively. It achieves new state-of-the-art on summarization, code comment generation (without external data) and data-to-text generation.

paragraphs: Text generators produce sequences one step at a time, making sequence-level training signals valuable. Contrastive learning offers such a signal by teaching a model to distinguish between examples. The paper investigates why earlier uses of contrastive learning for generation often performed poorly despite their potential to alleviate exposure bias.

CoNT addresses three parts of the generation pipeline together: how contrastive examples are constructed, which contrastive loss is used, and how decoding is performed. This scope matters because the proposed framework treats the training examples, learning objective, and generation procedure as connected sources of performance, rather than focusing on the objective alone.

summary.tldr: CoNT improves text generation by jointly addressing contrastive example construction, training loss, and decoding.

title: CoNT: Contrastive Neural Text Generation

abstract: A central issue in machine learning is how to train models on sensitive user data. Industry has widely adopted a simple algorithm: Stochastic Gradient Descent with noise (a.k.a. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics). However, foundational theoretical questions about this algorithm's privacy loss remain open---even in the seemingly simple setting of smooth convex losses over a bounded domain. Our main result resolves these questions: for a large range of parameters, we characterize the differential privacy up to a constant. This result reveals that all previous analyses for this setting have the wrong qualitative behavior. Specifically, while previous privacy analyses increase ad infinitum in the number of iterations, we show that after a small burn-in period, running SGD longer leaks no further privacy. Our analysis departs from previous approaches based on fast mixing, instead using techniques based on optimal transport (namely, Privacy Amplification by Iteration) and the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism (namely, Privacy Amplification by Sampling). Our techniques readily extend to other settings.
