paragraphs: Adding noise to stochastic gradient descent is a widely used way to train on sensitive data, but understanding the resulting privacy loss remains a theoretical challenge. This paper analyzes smooth convex losses over a bounded domain. For a broad range of parameters, it characterizes differential privacy up to a constant factor.

The result changes the qualitative picture of how privacy depends on training duration in this setting. Earlier analyses predict privacy loss that grows indefinitely with the number of iterations. The authors show instead that, after a short burn-in period, continuing to run the algorithm leaks no further privacy. The stated setting and parameter range are central to this conclusion.

The analysis combines privacy amplification through iteration, using optimal transport, with privacy amplification through sampling via the sampled Gaussian mechanism. This differs from approaches relying on fast mixing. The authors also state that their techniques extend readily to other settings. The main contribution is a sharper account of privacy over time for the specified noisy optimization problem.
summary.tldr: For smooth convex losses on a bounded domain and a broad parameter range, noisy SGD's privacy loss stops increasing after a short burn-in.

title: Privacy of Noisy Stochastic Gradient Descent: More Iterations without More Privacy Loss

abstract: Pre-training video transformers on extra large-scale datasets is generally required to achieve premier performance on relatively small datasets. In this paper, we show that video masked autoencoders (VideoMAE) are data-efficient learners for self-supervised video pre-training (SSVP). We are inspired by the recent ImageMAE and propose customized video tube masking with an extremely high ratio. This simple design makes video reconstruction a more challenging and meaningful self-supervision task, thus encouraging extracting more effective video representations during the pre-training process. We obtain three important findings with VideoMAE: (1) An extremely high proportion of masking ratio (i.e., 90% to 95%) still yields favorable performance for VideoMAE. The temporally redundant video content enables higher masking ratio than that of images. (2) VideoMAE achieves impressive results on very small datasets (i.e., around 3k-4k videos) without using any extra data. This is partially ascribed to the challenging task of video reconstruction to enforce high-level structure learning. (3) VideoMAE shows that data quality is more important than data quantity for SSVP. Domain shift between pre-training and target datasets is an important factor. Notably, our VideoMAE with the vanilla ViT backbone can achieve 87.4% on Kinects-400, 75.4% on Something-Something V2, 91.3% on UCF101, and 62.6% on HMDB51, without using any extra data. Code is available at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/VideoMAE.

paragraphs: VideoMAE studies whether video transformers can learn useful representations without extra large-scale pretraining datasets. It uses self-supervised reconstruction: the model learns from videos by recovering hidden content. The proposed tube-masking design removes an unusually high fraction of the video, making reconstruction a demanding task that encourages useful representation learning.

Masking 90% to 95% of the input still produces favorable performance. The authors explain that video's temporal redundancy permits more aggressive masking than images. They also obtain strong results with roughly 3,000 to 4,000 videos and no extra data, attributing part of that effectiveness to reconstruction requiring the model to learn high-level structure.

The experiments additionally emphasize data quality and the mismatch between pretraining and target domains. Using a standard vision-transformer backbone, VideoMAE reports results across four video benchmarks without extra data. Taken together, the findings support highly masked reconstruction as a data-efficient pretraining strategy and show why the suitability of the training videos matters alongside their number.
summary.tldr: VideoMAE learns useful video representations by reconstructing inputs with 90–95% masking, achieving strong results even with small datasets.

title: VideoMAE: Masked Autoencoders are Data-Efficient Learners for Self-Supervised Video Pre-Training

abstract: Multi-label classification, which predicts a set of labels for an input, has many applications. However, multiple recent studies showed that multi-label classification is vulnerable to adversarial examples. In particular, an attacker can manipulate the labels predicted by a multi-label classifier for an input via adding carefully crafted, human-imperceptible perturbation to it. Existing provable defenses for multi-class classification achieve sub-optimal provable robustness guarantees when generalized to multi-label classification. In this work, we propose MultiGuard, the first provably robust defense against adversarial examples to multi-label classification. Our MultiGuard leverages randomized smoothing, which is the state-of-the-art technique to build provably robust classifiers. Specifically, given an arbitrary multi-label classifier, our MultiGuard builds a smoothed multi-label classifier via adding random noise to the input. We consider isotropic Gaussian noise in this work. Our major theoretical contribution is that we show a certain number of ground truth labels of an input are provably in the set of labels predicted by our MultiGuard when the $\ell_2$-norm of the adversarial perturbation added to the input is bounded. Moreover, we design an algorithm to compute our provable robustness guarantees. Empirically, we evaluate our MultiGuard on VOC 2007, MS-COCO, and NUS-WIDE benchmark datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/quwenjie/MultiGuard

paragraphs: Multi-label classification predicts a set of labels for each input. Carefully chosen, visually imperceptible changes can manipulate that set. The paper argues that adapting existing provable defenses from multiclass classification produces suboptimal guarantees for this setting and introduces MultiGuard to address the multi-label problem directly.

MultiGuard wraps an arbitrary multi-label classifier with randomized smoothing, using isotropic Gaussian noise on the input. Its main theorem guarantees that a certain number of an input's true labels remain in the predicted set when the adversarial perturbation has bounded Euclidean, or l2, norm. This expresses protection in terms of retained correct labels.

The authors also provide an algorithm for computing the robustness guarantees and evaluate the method on VOC 2007, MS-COCO, and NUS-WIDE. The guarantee is specifically about how many true labels remain present within the permitted perturbation size; it does not assert that every predicted label is unchanged. That formulation makes the certificate directly relevant to predictions that can contain multiple simultaneous labels.
summary.tldr: MultiGuard certifies that a certain number of true labels survive adversarial perturbations with bounded l2 norm.

title: MultiGuard: Provably Robust Multi-label Classification against Adversarial Examples

abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is an imaging modality that provides unique insights into the dynamics of proteins and other building blocks of life. The algorithmic challenge of jointly estimating the poses, 3D structure, and conformational heterogeneity of a biomolecule from millions of noisy and randomly oriented 2D projections in a computationally efficient manner, however, remains unsolved. Our method, cryoFIRE, performs ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction with unknown poses in an amortized framework, thereby avoiding the computationally expensive step of pose search while enabling the analysis of conformational heterogeneity. Poses and conformation are jointly estimated by an encoder while a physics-based decoder aggregates the images into an implicit neural representation of the conformational space. We show that our method can provide one order of magnitude speedup on datasets containing millions of images, without any loss of accuracy. We validate that the joint estimation of poses and conformations can be amortized over the size of the dataset. For the first time, we prove that an amortized method can extract interpretable dynamic information from experimental datasets.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy produces noisy two-dimensional views of biomolecules in many unknown orientations. Reconstructing a molecule requires working out both how each image is oriented and what three-dimensional structure it depicts. When molecules also change conformation, the reconstruction must distinguish those structural changes from differences caused by viewing direction.

cryoFIRE tackles these unknowns together. An encoder estimates each image’s pose and conformation, while a decoder based on imaging physics combines the observations into an implicit neural representation of conformational variation. The approach is amortized: a shared inference model estimates these quantities across the dataset, avoiding an expensive pose-search step for individual images. It supports reconstruction from scratch with unknown poses.

The authors report that this approach can deliver an order-of-magnitude speedup on datasets containing millions of images without losing accuracy. They also demonstrate that jointly estimating pose and conformation can be amortized across the dataset, and that the resulting method extracts interpretable information about molecular dynamics from experimental data. The contribution therefore connects computational efficiency with recovering meaningful structural variation.
summary.tldr: cryoFIRE jointly estimates molecular poses and conformations with shared neural inference, enabling faster heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction.

title: Amortized Inference for Heterogeneous Reconstruction in Cryo-EM

abstract: In this paper, we address monocular depth estimation with deep neural networks. To enable training of deep monocular estimation models with various sources of datasets, state-of-the-art methods adopt image-level normalization strategies to generate affine-invariant depth representations. However, learning with the image-level normalization mainly emphasizes the relations of pixel representations with the global statistic in the images, such as the structure of the scene, while the fine-grained depth difference may be overlooked. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-scale depth normalization method that hierarchically normalizes the depth representations based on spatial information and depth distributions. Compared with previous normalization strategies applied only at the holistic image level, the proposed hierarchical normalization can effectively preserve the fine-grained details and improve accuracy. We present two strategies that define the hierarchical normalization contexts in the depth domain and the spatial domain, respectively. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed normalization strategy remarkably outperforms previous normalization methods, and we set new state-of-the-art on five zero-shot transfer benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single image becomes more challenging when training data come from different sources. Existing approaches use image-level normalization to make depth representations insensitive to changes in overall scale and offset. The paper argues that this emphasizes relationships to whole-image statistics, such as scene structure, while potentially overlooking small depth differences.

The proposed method normalizes depth representations hierarchically at multiple scales. It defines normalization contexts in two ways: through spatial information and through the distribution of depth values. This gives the learning process more localized reference contexts than a single statistic for the entire image, helping preserve fine-grained depth structure.

Experiments show improved accuracy and better retention of detail compared with previous normalization strategies. The authors report state-of-the-art results on five zero-shot transfer benchmark datasets. Those results make the normalization choice relevant beyond fitting a training source: in the reported evaluations, the learned models also transfer effectively to new datasets. The contribution centers on how depth targets are normalized to support both broad structure and finer differences.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical depth normalization preserves finer depth differences and improves single-image depth estimation across five zero-shot transfer benchmarks.

title: Hierarchical Normalization for Robust Monocular Depth Estimation

abstract: The receptive field (RF), which determines the region of time series to be “seen” and used, is critical to improve the performance for time series classification (TSC). However, the variation of signal scales across and within time series data, makes it challenging to decide on proper RF sizes for TSC. In this paper, we propose a dynamic sparse network (DSN) with sparse connections for TSC, which can learn to cover various RF without cumbersome hyper-parameters tuning. The kernels in each sparse layer are sparse and can be explored under the constraint regions by dynamic sparse training, which makes it possible to reduce the resource cost. The experimental results show that the proposed DSN model can achieve state-of-art performance on both univariate and multivariate TSC datasets with less than 50% computational cost compared with recent baseline methods, opening the path towards more accurate resource-aware methods for time series analyses. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/QiaoXiao7282/DSN.

The kernels in each sparse layer are sparse and can be explored under the constraint regions by dynamic sparse training, which makes it possible to reduce the resource cost. The experimental results show that the proposed DSN model can achieve state-of-art performance on both univariate and multivariate TSC datasets with less than 50% computational cost compared with recent baseline methods, opening the path towards more accurate resource-aware methods for time series analyses. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/QiaoXiao7282/DSN.

paragraphs: A time-series classifier must decide how much of a signal to consider when recognizing a pattern. This span is its receptive field. Choosing an appropriate span is difficult because useful patterns can occur at different scales, both across examples and within one signal. A manually chosen receptive field can therefore be an awkward fit for varied data.

The paper proposes a dynamic sparse network that learns connections covering different receptive fields. Its layers use sparse kernels, and dynamic sparse training explores their connections within constrained regions. This makes the choice of what parts of the signal to use part of training, reducing the need for cumbersome receptive-field hyperparameter tuning while creating opportunities to reduce resource use.

Experiments report state-of-the-art classification performance on both single-variable and multiple-variable time-series datasets. The reported computational cost is less than half that of recent baseline methods. These results suggest that sparse, adaptable connections can support both accuracy and efficiency in the evaluated tasks, rather than requiring dense computation to capture patterns at multiple scales.
summary.tldr: A dynamic sparse network learns which signal spans to use, achieving reported state-of-the-art time-series classification with less than half the baseline computational cost.

title: Dynamic Sparse Network for Time Series Classification: Learning What to “See”

abstract: The support/query episodic training strategy has been widely applied in modern meta learning algorithms. Supposing the $n$ training episodes and the test episodes are sampled independently from the same environment, previous work has derived a generalization bound of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ for smooth non-convex functions via algorithmic stability analysis. In this paper, we provide fine-grained analysis of stability and generalization for modern meta learning algorithms by considering more general situations. Firstly, we develop matching lower and upper stability bounds for meta learning algorithms with two types of loss functions: (1) nonsmooth convex functions with $\alpha$-H{\"o}lder continuous subgradients $(\alpha \in [0,1))$; (2) smooth (including convex and non-convex) functions. Our tight stability bounds show that, in the nonsmooth convex case, meta learning algorithms can be inherently less stable than in the smooth convex case. For the smooth non-convex functions, our stability bound is sharper than the existing one, especially in the setting where the number of iterations is larger than the number $n$ of training episodes. Secondly, we derive improved generalization bounds for meta learning algorithms that hold with high probability. Specifically, we first demonstrate that, under the independent episode environment assumption, the generalization bound of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ via algorithmic stability analysis is near optimal. To attain faster convergence rate, we show how to yield a deformed generalization bound of $O(\ln{n}/n)$ with the curvature condition of loss functions. Finally, we obtain a generalization bound for meta learning with dependent episodes whose dependency relation is characterized by a graph. Experiments on regression problems are conducted to verify our theoretical results.

Earlier analysis assumed independently sampled training and test episodes from the same environment and obtained generalization bounds scaling as one over the square root of the number of training episodes.

The bounds show that nonsmooth convex problems can be inherently less stable than smooth convex ones. For smooth nonconvex losses, the analysis improves existing stability bounds, particularly when training iterations outnumber training episodes.

With an additional curvature condition, a deformed generalization bound achieves a faster logarithmic-over-linear rate. The analysis further covers episodes whose dependencies are represented by a graph, and regression experiments support the theoretical results.
summary.tldr: Sharper stability bounds explain how loss smoothness, curvature, and episode dependence affect meta-learning generalization.

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Stability and Generalization for Modern Meta Learning Algorithms

abstract: Variational quantum circuits have been widely employed in quantum simulation and quantum machine learning in recent years. However, quantum circuits with random structures have poor trainability due to the exponentially vanishing gradient with respect to the circuit depth and the qubit number. This result leads to a general standpoint that deep quantum circuits would not be feasible for practical tasks. In this work, we propose an initialization strategy with theoretical guarantees for the vanishing gradient problem in general deep quantum circuits. Specifically, we prove that under proper Gaussian initialized parameters, the norm of the gradient decays at most polynomially when the qubit number and the circuit depth increase. Our theoretical results hold for both the local and the global observable cases, where the latter was believed to have vanishing gradients even for very shallow circuits. Experimental results verify our theoretical findings in quantum simulation and quantum chemistry.

paragraphs: Variational quantum circuits learn by adjusting circuit parameters, but this becomes difficult when the gradients guiding those adjustments become extremely small. The paper addresses the barren plateau problem, in which gradients can shrink exponentially as circuit depth and the number of qubits increase. This behavior has contributed to doubts about the practical trainability of deep quantum circuits.

The authors propose initializing the parameters with appropriately chosen Gaussian distributions. Under this initialization, they prove that the gradient norm decreases at most polynomially as depth and qubit count grow. The choice of initialization is therefore central to the guarantee: the result does not say that arbitrary random initial parameters avoid exponentially small gradients.

The theory covers both local and global observables, including the global case previously believed to suffer vanishing gradients even in very shallow circuits. Experiments in quantum simulation and quantum chemistry support the theoretical findings. The contribution challenges the idea that depth itself makes these circuits impractical by showing that a suitable starting parameter distribution can substantially change how the gradient scales.
summary.tldr: Proper Gaussian initialization provably prevents gradient norms from decaying faster than polynomially as quantum circuits become deeper and contain more qubits.

title: Escaping from the Barren Plateau via Gaussian Initializations in Deep Variational Quantum Circuits

abstract: We propose an adaptive variance-reduction method, called AdaSpider, for minimization of $L$-smooth, non-convex functions with a finite-sum structure. In essence, AdaSpider combines an AdaGrad-inspired (Duchi et al., 2011), but a fairly distinct, adaptive step-size schedule with the recursive \textit{stochastic path integrated estimator} proposed in (Fang et al., 2018). To our knowledge, AdaSpider is the first parameter-free non-convex variance-reduction method in the sense that it does not require the knowledge of problem-dependent parameters, such as smoothness constant $L$, target accuracy $\epsilon$ or any bound on gradient norms. In doing so, we are able to compute an $\epsilon$-stationary point with $\tilde{O}\left(n + \sqrt{n}/\epsilon^2\right)$ oracle-calls, which matches the respective lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: AdaSpider addresses optimization problems whose objective is a finite sum of smooth, potentially non-convex functions. Such problems require deciding both how to estimate useful gradients and how far to move at each step. The paper combines an adaptive step-size rule inspired by AdaGrad with a recursive stochastic gradient estimator designed to reduce variance.

The main contribution is that this combination does not require advance knowledge of several problem-dependent quantities. These include the smoothness constant, the desired accuracy, and bounds on gradient magnitudes. The authors describe AdaSpider as the first non-convex variance-reduction method to be parameter-free in this particular sense. Its step-size schedule is inspired by, but substantially different from, AdaGrad's.

For a sum with n terms, the method reaches an epsilon-stationary point using roughly n plus square root of n divided by epsilon squared oracle calls, apart from logarithmic factors. A stationary-point guarantee concerns making the gradient small rather than finding a global minimum. The stated complexity matches the relevant lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that this adaptivity preserves a strong theoretical efficiency guarantee.
summary.tldr: AdaSpider combines adaptive steps and variance reduction to reach approximate stationary points with near-optimal oracle complexity without knowing key problem parameters.

title: Adaptive Stochastic Variance Reduction for Non-convex Finite-Sum Minimization

abstract: High model performance, on average, can hide that models may systematically underperform on subgroups of the data. We consider the tabular setting, which surfaces the unique issue of outcome heterogeneity - this is prevalent in areas such as healthcare, where patients with similar features can have different outcomes, thus making reliable predictions challenging. To tackle this, we propose Data-IQ, a framework to systematically stratify examples into subgroups with respect to their outcomes. We do this by analyzing the behavior of individual examples during training, based on their predictive confidence and, importantly, the aleatoric (data) uncertainty. Capturing the aleatoric uncertainty permits a principled characterization and then subsequent stratification of data examples into three distinct subgroups (Easy, Ambiguous, Hard). We experimentally demonstrate the benefits of Data-IQ on four real-world medical datasets. We show that Data-IQ's characterization of examples is most robust to variation across similarly performant (yet different models), compared to baselines. Since Data-IQ can be used with any ML model (including neural networks, gradient boosting etc.), this property ensures consistency of data characterization, while allowing flexible model selection. Taking this a step further, we demonstrate that the subgroups enable us to construct new approaches to both feature acquisition and dataset selection. Furthermore, we highlight how the subgroups can inform reliable model usage, noting the significant impact of the Ambiguous subgroup on model generalization.

paragraphs: Data-IQ examines a problem hidden by average prediction scores: a model can perform well overall while struggling systematically on particular examples. In tabular data, people or cases with similar recorded features can have different outcomes. This outcome heterogeneity makes it useful to distinguish difficult prediction problems from examples whose outcomes are inherently ambiguous given the available data.

The framework tracks individual examples during training, using predictive confidence alongside aleatoric uncertainty, meaning uncertainty associated with the data. It uses these signals to organize examples into Easy, Ambiguous, and Hard groups. The method is designed to work with different kinds of machine-learning models, including neural networks and gradient boosting.

Their findings highlight the Ambiguous group as consequential for generalization, making the grouping useful for understanding where and how a model can be used reliably.
summary.tldr: Data-IQ uses training behavior and data uncertainty to group tabular examples and reveal differences hidden by average model performance.

title: Data-IQ: Characterizing subgroups with heterogeneous outcomes in tabular data

abstract: Differentiable simulations of optical systems can be combined with deep learning-based reconstruction networks to enable high performance computational imaging via end-to-end (E2E) optimization of both the optical encoder and the deep decoder. This has enabled imaging applications such as 3D localization microscopy, depth estimation, and lensless photography via the optimization of local optical encoders. More challenging computational imaging applications, such as 3D snapshot microscopy which compresses 3D volumes into single 2D images, require a highly non-local optical encoder. We show that existing deep network decoders have a locality bias which prevents the optimization of such highly non-local optical encoders. We address this with a decoder based on a shallow neural network architecture using global kernel Fourier convolutional neural networks (FourierNets). We show that FourierNets surpass existing deep network based decoders at reconstructing photographs captured by the highly non-local DiffuserCam optical encoder. Further, we show that FourierNets enable E2E optimization of highly non-local optical encoders for 3D snapshot microscopy. By combining FourierNets with a large-scale multi-GPU differentiable optical simulation, we are able to optimize non-local optical encoders 170$\times$ to 7372$\times$ larger than prior state of the art, and demonstrate the potential for ROI-type specific optical encoding with a programmable microscope.

paragraphs: Computational imaging can jointly optimize an optical system and a neural network that reconstructs images from its measurements. Some applications require optical encoders that mix information across distant locations. The paper identifies a locality bias in existing deep decoders that prevents effective optimization of these highly non-local encoders, including those needed to compress a 3D volume into one 2D image.

The authors introduce FourierNets, shallow reconstruction networks using global-kernel Fourier convolutions. Their broad spatial operations address the mismatch between non-local optical measurements and locally biased decoders. FourierNets outperform existing deep-network decoders when reconstructing photographs captured with the highly non-local DiffuserCam encoder.

The method also enables joint optimization of non-local encoders for 3D snapshot microscopy. Combined with a large, multi-GPU differentiable optical simulation, it supports encoders reported to be 170 to 7,372 times larger than prior state of the art. The results connect decoder design to which optical systems can be optimized.
summary.tldr: FourierNets use global convolutions to reconstruct non-local optical measurements and enable optimization of much larger computational-imaging encoders.

title: FourierNets enable the design of highly non-local optical encoders for computational imaging

abstract: Effective exploration is a challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Novelty-based exploration methods can suffer in high-dimensional state spaces, such as continuous partially-observable 3D environments. We address this challenge by defining novelty using semantically meaningful state abstractions, which can be found in learned representations shaped by natural language. In particular, we evaluate vision-language representations, pretrained on natural image captioning datasets. We show that these pretrained representations drive meaningful, task-relevant exploration and improve performance on 3D simulated environments. We also characterize why and how language provides useful abstractions for exploration by considering the impacts of using representations from a pretrained model, a language oracle, and several ablations. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach with on- and off-policy RL algorithms and in two very different task domains---one that stresses the identification and manipulation of everyday objects, and one that requires navigational exploration in an expansive world. Our results suggest that using language-shaped representations could improve exploration for various algorithms and agents in challenging environments.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning often rewards encountering novel states, but novelty is difficult to define in complex visual environments. This paper measures novelty using semantically meaningful abstractions shaped by natural language. The approach uses pretrained vision-language representations to describe states in terms that can be more relevant to the task.

The representations come from models pretrained on natural image-captioning datasets. The authors show that they guide meaningful exploration and improve performance in simulated 3D environments. They investigate language's contribution by comparing pretrained representations, a language oracle, and several ablations, aiming to understand how the abstraction influences exploration behavior.

The evaluation includes both on-policy and off-policy reinforcement-learning algorithms and two distinct task domains. One emphasizes recognizing and manipulating everyday objects; the other requires navigation through a large world. Results across these settings suggest that language-shaped representations could benefit different algorithms and agents. The broader implication remains a possibility supported by these experiments, while the demonstrated gains concern the tested simulated environments.
summary.tldr: Pretrained language-shaped visual representations make novelty more task-relevant and improve exploration in tested 3D reinforcement-learning environments.

title: Semantic Exploration from Language Abstractions and Pretrained Representations

abstract: The dominant paradigm for neural text generation nowadays is seq2seq learning with large-scale pretrained language models. However, it is usually difficult to manually constrain the generation process of these models. Prior studies have introduced Lexically Constrained Decoding (LCD) to ensure the presence of pre-specified words or phrases in the output. However, simply applying lexical constraints has no guarantee of the grammatical or semantic relations between words. Thus, more elaborate constraints are needed. To this end, we first propose a new constrained decoding scenario named Relation-Constrained Decoding (RCD), which requires the model's output to contain several given word pairs with respect to the given relations between them. For this scenario, we present a novel plug-and-play decoding algorithm named RElation-guided probability Surgery and bEam ALlocation (RESEAL), which can handle different categories of relations, e.g., syntactical relations or factual relations. Moreover, RESEAL can adaptively "reseal" the relations to form a high-quality sentence, which can be applied to the inference stage of any autoregressive text generation model. To evaluate our method, we first construct an RCD benchmark based on dependency relations from treebanks with annotated dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can achieve better preservation of the input dependency relations compared to previous methods. To further illustrate the effectiveness of RESEAL, we apply our method to three downstream tasks: sentence summarization, fact-based text editing, and data-to-text generation. We observe an improvement in generation quality. The source code is available at https://github.com/CasparSwift/RESEAL.

paragraphs: Requiring generated text to contain particular words does not ensure that those words express the intended relationship. A sentence can include all requested terms while getting its grammar or facts wrong. The paper introduces relation-constrained decoding, where output must contain specified word pairs connected by specified relations.

Its RESEAL algorithm guides generation through probability adjustments and beam allocation. It can handle different kinds of relations, including syntactic and factual ones, and adaptively assembles those relations into a sentence. The method is designed as a plug-and-play addition at inference time for autoregressive text generators.

The authors build a benchmark from treebanks with annotated grammatical dependencies and show better preservation of input dependency relations than previous methods. They also apply RESEAL to summarization, fact-based text editing, and data-to-text generation, reporting improved generation quality. These results support making relationships explicit in decoding, so that control concerns how requested words connect as well as whether they appear.
summary.tldr: RESEAL guides autoregressive text generation to preserve specified relationships between words, improving relation preservation and quality in evaluated tasks.

title: Relation-Constrained Decoding for Text Generation

abstract: Continual learning is an emerging paradigm in machine learning, wherein a model is exposed in an online fashion to data from multiple different distributions (i.e. environments), and is expected to adapt to the distribution change. Precisely, the goal is to perform well in the new environment, while simultaneously retaining the performance on the previous environments (i.e. avoid ``catastrophic forgetting'').While this setup has enjoyed a lot of attention in the applied community, there hasn't be theoretical work that even formalizes the desired guarantees. In this paper, we propose a framework for continual learning through the framework of feature extraction---namely, one in which features, as well as a classifier, are being trained with each environment. When the features are linear, we design an efficient gradient-based algorithm $\mathsf{DPGrad}$, that is guaranteed to perform well on the current environment, as well as avoid catastrophic forgetting. In the general case, when the features are non-linear, we show such an algorithm cannot exist, whether efficient or not.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to adapt as data arrives from different environments while retaining performance on earlier ones. These two demands can conflict: learning the current environment may erase useful earlier behavior. This paper gives a theoretical framework for expressing both goals through feature extraction.

In the framework, learning each environment updates both a feature representation and a classifier. For linear features, the authors introduce DPGrad, an efficient gradient-based algorithm. Within their formalization, it comes with guarantees for performing well in the current environment while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. The contribution is therefore a defined learning setup together with an algorithm that satisfies its requirements.

The nonlinear case exposes a fundamental obstruction. For the general setting with nonlinear features, the authors show that an algorithm providing the same guarantees cannot exist, even without a computational-efficiency requirement. This separates an efficiently solvable linear case from a general impossibility result. The distinction concerns the paper’s formal guarantees; it does not claim that every practical use of nonlinear continual learning must fail.
summary.tldr: A feature-extraction framework yields a guaranteed continual-learning algorithm for linear features and an impossibility result for the general nonlinear case.

title: Continual learning: a feature extraction formalization, an efficient algorithm, and fundamental obstructions

abstract: Recovering a skeletal shape from a monocular video is a longstanding challenge. Prevailing nonrigid animal reconstruction methods often adopt a control-point driven animation model and optimize bone transforms individually without considering skeletal topology, yielding unsatisfactory shape and articulation. In contrast, humans can easily infer the articulation structure of an unknown character by associating it with a seen articulated object in their memory. Inspired by this fact, we present CASA, a novel category-agnostic articulated animal reconstruction method. Our method consists of two components, a video-to-shape retrieval process and a neural inverse graphics framework. During inference, CASA first finds a matched articulated shape from a 3D character assets bank so that the input video scores highly with the rendered image, according to a pretrained image-language model. It then integrates the retrieved character into an inverse graphics framework and jointly infers the shape deformation, skeleton structure, and skinning weights through optimization. Experiments validate the efficacy of our method in shape reconstruction and articulation. We further show that we can use the resulting skeletal-animated character for re-animation.

Inspired by this fact, we present CASA, a novel category-agnostic articulated animal reconstruction method. Our method consists of two components, a video-to-shape retrieval process and a neural inverse graphics framework. paragraphs: Recovering an animal’s three-dimensional shape and movable skeleton from a single-camera video requires understanding how its parts connect and move. The paper argues that optimizing individual bone transformations without considering their connections can produce poor shape and articulation. CASA instead begins with an existing articulated character that provides useful structural information.

Its first stage searches a bank of three-dimensional character assets. A pretrained image-language model scores how well rendered views of candidate characters match the input video. The retrieved character then enters a neural inverse-graphics framework, which works backward from observed images to estimate the underlying animated model.

Within this framework, CASA jointly optimizes shape deformation, skeletal structure, and skinning weights—the quantities that determine how the surface follows the skeleton. This couples appearance and articulation instead of treating bone movements independently. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness for shape reconstruction and articulation, and the authors demonstrate re-animation of the reconstructed character. The output can therefore serve as a movable character, beyond representing the observed shape.
summary.tldr: CASA retrieves an articulated character and jointly adapts its shape and skeleton to reconstruct a re-animatable animal from video.

title: CASA: Category-agnostic Skeletal Animal Reconstruction

abstract: Deep and wide neural networks successfully fit very complex functions today, but dense models are starting to be prohibitively expensive for inference. To mitigate this, one promising research direction is networks that activate a sparse subgraph of the network. The subgraph is chosen by a data-dependent routing function, enforcing a fixed mapping of inputs to subnetworks (e.g., the Mixture of Experts (MoE) paradigm in Switch Transformers). However, there is no theoretical grounding for these sparsely activated models. As our first contribution, we present a formal model of data-dependent sparse networks that captures salient aspects of popular architectures. Then, we show how to construct sparse networks that provably match the approximation power and total size of dense networks on Lipschitz functions. The sparse networks use much fewer inference operations than dense networks, leading to a faster forward pass. The key idea is to use locality sensitive hashing on the input vectors and then interpolate the function in subregions of the input space. This offers a theoretical insight into why sparse networks work well in practice. Finally, we present empirical findings that support our theory; compared to dense networks, sparse networks give a favorable trade-off between number of active units and approximation quality.
originalAbstract: Deep and wide neural networks successfully fit very complex functions today, but dense models are starting to be prohibitively expensive for inference. To mitigate this, one promising research direction is networks that activate a sparse subgraph of the network. The subgraph is chosen by a data-dependent routing function, enforcing a fixed mapping of inputs to subnetworks (e.g., the Mixture of Experts (MoE) paradigm in Switch Transformers). However, there is no theoretical grounding for these sparsely activated models. As our first contribution, we present a formal model of data-dependent sparse networks that captures salient aspects of popular architectures. Then, we show how to construct sparse networks that provably match the approximation power and total size of dense networks on Lipschitz functions. The sparse networks use much fewer inference operations than dense networks, leading to a faster forward pass. The key idea is to use locality sensitive hashing on the input vectors and then interpolate the function in subregions of the input space. This offers a theoretical insight into why sparse networks work well in practice. Finally, we present empirical findings that support our theory; compared to dense networks, sparse networks give a favorable trade-off between number of active units and approximation quality.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can represent complicated functions, but evaluating every part of a dense network can make inference expensive. Sparsely activated networks address this by routing each input through only part of the model. This paper develops a formal description of that arrangement, capturing important features of architectures in which the input determines which subnetwork is used.

The main theoretical result is a construction of sparse networks that match dense networks in approximation power and total size for Lipschitz functions, whose outputs change at a bounded rate as inputs change. These sparse constructions require substantially fewer operations during inference. The central technique uses locality sensitive hashing to organize inputs, followed by interpolation within different parts of the input space.

This distinguishes the total capacity a network stores from the amount of computation it uses for one prediction. The result supplies a theoretical explanation for how sparse activation can preserve approximation quality while reducing active computation. Experiments support this account by showing a favorable balance between the number of active units and approximation quality.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs sparse networks that match dense-network approximation power for Lipschitz functions while using fewer inference operations.

title: A Theoretical View on Sparsely Activated Networks

abstract: We propose a model-based reinforcement learning framework to derive untargeted poisoning attacks against federated learning (FL) systems. Our framework first approximates the distribution of the clients' aggregated data using model updates from the server. The learned distribution is then used to build a simulator of the FL environment, which is utilized to learn an adaptive attack policy through reinforcement learning. Our framework is capable of learning strong attacks automatically even when the server adopts a robust aggregation rule. We further derive an upper bound on the attacker's performance loss due to inaccurate distribution estimation. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed attack framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art poisoning attacks. This indicates the importance of developing adaptive defenses for FL systems.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines contributions from multiple clients, creating opportunities for poisoned contributions to damage the learned model. This paper studies untargeted poisoning through a model-based reinforcement learning framework. Its central idea is to learn an adaptive attack policy using an approximation of the federated training environment.

The framework first estimates the distribution of the clients' combined data from server model updates. That estimated distribution supports a simulator in which reinforcement learning can train the attack policy. The authors report that the framework can automatically learn strong attacks even when the server uses a robust aggregation rule, indicating that adaptation can expose weaknesses in the evaluated defenses.

The paper also derives an upper bound on how much an attacker's performance can deteriorate because the estimated data distribution is inaccurate. Experiments on real-world datasets report significant improvements over leading poisoning attacks. Together, the analysis and experiments connect the quality of the simulated environment to attack effectiveness and motivate defenses that account for attackers learning and adapting to the federated system.
summary.tldr: A learned simulator enables reinforcement learning to produce adaptive federated-learning poisoning attacks that outperform evaluated alternatives.

title: Learning to Attack Federated Learning: A Model-based Reinforcement Learning Attack Framework

abstract: Explainable recommendation has attracted much attention from the industry and academic communities. It has shown great potential to improve the recommendation persuasiveness, informativeness and user satisfaction. In the past few years, while a lot of promising explainable recommender models have been proposed, the datasets used to evaluate them still suffer from several limitations, for example, the explanation ground truths are not labeled by the real users, the explanations are mostly single-modal and around only one aspect. To bridge these gaps, in this paper, we build a new explainable recommendation dataset, which, to our knowledge, is the first contribution that provides a large amount of real user labeled multi-modal and multi-aspect explaination ground truths. In specific, we firstly develop a video recommendation platform, where a series of questions around the recommendation explainability are carefully designed. Then, we recruit about 3000 high-quality labelers with different backgrounds to use the system, and collect their behaviors and feedback to our questions. In this paper, we detail the construction process of our dataset and also provide extensive analysis on its characteristics. In addition, we develop a library, where ten well-known explainable recommender models are implemented in a unified framework. Based on this library, we build several benchmarks for different explainable recommendation tasks. At last, we present many new opportunities brought by our dataset, which are expected to promote the field of explainable recommendation. Our dataset, library and the related documents have been released at https://reasoner2023.github.io/.

paragraphs: Evaluating recommendation explanations requires evidence about what users actually find explanatory. Existing datasets often lack labels from real users, cover only one type of explanation, or focus on a single aspect. REASONER addresses these gaps by collecting user-labeled explanation ground truths that span multiple modalities and aspects within a video-recommendation setting.

The researchers build a recommendation platform with carefully designed questions about explainability. Approximately 3,000 labelers from different backgrounds use the system, providing both behavioral data and answers to those questions. The paper describes how the dataset was constructed and analyzes its characteristics, making the collection process part of the contribution alongside the resulting data.

The project also implements ten established explainable-recommendation models in a unified library and uses them to build benchmarks for different explanation tasks. This supplies a shared basis for evaluating methods against the richer user feedback. The dataset, library, and documentation are released publicly. The contribution is evaluation infrastructure intended to advance explainable recommendation, rather than a demonstrated claim that explanations necessarily improve every user’s decisions.
summary.tldr: REASONER supplies real-user explanation labels across multiple modalities and aspects, alongside a shared library and recommendation benchmarks.

title: REASONER: An Explainable Recommendation Dataset with Comprehensive Labeling Ground Truths

abstract: Attaining a high degree of user controllability in visual generation often requires intricate, fine-grained inputs like layouts. However, such inputs impose a substantial burden on users when compared to simple text inputs. To address the issue, we study how Large Language Models (LLMs) can serve as visual planners by generating layouts from text conditions, and thus collaborate with visual generative models. We propose LayoutGPT, a method to compose in-context visual demonstrations in style sheet language to enhance visual planning skills of LLMs. We show that LayoutGPT can generate plausible layouts in multiple domains, ranging from 2D images to 3D indoor scenes. LayoutGPT also shows superior performance in converting challenging language concepts like numerical and spatial relations to layout arrangements for faithful text-to-image generation. When combined with a downstream image generation model, LayoutGPT outperforms text-to-image models/systems by 20-40\% and achieves comparable performance as human users in designing visual layouts for numerical and spatial correctness. Lastly, LayoutGPT achieves comparable performance to supervised methods in 3D indoor scene synthesis, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential in multiple visual domains.

paragraphs: Detailed layouts can give users substantial control over generated visuals, but specifying them requires more effort than writing a text description. LayoutGPT explores whether a large language model can take on this planning work. It translates textual conditions into layouts that can guide visual generation, connecting language-based requests with explicit spatial arrangements.

The method presents in-context visual demonstrations in a style sheet language to strengthen the language model's layout planning. It generates plausible arrangements for both two-dimensional images and three-dimensional indoor scenes. A central target is translating numerical and spatial language into arrangements that preserve the requested object counts and relationships.

Combined with an image-generation model, LayoutGPT reports a 20–40% improvement over compared text-to-image systems and performance comparable to human layout designers for numerical and spatial correctness. In three-dimensional indoor scene synthesis, it also performs comparably to supervised methods. These findings support using language models as visual planners, with an intermediate layout helping translate compositional requests into a form downstream generators can use.
summary.tldr: LayoutGPT turns text into visual layouts that improve numerical and spatial faithfulness in image and scene generation.

title: LayoutGPT: Compositional Visual Planning and Generation with Large Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models have revolutionized the image classification paradigm. Despite showing impressive zero-shot capabilities, a pre-defined set of categories, a.k.a. the vocabulary, is assumed at test time for composing the textual prompts. However, such assumption can be impractical when the semantic context is unknown and evolving. We thus formalize a novel task, termed as Vocabulary-free Image Classification (VIC), where we aim to assign to an input image a class that resides in an unconstrained language-induced semantic space, without the prerequisite of a known vocabulary. VIC is a challenging task as the semantic space is extremely large, containing millions of concepts, with hard-to-discriminate fine-grained categories. In this work, we first empirically verify that representing this semantic space by means of an external vision-language database is the most effective way to obtain semantically relevant content for classifying the image. We then propose Category Search from External Databases (CaSED), a method that exploits a pre-trained vision-language model and an external vision-language database to address VIC in a training-free manner. CaSED first extracts a set of candidate categories from captions retrieved from the database based on their semantic similarity to the image, and then assigns to the image the best matching candidate category according to the same vision-language model. Experiments on benchmark datasets validate that CaSED outperforms other complex vision-language frameworks, while being efficient with much fewer parameters, paving the way for future research in this direction.

paragraphs: Zero-shot image classifiers commonly still require a predefined list of categories at test time. That requirement becomes awkward when an image’s semantic context is unknown or changing. This paper introduces Vocabulary-free Image Classification, where the model must assign a category from a broad language-defined space without being given a known vocabulary.

The authors empirically identify an external vision-language database as the most effective way, among the approaches studied, to obtain relevant semantic content. Their training-free method, CaSED, retrieves captions that are semantically similar to the input image. It extracts candidate categories from those captions, then uses the same pretrained vision-language model to select the best-matching candidate.

This two-stage process makes an enormous category space manageable through image-relevant retrieval and selection. Benchmark experiments show CaSED outperforming other complex vision-language frameworks while using far fewer parameters and remaining efficient. The findings support database-assisted category discovery as a practical approach to classification when the category vocabulary is not supplied in advance.
summary.tldr: CaSED classifies images without a supplied category list by retrieving captions, extracting candidate labels, and ranking them without training.

title: Vocabulary-free Image Classification

abstract: Visual model-based RL methods typically encode image observations into low-dimensional representations in a manner that does not eliminate redundant information. This leaves them susceptible to spurious variations -- changes in task-irrelevant components such as background distractors or lighting conditions. In this paper, we propose a visual model-based RL method that learns a latent representation resilient to such spurious variations. Our training objective encourages the representation to be maximally predictive of dynamics and reward, while constraining the information flow from the observation to the latent representation. We demonstrate that this objective significantly bolsters the resilience of visual model-based RL methods to visual distractors, allowing them to operate in dynamic environments. We then show that while the learned encoder is able to operate in dynamic environments, it is not invariant under significant distribution shift. To address this, we propose a simple reward-free alignment procedure that enables test time adaptation of the encoder. This allows for quick adaptation to widely differing environments without having to relearn the dynamics and policy. Our effort is a step towards making model-based RL a practical and useful tool for dynamic, diverse domains and we show its effectiveness in simulation tasks with significant spurious variations.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement-learning systems can encode distracting details alongside information needed for action. Changes in backgrounds or lighting can then disrupt a learned model even when those details are irrelevant to the task. RePo addresses this by learning a compact representation designed to retain information useful for predicting dynamics and rewards.

Its objective encourages strong prediction while restricting information flowing from images into the latent representation. The reported results show substantially improved resilience to visual distractors in dynamic environments. The paper also identifies a remaining limit: the learned encoder is not invariant to substantial distribution shifts, so resistance to distractors does not eliminate the need for adaptation.

To handle larger shifts, RePo adds a reward-free alignment procedure that adapts the encoder at test time. This allows quick adjustment to substantially different environments without relearning the dynamics model or policy. Simulation results with significant irrelevant visual variation support the combined approach, linking selective representation learning with targeted adaptation when the visual environment changes.
summary.tldr: RePo limits irrelevant visual information in model-based reinforcement learning and adds reward-free encoder adaptation for larger distribution shifts.

title: RePo: Resilient Model-Based Reinforcement Learning by Regularizing Posterior Predictability

abstract: Existing point cloud based 3D detectors are designed for the particular scene, either indoor or outdoor ones. Because of the substantial differences in object distribution and point density within point clouds collected from various environments, coupled with the intricate nature of 3D metrics, there is still a lack of a unified network architecture that can accommodate diverse scenes. In this paper, we propose Uni3DETR, a unified 3D detector that addresses indoor and outdoor 3D detection within the same framework. Specifically, we employ the detection transformer with point-voxel interaction for object prediction, which leverages voxel features and points for cross-attention and behaves resistant to the discrepancies from data. We then propose the mixture of query points, which sufficiently exploits global information for dense small-range indoor scenes and local information for large-range sparse outdoor ones. Furthermore, our proposed decoupled IoU provides an easy-to-optimize training target for localization by disentangling the $xy$ and $z$ space. Extensive experiments validate that Uni3DETR exhibits excellent performance consistently on both indoor and outdoor 3D detection. In contrast to previous specialized detectors, which may perform well on some particular datasets but suffer a substantial degradation on different scenes, Uni3DETR demonstrates the strong generalization ability under heterogeneous conditions (Fig. 1).

paragraphs: Indoor and outdoor point clouds differ substantially in point density, spatial extent, and object distribution. These differences have encouraged specialized 3D detectors. Uni3DETR proposes one detection framework that accommodates both settings, aiming to maintain strong performance across heterogeneous scenes.

Its detection transformer combines points and voxel features through cross-attention for object prediction. A mixture of query points draws on global information for dense, small-range indoor scenes and local information for sparse, large-range outdoor scenes. The training objective also decouples intersection-over-union calculations across the horizontal xy plane and vertical z direction, providing an easier-to-optimize localization target.

Experiments report consistently strong indoor and outdoor detection performance and strong generalization under heterogeneous conditions. The authors contrast this behavior with specialized detectors that can degrade substantially when evaluated on different kinds of scenes. The stated contribution is architectural unity across those environments, supported by mechanisms that address feature interaction, query coverage, and the optimization of 3D localization.
summary.tldr: Uni3DETR unifies indoor and outdoor point-cloud detection through point-voxel attention, mixed query points, and a decoupled localization objective.

title: Uni3DETR: Unified 3D Detection Transformer

abstract: Modern successes of diffusion models in learning complex, high-dimensional data distributions are attributed, in part, to their capability to construct diffusion processes with analytic transition kernels and score functions. The tractability results in a simulation-free framework with stable regression losses, from which reversed, generative processes can be learned at scale. However, when data is confined to a constrained set as opposed to a standard Euclidean space, these desirable characteristics appear to be lost based on prior attempts. In this work, we propose Mirror Diffusion Models (MDM), a new class of diffusion models that generate data on convex constrained sets without losing any tractability. This is achieved by learning diffusion processes in a dual space constructed from a mirror map, which, crucially, is a standard Euclidean space. We derive efficient computation of mirror maps for popular constrained sets, such as simplices and $\ell_2$-balls, showing significantly improved performance of MDM over existing methods. For safety and privacy purposes, we also explore constrained sets as a new mechanism to embed invisible but quantitative information (i.e., watermarks) in generated data, for which MDM serves as a compelling approach. Our work brings new algorithmic opportunities for learning tractable diffusion on complex domains.

paragraphs: Diffusion models benefit from mathematical expressions that make their noise processes and training objectives tractable. Those advantages become harder to retain when generated data must remain inside a constrained set. This paper introduces Mirror Diffusion Models to handle convex constraints while preserving the tractability that makes ordinary diffusion training practical.

The method uses a mirror map to construct a dual space that is an ordinary Euclidean space. It learns the diffusion process there, enabling constrained generation through this alternative representation. The authors derive efficient ways to compute mirror maps for common constraint sets, including simplices and Euclidean balls, and report substantially improved performance over existing methods.

The paper also explores using constraints to embed invisible, quantitative information in generated data as watermarks. Mirror Diffusion Models provide a way to generate within the sets used for that purpose. This is presented as a potential mechanism for safety and privacy applications, alongside the main contribution of retaining manageable diffusion learning on convex constrained domains.
summary.tldr: Mirror Diffusion Models use a transformed Euclidean space to enable tractable generation under convex constraints, including explored watermarking applications.

title: Mirror Diffusion Models for Constrained and Watermarked Generation

abstract: The performance of deep learning models heavily relies on the quality of the training data. Inadequacies in the training data, such as corrupt input or noisy labels, can lead to the failure of model generalization. Recent studies propose repairing the model by identifying the training samples that contribute to the failure and removing their influence from the model. However, it is important to note that the identified data may contain both beneficial and detrimental information. Simply erasing the information of the identified data from the model can have a negative impact on its performance, especially when accurate data is mistakenly identified as detrimental and removed. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages the knowledge obtained from a retained clean set. Our method first identifies harmful data by utilizing the clean set, then separates the beneficial and detrimental information within the identified data. Finally, we utilize the extracted beneficial information to enhance the model's performance. Through empirical evaluations, we demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches in both identifying harmful data and rectifying model failures. Particularly in scenarios where identification is challenging and a significant amount of benign data is involved, our method improves performance while the baselines deteriorate due to the erroneous removal of beneficial information.

paragraphs: This paper addresses repairing neural networks trained on problematic data, such as corrupted inputs or noisy labels. Existing repair approaches identify harmful training examples and remove their influence. The authors point out that a flagged example may contain useful information as well as harmful information, and clean examples can also be flagged mistakenly.

Their method uses knowledge from a retained clean dataset to guide repair. It first identifies potentially harmful examples, then separates beneficial and detrimental information within them. The extracted beneficial information is used to improve the model. This makes the repair process sensitive to the information inside an example rather than treating identification as sufficient reason to erase its full contribution.

Empirical evaluations show improvements over baseline methods in both harmful-data identification and model repair. The advantage is especially clear when identification is difficult and many benign examples are implicated: the proposed method improves performance while baselines deteriorate after removing useful information. The findings support preserving valuable training signals during repair, with the retained clean set supplying the guiding knowledge.
summary.tldr: A clean-set-guided repair method separates useful and harmful information in flagged training data, improving repair while retaining beneficial signals.

title: Retaining Beneficial Information from Detrimental Data for Neural Network Repair

abstract: The offline reinforcement learning (RL) problem is often motivated by the need to learn data-driven decision policies in financial, legal and healthcare applications. However, the learned policy could retain sensitive information of individuals in the training data (e.g., treatment and outcome of patients), thus susceptible to various privacy risks. We design offline RL algorithms with differential privacy guarantees which provably prevent such risks. These algorithms also enjoy strong instance-dependent learning bounds under both tabular and linear Markov Decision Process (MDP) settings. Our theory and simulation suggest that the privacy guarantee comes at (almost) no drop in utility comparing to the non-private counterpart for a medium-size dataset.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns decision policies from previously collected data. In applications involving sensitive records, the resulting policy may retain information about individuals, including their treatments and outcomes. This paper addresses privacy at the level of the learning algorithm, so that producing a useful policy also comes with a formal privacy guarantee.

The authors design offline reinforcement-learning algorithms with differential privacy guarantees and establish learning bounds that depend on the particular problem instance. Their analysis covers both tabular Markov decision processes and linear Markov decision processes. These results connect the privacy protection to guarantees about how well the algorithms learn within the two settings studied.

The theory and simulations suggest that, for a medium-size dataset, the privacy guarantee can come with almost no reduction in utility relative to a non-private counterpart. This is a qualified finding about the analyzed and simulated settings, rather than a claim that privacy is always cost-free. Its significance is that formal privacy protection and useful offline policy learning can coexist with a small observed or predicted utility penalty.
summary.tldr: Differentially private offline-RL algorithms achieve instance-dependent learning guarantees, with theory and simulations suggesting almost no utility loss for medium-size datasets.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Differential Privacy

abstract: Recent work has shown that language models' (LMs) prompt-based learning capabilities make them well suited for automating data labeling in domains where manual annotation is expensive. The challenge is that while writing an initial prompt is cheap, improving a prompt is costly---practitioners often require significant labeled data in order to evaluate the impact of prompt modifications. Our work asks whether it is possible to improve prompt-based learning _without_ additional labeled data. We approach this problem by attempting to modify the predictions of a prompt, rather than the prompt itself. Our intuition is that accurate predictions should also be consistent: samples which are similar under some feature representation should receive the same prompt prediction. We propose Embroid, a method which computes multiple representations of a dataset under different embedding functions, and uses the consistency between the LM predictions for neighboring samples to identify mispredictions. Embroid then uses these neighborhoods to create additional predictions for each sample, and combines these predictions with a simple latent variable graphical model in order to generate a final corrected prediction. In addition to providing a theoretical analysis of Embroid, we conduct a rigorous empirical evaluation across six different LMs and up to 95 different tasks. We find that (1) Embroid substantially improves performance over original prompts (e.g., by an average of 7.3 points on GPT-JT), (2) also realizes improvements for more sophisticated prompting strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought), and (3) can be specialized to domains like law through the embedding functions.

We find that (1) Embroid substantially improves performance over original prompts (e.g., by an average of 7.3 points on GPT-JT), (2) also realizes improvements for more sophisticated prompting strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought), and (3) can be specialized to domains like law through the embedding functions.

paragraphs: Language models can label data from a prompt, but improving that prompt often requires labeled examples to judge whether a revision helped. Embroid approaches this cost from a different direction: it keeps the prompt and corrects its predictions without additional labeled data. Its guiding intuition is that samples with similar representations should receive consistent predictions.

The method embeds the dataset in several different representation spaces and examines predictions among neighboring samples. Disagreement within these neighborhoods helps identify possible mistakes. Embroid then creates additional predictions from neighborhood information and combines them with a latent-variable graphical model to produce a corrected label. Multiple embeddings provide several views of which samples should be treated as similar.

The paper includes theoretical analysis and evaluation across six language models and up to 95 tasks. It reports improvements over original prompts, including an average gain of 7.3 points for GPT-JT, and gains with more sophisticated prompting such as chain-of-thought. Domain-specific embeddings can also specialize the method, including for law. These findings support prediction consistency as a useful source of improvement without collecting extra labels.
summary.tldr: Embroid improves prompt-based classification without extra labels by combining predictions from neighborhoods in multiple embedding spaces.

title: Embroid: Unsupervised Prediction Smoothing Can Improve Few-Shot Classification

abstract: Recent Diffusion Transformers (i.e., DiT) have demonstrated their powerful effectiveness in generating high-quality 2D images. However, it is unclear how the Transformer architecture performs equally well in 3D shape generation, as previous 3D diffusion methods mostly adopted the U-Net architecture. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel Diffusion Transformer for 3D shape generation, named DiT-3D, which can directly operate the denoising process on voxelized point clouds using plain Transformers. Compared to existing U-Net approaches, our DiT-3D is more scalable in model size and produces much higher quality generations.Specifically, the DiT-3D adopts the design philosophy of DiT but modifies it by incorporating 3D positional and patch embeddings to aggregate input from voxelized point clouds.To reduce the computational cost of self-attention in 3D shape generation, we incorporate 3D window attention into Transformer blocks, as the increased 3D token length resulting from the additional dimension of voxels can lead to high computation.Finally, linear and devoxelization layers are used to predict the denoised point clouds. In addition, we empirically observe that the pre-trained DiT-2D checkpoint on ImageNet can significantly improve DiT-3D on ShapeNet.Experimental results on the ShapeNet dataset demonstrate that the proposed DiT-3D achieves state-of-the-art performance in high-fidelity and diverse 3D point cloud generation.

paragraphs: DiT-3D investigates whether the Transformer architecture used successfully in two-dimensional diffusion generation can also generate high-quality three-dimensional shapes. Earlier 3D diffusion approaches mainly used U-Nets. The proposed model instead performs denoising directly on voxelized point clouds using plain Transformers.

The architecture adapts the DiT design with three-dimensional positional and patch embeddings to organize the voxelized input. Because the additional spatial dimension creates longer token sequences, it uses 3D window attention to reduce the cost of self-attention. Linear and devoxelization layers then produce predictions of the denoised point clouds. These changes make the Transformer design applicable to the structure and computational demands of 3D inputs.

The authors report better model-size scalability and much higher generation quality than existing U-Net approaches. On ShapeNet, DiT-3D achieves state-of-the-art results for high-fidelity, diverse point cloud generation. They also empirically find that initializing from a DiT-2D checkpoint pretrained on ImageNet significantly improves performance on ShapeNet, showing useful transfer from two-dimensional pretraining in this setting.
summary.tldr: DiT-3D adapts diffusion Transformers to voxelized point clouds and achieves strong 3D generation results, aided by 2D pretraining.

title: DiT-3D: Exploring Plain Diffusion Transformers for 3D Shape Generation

abstract: Scaling hyperparameter optimisation to very large datasets remains an open problem in the Gaussian process community. This paper focuses on iterative methods, which use linear system solvers, like conjugate gradients, alternating projections or stochastic gradient descent, to construct an estimate of the marginal likelihood gradient. We discuss three key improvements which are applicable across solvers: (i) a pathwise gradient estimator, which reduces the required number of solver iterations and amortises the computational cost of making predictions, (ii) warm starting linear system solvers with the solution from the previous step, which leads to faster solver convergence at the cost of negligible bias, (iii) early stopping linear system solvers after a limited computational budget, which synergises with warm starting, allowing solver progress to accumulate over multiple marginal likelihood steps. These techniques provide speed-ups of up to $72\times$ when solving to tolerance, and decrease the average residual norm by up to $7\times$ when stopping early.
