paragraphs: Training Gaussian-process hyperparameters on very large datasets can require expensive repeated linear-system solves. Iterative approaches use solvers such as conjugate gradients, alternating projections, or stochastic gradient descent to estimate the marginal-likelihood gradient. This paper proposes three improvements that apply across these solvers and make better use of computation during hyperparameter optimization.

First, a pathwise gradient estimator reduces the number of solver iterations needed and spreads out the computational cost of prediction. Second, warm starting uses the previous optimization step's solution as the next solver's starting point. This accelerates convergence with a reported negligible bias. Third, early stopping limits the computation spent on each solve.

Warm starting and early stopping reinforce each other: progress from a partially completed solve can carry into later marginal-likelihood steps. The reported techniques deliver speedups of up to 72 times when solving to a specified tolerance and reduce average residual norm by up to seven times when stopping early. These are maximum reported gains, demonstrating the potential value of carrying solver progress across optimization steps.
summary.tldr: A pathwise estimator, warm starts, and early stopping accelerate iterative Gaussian-process hyperparameter optimization by reusing computational progress.

title: Improving Linear System Solvers for Hyperparameter Optimisation in Iterative Gaussian Processes

abstract: Cech Persistence diagrams (PDs) are topological descriptors routinely used to capture the geometry of complex datasets. They are commonly compared using the Wasserstein distances $\mathrm{OT}_p$; however, the extent to which PDs are stable with respect to these metrics remains poorly understood. We partially close this gap by focusing on the case where datasets are sampled on an $m$-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$. Under this manifold hypothesis, we show that convergence with respect to the $\mathrm{OT}_p$ metric happens exactly when $p>m$. We also provide improvements upon the bottleneck stability theorem in this case and prove new laws of large numbers for the total $\alpha$-persistence of PDs. Finally, we show how these theoretical findings shed new light on the behavior of the feature maps on the space of PDs that are used in ML-oriented applications of Topological Data Analysis.

paragraphs: Čech persistence diagrams summarize geometric and topological structure in data. They are often compared with Wasserstein distances, but understanding stability under those distances requires more than knowing that the diagrams are useful descriptors. This paper studies that issue when data are sampled from an m-dimensional submanifold of an ambient Euclidean space.

Under this manifold hypothesis, the authors establish that convergence in the Wasserstein metric OT_p occurs exactly when p exceeds m. The threshold therefore depends on the manifold's intrinsic dimension. This gives a precise condition for convergence in the studied setting, rather than a general stability assertion for every choice of metric exponent.

The paper also strengthens bottleneck stability results in this setting and proves laws of large numbers for total alpha-persistence, an aggregate summary of persistence. Finally, it connects these theoretical results to feature maps used in machine-learning applications of topological data analysis. Together, the findings clarify how sampling geometry influences both diagram comparison and representations built from diagrams.
summary.tldr: For the studied manifold sampling setting, Čech persistence diagrams converge in Wasserstein OT_p exactly when p exceeds the manifold dimension.

title: Wasserstein convergence of Cech persistence diagrams for samplings of submanifolds

abstract: Label Distribution Learning (LDL) has been extensively studied in IID data applications such as computer vision, thanks to its more generic setting over single-label and multi-label classification. This paper advances LDL into graph domains and aims to tackle a novel and fundamentalheterogeneous graph label distribution learning (HGDL) problem.We argue that the graph heterogeneity reflected on node types, node attributes, and neighborhood structures can impose significant challenges for generalizing LDL onto graphs. To address the challenges, we propose a new learning framework with two key components: 1) proactive graph topology homogenization, and 2) topology and content consistency-aware graph transformer. Specifically, the former learns optimal information aggregation between meta-paths, so that the nodeheterogeneity can be proactively addressed prior to the succeeding embedding learning; the latter leverages an attention mechanism to learn consistency between meta-path and node attributes, allowing network topology and nodal attributes to be equally emphasized during the label distribution learning. By using KL-divergence and additional constraints, \method~delivers an end-to-end solution for learning and predicting label distribution for nodes. Both theoretical and empirical studies substantiate the effectiveness of our HGDL approach.Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Listener-Watcher/HGDL.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how strongly several labels apply to an example, rather than assigning only one label or a set of labels. This paper brings that problem to heterogeneous graphs, where nodes can differ in type, attributes, and surrounding connections. Those differences complicate how information should be combined to predict a node's label distribution.

The proposed framework first learns how to aggregate information across meta-paths, which describe different patterns of connections through the graph. This topology homogenization addresses heterogeneity before node representations are learned. A graph transformer then uses attention to capture consistency between these structural patterns and node attributes, giving both topology and content a role in prediction.

Training combines KL divergence with additional constraints to learn the system end to end. The authors report theoretical and empirical support for the approach. Its central contribution is a framework that explicitly handles heterogeneous graph structure while preserving the richer prediction target of a distribution over labels.
summary.tldr: HGDL predicts label distributions on heterogeneous graphs by coordinating structural aggregation with attention to node attributes.

title: HGDL: Heterogeneous Graph Label Distribution Learning

abstract: Inferring the synaptic plasticity rules that govern learning in the brain is a key challenge in neuroscience. We present a novel computational method to infer these rules from experimental data, applicable to both neural and behavioral data. Our approach approximates plasticity rules using a parameterized function, employing either truncated Taylor series for theoretical interpretability or multilayer perceptrons. These plasticity parameters are optimized via gradient descent over entire trajectories to align closely with observed neural activity or behavioral learning dynamics. This method can uncover complex rules that induce long nonlinear time dependencies, particularly involving factors like postsynaptic activity and current synaptic weights. We validate our approach through simulations, successfully recovering established rules such as Oja's, as well as more intricate plasticity rules with reward-modulated terms. We assess the robustness of our technique to noise and apply it to behavioral data from \textit{Drosophila} in a probabilistic reward-learning experiment. Notably, our findings reveal an active forgetting component in reward learning in flies, improving predictive accuracy over previous models. This modeling framework offers a promising new avenue for elucidating the computational principles of synaptic plasticity and learning in the brain.

paragraphs: Synaptic plasticity rules describe how connections between neurons change during learning. This paper develops a method for inferring those rules from observed neural activity or behavior. The approach fits a model of the learning process to entire trajectories, making changes over time central to the inference.

The unknown rule is represented either by a truncated Taylor series, chosen for theoretical interpretability, or by a multilayer perceptron. Gradient descent adjusts its parameters so the modeled trajectory matches the observations. This allows the method to capture complex nonlinear dependencies involving postsynaptic activity, current connection weights, and effects that unfold over long periods.

In simulations, the method recovers established rules such as Oja's rule and more complex rules involving reward modulation. The authors also assess noise robustness and apply the approach to fruit-fly behavior in a probabilistic reward-learning experiment. That analysis identifies an active forgetting component and improves predictive accuracy over previous models, illustrating how fitting learning dynamics can reveal useful components of a plasticity model.
summary.tldr: Fitting parameterized plasticity rules to whole learning trajectories recovers simulated rules and identifies an active forgetting component in fruit-fly reward learning.

title: Model Based Inference of Synaptic Plasticity Rules

abstract: It is generally accepted that starting neural networks training with large learning rates (LRs) improves generalization. Following a line of research devoted to understanding this effect, we conduct an empirical study in a controlled setting focusing on two questions: 1) how large an initial LR is required for obtaining optimal quality, and 2) what are the key differences between models trained with different LRs? We discover that only a narrow range of initial LRs slightly above the convergence threshold lead to optimal results after fine-tuning with a small LR or weight averaging. By studying the local geometry of reached minima, we observe that using LRs from this optimal range allows for the optimization to locate a basin that only contains high-quality minima. Additionally, we show that these initial LRs result in a sparse set of learned features, with a clear focus on those most relevant for the task. In contrast, starting training with too small LRs leads to unstable minima and attempts to learn all features simultaneously, resulting in poor generalization. Conversely, using initial LRs that are too large fails to detect a basin with good solutions and extract meaningful patterns from the data.

paragraphs: Starting neural-network training with a large learning rate is often associated with better generalization, but the useful range is unclear. This paper conducts a controlled empirical study of how initial learning rates affect final model quality and the kinds of solutions learned. It examines both the geometry of reached minima and the features acquired during training.

The best outcomes occur in a narrow range slightly above the convergence threshold, followed by small-learning-rate fine-tuning or weight averaging. In the studied setting, these initial rates guide optimization into a basin containing only high-quality minima. They also produce a sparse set of learned features concentrated on those most relevant to the task.

Initial rates that are too small instead lead to unstable minima and attempts to learn all features simultaneously, with poorer generalization. Rates that are too large fail to locate good solution basins or extract meaningful patterns. These observations explain why increasing the initial rate can help only within a suitable range in the controlled experiments.
summary.tldr: A controlled study finds that a narrow initial-learning-rate range favors useful features and good solution basins, while smaller or larger rates perform worse.

title: Where Do Large Learning Rates Lead Us?

abstract: Learning world models offers a promising avenue for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning with sparse rewards. By allowing agents to plan actions or exploratory goals without direct interaction with the environment, world models enhance exploration efficiency. The quality of a world model hinges on the richness of data stored in the agent's replay buffer, with expectations of reasonable generalization across the state space surrounding recorded trajectories. However, challenges arise in generalizing learned world models to state transitions backward along recorded trajectories or between states across different trajectories, hindering their ability to accurately model real-world dynamics. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel goal-directed exploration algorithm, MUN (short for "World Models for Unconstrained Goal Navigation"). This algorithm is capable of modeling state transitions between arbitrary subgoal states in the replay buffer, thereby facilitating the learning of policies to navigate between any "key" states. Experimental results demonstrate that MUN strengthens the reliability of world models and significantly improves the policy's capacity to generalize across new goal settings.

paragraphs: World models help reinforcement-learning agents plan and explore by predicting how an environment changes. Their usefulness depends on the experiences stored in the replay buffer. This paper focuses on a gap in generalization: a model may struggle with transitions backward along a recorded trajectory or between states drawn from different trajectories.

MUN is a goal-directed exploration algorithm designed to model transitions between arbitrary subgoal states within that buffer. It supports learning policies that navigate between key states, extending the connections an agent can make among its recorded experiences. This is particularly relevant when rewards are sparse and effective exploration is difficult.

The experiments report more reliable world models and substantially better policy generalization to new goal settings. The result supports learning useful connections across stored experiences, including connections that are difficult for existing world models. The scope of the stated capability is navigation among subgoal states in the replay buffer; the method's name does not imply unrestricted knowledge of every possible environment state.
summary.tldr: MUN improves goal navigation by learning transitions among subgoal states across an agent's stored trajectories.

title: Learning World Models for Unconstrained Goal Navigation

abstract: It is important to estimate an accurate signed distance function (SDF) from a point cloud in many computer vision applications. The latest methods learn neural SDFs using either a data-driven based or an overfitting-based strategy. However, these two kinds of methods are with either poor generalization or slow convergence, which limits their capability under challenging scenarios like highly noisy point clouds. To resolve this issue, we propose a method to prompt pros of both data-driven based and overfitting-based methods for better generalization, faster inference, and higher accuracy in learning neural SDFs. We introduce a novel statistical reasoning algorithm in local regions which is able to finetune data-driven based priors without signed distance supervision, clean point cloud, or point normals. This helps our method start with a good initialization, and converge to a minimum in a much faster way. Our numerical and visual comparisons with the stat-of-the-art methods show our superiority over these methods in surface reconstruction and point cloud denoising on widely used shape and scene benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/chenchao15/LocalN2NM.

paragraphs: A signed distance function represents a surface through distances whose signs distinguish its two sides. Estimating one from noisy point measurements is useful for reconstruction and denoising. The paper addresses a trade-off between data-driven methods that can generalize poorly and methods fitted to individual point clouds that can converge slowly, especially under heavy noise.

The proposed approach starts from a data-driven prior and fine-tunes it to a single noisy point cloud. A statistical reasoning algorithm operating in local regions makes this adaptation possible without signed-distance supervision, a clean point cloud, or point normals. The prior supplies a useful initialization, helping the subsequent fitting process converge much faster.

Numerical and visual comparisons on widely used shape and scene benchmarks show advantages over the compared state-of-the-art methods in surface reconstruction and point-cloud denoising. The approach combines knowledge learned from data with adjustment to the particular observed object or scene. Its reported benefits include better generalization, faster inference, and greater accuracy in learning neural signed distance functions.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning learned priors through local statistical reasoning improves signed-distance estimation from a single noisy point cloud.

title: Inferring Neural Signed Distance Functions by Overfitting on Single Noisy Point Clouds through Finetuning Data-Driven based Priors

abstract: Recent progress in Neural Causal Models (NCMs) showcased how identification and partial identification of causal effects can be automatically carried out via training of neural generative models that respect the constraints encoded in a given causal graph [Xia et al. 2022, Balazadeh et al. 2022]. However, formal consistency of these methods has only been proven for the case of discrete variables or only for linear causal models. In this work, we prove the consistency of partial identification via NCMs in a general setting with both continuous and categorical variables. Further, our results highlight the impact of the design of the underlying neural network architecture in terms of depth and connectivity as well as the importance of applying Lipschitz regularization in the training phase. In particular, we provide a counterexample showing that without Lipschitz regularization this method may not be asymptotically consistent. Our results are enabled by new results on the approximability of Structural Causal Models (SCMs) via neural generative models, together with an analysis of the sample complexity of the resulting architectures and how that translates into an error in the constrained optimization problem that defines the partial identification bounds.

paragraphs: Neural causal models use generative networks constrained by a causal graph to estimate causal effects or bounds on those effects. Partial identification concerns the latter situation, where the available constraints support a range rather than a single answer. This paper asks whether neural estimates of those bounds are formally consistent as the available data grows.

Earlier consistency results covered discrete variables or linear causal models. The authors extend the analysis to a general setting containing both continuous and categorical variables. Their proof connects the ability of neural generative models to approximate structural causal models with sample complexity, then follows how those errors affect the constrained optimization defining the causal bounds.

The results show that network depth, connectivity, and Lipschitz regularization matter for consistency. A counterexample demonstrates that without this regularization, the method may fail to become consistent even asymptotically. The contribution therefore includes both a broader theoretical guarantee and a concrete reason to treat architecture and training regularization as part of the causal estimation method.
summary.tldr: The paper proves neural causal partial-identification consistency in a broader setting and shows why architecture and Lipschitz regularization matter.

title: Consistency of Neural Causal Partial Identification

abstract: This paper introduces an innovative approach to classification called Credal Deep Ensembles (CreDEs), namely, ensembles of novel Credal-Set Neural Networks (CreNets). CreNets are trained to predict a lower and an upper probability bound for each class, which, in turn, determine a convex set of probabilities (credal set) on the class set. The training employs a loss inspired by distributionally robust optimization which simulates the potential divergence of the test distribution from the training distribution, in such a way that the width of the predicted probability interval reflects the epistemic uncertainty about the future data distribution. Ensembles can be constructed by training multiple CreNets, each associated with a different random seed, and averaging the outputted intervals. Extensive experiments are conducted on various out-of-distributions (OOD) detection benchmarks (CIFAR10/100 vs SVHN/Tiny-ImageNet, CIFAR10 vs CIFAR10-C, ImageNet vs ImageNet-O) and using different network architectures (ResNet50, VGG16, and ViT Base). Compared to Deep Ensemble baselines, CreDEs demonstrate higher test accuracy, lower expected calibration error, and significantly improved epistemic uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Credal Deep Ensembles represent classification uncertainty through probability intervals. Each constituent network, called a CreNet, predicts a lower and upper probability for every class. Together, these bounds define a convex collection of possible class-probability distributions, known as a credal set. This gives the model a way to express uncertainty about which probability distribution is appropriate.

Training uses a loss inspired by distributionally robust optimization. It simulates possible differences between training and test distributions so that interval width reflects epistemic uncertainty about future data. Multiple CreNets are trained with different random seeds, and their predicted intervals are averaged to form the ensemble. Thus, uncertainty representation is built into each network as well as into the ensemble.

The authors evaluate the method on several out-of-distribution detection benchmarks using ResNet50, VGG16, and ViT Base architectures. Relative to the tested Deep Ensemble baselines, they report higher test accuracy, lower expected calibration error, and substantially better epistemic uncertainty estimation. These findings support probability intervals as a useful representation when the future data distribution may differ from the training distribution.
summary.tldr: Credal Deep Ensembles predict class-probability intervals and improve accuracy, calibration, and epistemic uncertainty estimation over tested ensemble baselines.

title: Credal Deep Ensembles for Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: We propose a novel inference technique based on a pretrained diffusion model for text-conditional video generation. Our approach, called FIFO-Diffusion, is conceptually capable of generating infinitely long videos without additional training. This is achieved by iteratively performing diagonal denoising, which simultaneously processes a series of consecutive frames with increasing noise levels in a queue; our method dequeues a fully denoised frame at the head while enqueuing a new random noise frame at the tail. However, diagonal denoising is a double-edged sword as the frames near the tail can take advantage of cleaner frames by forward reference but such a strategy induces the discrepancy between training and inference. Hence, we introduce latent partitioning to reduce the training-inference gap and lookahead denoising to leverage the benefit of forward referencing. Practically, FIFO-Diffusion consumes a constant amount of memory regardless of the target video length given a baseline model, while well-suited for parallel inference on multiple GPUs. We have demonstrated the promising results and effectiveness of the proposed methods on existing text-to-video generation baselines. Generated video examples and source codes are available at our project page.

title: FIFO-Diffusion: Generating Infinite Videos from Text without Training

abstract: Creating realistic avatars from a single RGB image is an attractive yet challenging problem. To deal with challenging loose clothing or occlusion by interaction objects, we leverage powerful shape prior from 2D diffusion models pretrained on large datasets. Although 2D diffusion models demonstrate strong generalization capability, they cannot provide multi-view shape priors with guaranteed 3D consistency. We propose Human-3Diffusion: Realistic Avatar Creation via Explicit 3D Consistent Diffusion. Our key insight is that 2D multi-view diffusion and 3D reconstruction models provide complementary information for each other. By coupling them in a tight manner, we can fully leverage the potential of both models. We introduce a novel image-conditioned generative 3D Gaussian Splats reconstruction model that leverages the prior from 2D multi-view diffusion models, and provides an explicit 3D representation, which further guides the 2D reverse sampling processto have better 3D consistency. Experiments show that our proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods and enables the creation of realistic avatars from a single RGB image, achieving high-fidelity in both geometry and appearance. Extensive ablations also validate the efficacy of our design, (1) multi-view 2D priors conditioning in generative 3D reconstruction and (2) consistency refinement of sampling trajectory via the explicit 3D representation. Our code and models are released at https://yuxuan-xue.com/human-3diffusion/.

paragraphs: Creating a realistic avatar from one color image is difficult when clothing is loose or objects obscure parts of the person. Pretrained 2D diffusion models provide useful shape information, but the views they generate do not inherently come with guaranteed 3D consistency. Human-3Diffusion addresses this by coupling multi-view image generation with explicit 3D reconstruction.

The method introduces an image-conditioned generative reconstruction model based on 3D Gaussian Splats. This model uses information from multi-view 2D diffusion to construct a 3D representation. That representation then guides the diffusion model's reverse sampling process toward better agreement across views. Information therefore flows in both directions: image-generation priors inform reconstruction, and reconstructed geometry helps refine image generation.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods and realistic avatars with high fidelity in geometry and appearance from a single image. Ablations support both conditioning reconstruction on multi-view priors and refining the sampling trajectory through explicit 3D information. These findings support the paper's central idea that closely coupling the two models can make their complementary information more useful.
summary.tldr: Human-3Diffusion couples multi-view diffusion with 3D Gaussian reconstruction to create realistic single-image avatars with improved cross-view consistency.

title: Human-3Diffusion: Realistic Avatar Creation via Explicit 3D Consistent Diffusion Models

abstract: We introduce QuaRot, a new Quantization scheme based on Rotations, which is able to quantize LLMs end-to-end, including all weights, activations, and KV cache in 4 bits. QuaRot rotates LLMs in a way that removes outliers from the hidden state without changing the output, making quantization easier. This computational invariance is applied to the hidden state (residual) of the LLM, as well as to the activations of the feed-forward components, aspects of the attention mechanism, and to the KV cache. The result is a quantized model where all matrix multiplications are performed in 4 bits, without any channels identified for retention in higher precision. Our 4-bit quantized LLAMA2-70B model has losses of at most 0.47 WikiText-2 perplexity and retains 99% of the zero-shot performance. We also show that QuaRot can provide lossless 6 and 8 bit LLAMA-2 models without any calibration data using round-to-nearest quantization. Code is available at github.com/spcl/QuaRot.

paragraphs: QuaRot makes language models easier to quantize by rotating their internal representations to remove hidden-state outliers. The rotations preserve the model’s output before quantization. This distinction matters: reorganizing the computation does not itself change the answer, while the subsequent reduction in numerical precision can introduce an accuracy loss.

The approach applies this invariance to residual hidden states, feed-forward activations, parts of attention, and the key-value cache. It quantizes weights, activations, and that cache to four bits. All matrix multiplications then operate in four bits, without keeping selected channels at higher precision to accommodate outliers.

For the reported four-bit LLAMA2-70B model, the WikiText-2 perplexity loss is at most 0.47, and the model retains 99% of its zero-shot performance. The authors also demonstrate lossless six- and eight-bit LLAMA-2 models using round-to-nearest quantization without calibration data. The findings show how an output-preserving change of representation can support aggressive precision reduction with small reported losses in the four-bit setting.
summary.tldr: QuaRot removes internal outliers through output-preserving rotations, enabling end-to-end four-bit language-model inference with small reported performance losses.

title: QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs

abstract: Object-centric learning (OCL) aims to learn representations of individual objects within visual scenes without manual supervision, facilitating efficient and effective visual reasoning. Traditional OCL methods primarily employ bottom-up approaches that aggregate homogeneous visual features to represent objects. However, in complex visual environments, these methods often fall short due to the heterogeneous nature of visual features within an object. To address this, we propose a novel OCL framework incorporating a top-down pathway. This pathway first bootstraps the semantics of individual objects and then modulates the model to prioritize features relevant to these semantics. By dynamically modulating the model based on its own output, our top-down pathway enhances the representational quality of objects. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple synthetic and real-world object-discovery benchmarks.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning tries to discover individual objects in images without manual supervision. Many approaches build object representations by gathering visual features that resemble one another. This becomes difficult when different parts of the same object have very different appearances: visual similarity alone may provide an incomplete basis for deciding which features belong together.

The paper adds a top-down pathway that uses the model’s developing interpretation of an object to guide feature processing. It first builds an initial estimate of the object’s semantics, then adjusts the model to emphasize features relevant to that estimate. The model therefore uses its own output as a signal for improving the representation it constructs.

This self-modulation connects object interpretation with feature selection, addressing the mismatch between internally varied objects and grouping based on homogeneous features. The authors report state-of-the-art results across multiple synthetic and real-world object-discovery benchmarks. These findings support the value of adding semantic feedback to unsupervised object representation learning.
summary.tldr: A top-down feedback pathway uses a model’s own object interpretations to improve unsupervised object discovery.

title: Bootstrapping Top-down Information for Self-modulating Slot Attention

abstract: Signed graphs can model friendly or antagonistic relations where edges are annotated with a positive or negative sign. The main downstream task in signed graph analysis is $\textit{link sign prediction}$. Signed Graph Neural Networks (SGNNs) have been widely used for signed graph representation learning. While significant progress has been made in SGNNs research, two issues (i.e., graph sparsity and unbalanced triangles) persist in the current SGNN models. We aim to alleviate these issues through data augmentation ($\textit{DA}$) techniques which have demonstrated effectiveness in improving the performance of graph neural networks. However, most graph augmentation methods are primarily aimed at graph-level and node-level tasks (e.g., graph classification and node classification) and cannot be directly applied to signed graphs due to the lack of side information (e.g., node features and label information) in available real-world signed graph datasets. Random $\textit{DropEdge} $is one of the few $\textit{DA}$ methods that can be directly used for signed graph data augmentation, but its effectiveness is still unknown. In this paper, we first provide the generalization bound for the SGNN model and demonstrate from both experimental and theoretical perspectives that the random $\textit{DropEdge}$ cannot improve the performance of link sign prediction. Therefore, we propose a novel signed graph augmentation method, $\underline{S}$igned $\underline{G}$raph $\underline{A}$ugmentation framework (SGA). Specifically, SGA first integrates a structure augmentation module to detect candidate edges solely based on network information. Furthermore, SGA incorporates a novel strategy to select beneficial candidates. Finally, SGA introduces a novel data augmentation perspective to enhance the training process of SGNNs. Experiment results on six real-world datasets demonstrate that SGA effectively boosts the performance of diverse SGNN models, achieving improvements of up to 32.3\% in F1-micro for SGCN on the Slashdot dataset in the link sign prediction task.

paragraphs: Signed graphs represent relationships as positive or negative, such as friendly or antagonistic connections. A central prediction task is determining a link's sign. The paper addresses two difficulties for signed graph neural networks: sparse connections and unbalanced triangles. Many graph augmentation techniques also require node features or labels that available signed graph datasets do not provide.

Random DropEdge, which removes connections during augmentation, can operate without that extra information. However, the authors derive a generalization bound and present theoretical and experimental evidence that this method does not improve link sign prediction in their studied setting. They introduce Signed Graph Augmentation, or SGA, to make augmentation depend on network structure rather than indiscriminate edge removal.

SGA identifies candidate edges using network information, selects candidates judged beneficial, and incorporates the augmentation into training. Experiments on six real-world datasets show improvements across several signed graph neural networks. The largest reported example is an improvement of up to 32.3% in F1-micro for SGCN on Slashdot. The result supports designing augmentation around signed relationship structure and the prediction task.
summary.tldr: SGA uses signed graph structure to select useful augmentations and improves link sign prediction where random DropEdge falls short.

title: DropEdge not Foolproof: Effective Augmentation Method for Signed Graph Neural Networks

abstract: From the onset of infanthood, humans naturally develop the ability to closely observe and interpret the visual gaze of others. This skill, known as gaze following, holds significance in developmental theory as it enables us to grasp another person’s mental state, emotions, intentions, and more. In computer vision, gaze following is defined as the prediction of the pixel coordinates where a person in the image is focusing their attention. Existing methods in this research area have predominantly centered on pinpointing the gaze target by predicting a gaze heatmap or gaze point. However, a notable drawback of this approach is its limited practical value in gaze applications, as mere localization may not fully capture our primary interest — understanding the underlying semantics, such as the nature of the gaze target, rather than just its 2D pixel location. To address this gap, we extend the gaze following task, and introduce a novel architecture that simultaneously predicts the localization and semantic label of the gaze target. We devise a pseudo-annotation pipeline for the GazeFollow dataset, propose a new benchmark, develop an experimental protocol and design a suitable baseline for comparison. Our method sets a new state-of-the-art on the main GazeFollow benchmark for localization and achieves competitive results in the recognition task on both datasets compared to the baseline, with 40% fewer parameters

paragraphs: Gaze-following systems typically predict the location in an image where a person is looking. A coordinate or heatmap answers where the gaze lands, but it does not directly identify the kind of target receiving attention. This paper extends the task to predict both the target's location and its semantic label.

The authors introduce an architecture that produces these two outputs together. To support training and evaluation, they build a pseudo-annotation pipeline for the GazeFollow dataset, introduce a new benchmark, define an experimental protocol, and construct a comparison baseline. These additions make recognition of the gaze target an explicit part of the task rather than leaving it outside the localization evaluation.

The method reports a new state of the art for localization on the main GazeFollow benchmark and competitive recognition results on both evaluated datasets, using 40% fewer parameters than the baseline. The findings suggest that adding semantic target prediction can coexist with strong localization in a smaller model, giving gaze-following outputs a more directly interpretable meaning.
summary.tldr: The paper extends gaze following to predict both where a person looks and the target's semantic label, with strong results using fewer parameters.

title: Toward Semantic Gaze Target Detection

abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is a crucial but challenging task in many high-dimensional learning problems to increase the confidence of a given predictor. We develop a new data-driven approach for UQ in regression that applies both to classical optimization approaches such as the LASSO as well as to neural networks. One of the most notable UQ techniques is the debiased LASSO, which modifies the LASSO to allow for the construction of asymptotic confidence intervals by decomposing the estimation error into a Gaussian and an asymptotically vanishing bias component. However, in real-world problems with finite-dimensional data, the bias term is often too significant to disregard, resulting in overly narrow confidence intervals. Our work rigorously addresses this issue and derives a data-driven adjustment that corrects the confidence intervals for a large class of predictors by estimating the means and variances of the bias terms from training data, exploiting high-dimensional concentration phenomena. This gives rise to non-asymptotic confidence intervals, which can help avoid overestimating certainty in critical applications such as MRI diagnosis. Importantly, our analysis extends beyond sparse regression to data-driven predictors like neural networks, enhancing the reliability of model-based deep learning. Our findings bridge the gap between established theory and the practical applicability of such methods.

paragraphs: Confidence intervals can convey excessive certainty when a theoretical approximation neglects an error that remains substantial in actual data. The paper examines this problem in high-dimensional regression. In particular, debiased LASSO separates estimation error into a Gaussian component and a bias component that vanishes asymptotically, but the latter may still matter in finite-dimensional settings.

The authors develop a data-driven adjustment that explicitly accounts for this remaining bias. They estimate the bias terms' means and variances from training data, using high-dimensional concentration phenomena. These estimates support confidence intervals that do not depend on simply treating the bias as negligible in an asymptotic limit.

The analysis covers a broad class of predictors, extending beyond sparse regression methods to neural networks. Its significance is therefore both statistical and practical: uncertainty estimates can reflect a source of error that conventional intervals may understate. The authors identify MRI diagnosis as an application where avoiding overstated certainty could matter, and connect the framework to more reliable model-based deep learning.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs non-asymptotic confidence intervals by estimating residual bias, extending uncertainty correction from sparse regression to neural-network predictors.

title: Non-Asymptotic Uncertainty Quantification in High-Dimensional Learning

abstract: This paper introduces the Quotient Bayesian Learning Rule, an extension of natural-gradient Bayesian updates to probability models that fall outside the exponential family. Building on the observation that many heavy-tailed and otherwise non-exponential distributions arise as marginals of minimal exponential families, we prove that such marginals inherit a unique Fisher–Rao information geometry via the quotient-manifold construction. Exploiting this geometry, we derive the Quotient Natural Gradient algorithm, which takes steepest-descent steps in the well-structured covering space, thereby guaranteeing parameterization-invariant optimization in the target space. Empirical results on the Student-$t$ distribution confirm that our method converges more rapidly and attains higher-quality solutions than previous variants of the Bayesian Learning Rule. These findings position quotient geometry as a unifying tool for efficient and principled inference across a broad class of latent-variable models.

paragraphs: The Quotient Bayesian Learning Rule extends natural-gradient Bayesian updates to probability distributions beyond the exponential family. The key observation is that many such distributions, including heavy-tailed ones, can be obtained by marginalizing a larger minimal exponential-family model. This gives the method access to a more structured representation of the target distribution.

The paper proves that these marginals inherit a unique Fisher–Rao information geometry through a quotient-manifold construction. Its Quotient Natural Gradient algorithm takes steepest-descent steps in the structured covering space. The resulting optimization in the target space is invariant to parameterization, meaning that the choice of coordinates does not determine the underlying update.

Experiments with the Student-t distribution show faster convergence and better solutions than earlier Bayesian Learning Rule variants. These results support the practical value of the geometric construction for that distribution. More broadly, the contribution provides a principled route for extending Bayesian learning updates to latent-variable models whose observable distributions fall outside the usual exponential-family setting.
summary.tldr: Quotient geometry extends parameterization-invariant Bayesian learning updates to non-exponential distributions represented as exponential-family marginals.

title: The Quotient Bayesian Learning Rule

abstract: Reconstructing 3D objects into editable programs is pivotal for applications like reverse engineering and shape editing. However, existing methods often rely on limited domain-specific languages (DSLs) and small-scale datasets, restricting their ability to model complex geometries and structures. To address these challenges, we introduce MeshLLM, a novel framework that reconstructs complex 3D objects from point clouds into editable Blender Python scripts. We develop a comprehensive set of expressive Blender Python APIs capable of synthesizing intricate geometries. Leveraging these APIs, we construct a large-scale paired object-code dataset, where the code for each object is decomposed into distinct semantic parts. Subsequently, we train a multimodal large language model (LLM) that translates 3D point cloud into executable Blender Python scripts. Our approach not only achieves superior performance in shape-to-code reconstruction tasks but also facilitates intuitive geometric and topological editing through convenient code modifications. Furthermore, our code-based representation enhances the reasoning capabilities of LLMs in 3D shape understanding tasks. Together, these contributions establish MeshLLM as a powerful and flexible solution for programmatic 3D shape reconstruction and understanding.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs 3D objects as editable programs from point clouds. Its framework, MeshLLM, generates executable Blender Python scripts, providing a programmatic representation of an object's geometry. The motivation is to support complex shapes while making the reconstructed result useful for reverse engineering and subsequent editing.

The researchers develop expressive Blender Python APIs and use them to build a large paired dataset of objects and code. Each object's code is divided into distinct semantic parts. A multimodal language model then learns to translate point clouds into scripts using this representation, connecting observed shape information with structured construction instructions.

The paper reports superior shape-to-code reconstruction performance and shows that code modifications enable geometric and topological editing. The contribution therefore extends beyond reconstructing an object's appearance: the generated script exposes a structured way to change and reason about the shape, with semantic parts helping organize that editable representation.
summary.tldr: MeshLLM converts point clouds into structured Blender Python programs that support 3D reconstruction, editing, and shape reasoning.

title: MeshCoder: LLM-Powered Structured Mesh Code Generation from Point Clouds

abstract: Channel permutation is a powerful technique for enhancing the accuracy of N:M sparse models by reordering the channels of weight matrices to prioritize the retention of important weights. However, traditional channel permutation methods rely on handcrafted quality metrics, which often fail to accurately capture the true impact of pruning on model performance. To address this limitation, we propose PermLLM, a novel post-training pruning framework that introduces learnable channel permutation (LCP) for N:M sparsity. LCP leverages Sinkhorn normalization to transform discrete permutation matrices into differentiable soft permutation matrices, enabling end-to-end optimization. Additionally, PermLLM incorporates an efficient block-wise channel permutation strategy, which significantly reduces the number of learnable parameters and computational complexity. PermLLM seamlessly integrates with existing one-shot pruning methods to adaptively optimize channel permutations, effectively mitigating pruning-induced errors. Extensive experiments on the LLaMA series, Qwen, and OPT models demonstrate that PermLLM achieves superior performance in optimizing N:M sparse models.

LCP leverages Sinkhorn normalization to transform discrete permutation matrices into differentiable soft permutation matrices, enabling end-to-end optimization. Additionally, PermLLM incorporates an efficient block-wise channel permutation strategy, which significantly reduces the number of learnable parameters and computational complexity. PermLLM seamlessly integrates with existing one-shot pruning methods to adaptively optimize channel permutations, effectively mitigating pruning-induced errors. paragraphs: Structured pruning removes model weights according to a prescribed sparsity pattern. Reordering the channels of a weight matrix can help important weights survive that process, but choosing a good ordering is difficult. PermLLM replaces handcrafted measures of ordering quality with a learnable channel-permutation procedure for N:M sparse language models.

The key obstacle is that permutations are discrete, making them difficult to optimize directly with gradients. PermLLM uses Sinkhorn normalization to form differentiable soft permutation matrices, enabling end-to-end optimization. It also organizes channel permutations block by block, reducing the number of learnable parameters and the computational complexity of the optimization.

The framework operates after training and integrates with existing one-shot pruning methods. Its purpose is to adapt channel orderings in ways that reduce errors introduced by pruning, rather than relying only on a manually chosen proxy for which arrangement is best. Experiments on the LLaMA series, Qwen, and OPT report superior performance in optimizing N:M sparse models, supporting learned channel arrangement as a useful component of post-training compression.
summary.tldr: PermLLM learns channel reorderings through differentiable soft permutations to reduce errors from structured language-model pruning.

title: PermLLM: Learnable Channel Permutation for N:M Sparse Large Language Models

abstract: Influence functions provide crucial insights into model training, but existing methods suffer from large computational costs and limited generalization. Particularly, recent works have proposed various metrics and algorithms to calculate the influence of data using language models, which do not scale well with large models and datasets. This is because of the expensive forward and backward passes required for computation, substantial memory requirements to store large models, and poor generalization of influence estimates to new data. In this paper, we explore the use of small neural networks -- which we refer to as the InfluenceNetwork -- to estimate influence values, achieving up to 99% cost reduction. Our evaluation demonstrates that influence values can be estimated with models just 0.0007% the size of full language models (we average across 1.5B-22B versions). We apply our algorithm of estimating influence values (called NN-CIFT: Neural Networks for effiCient Instruction Fine-Tuning) to the downstream task of subset selection for general instruction fine-tuning. In our study, we include four state-of-the-art influence functions and show no compromise in performance, despite large speedups, between NN-CIFT and the original influence functions. We provide an in-depth hyperparameter analyses of NN-CIFT. The code for our method can be found here: https://github.com/agarwalishika/NN-CIFT/tree/main.

paragraphs: Influence estimates help identify which training examples matter to a model, but computing them with large language models can be expensive. Repeated forward and backward passes and substantial memory requirements limit scalability. Existing approaches can also struggle to generalize influence estimates to new data.

The paper proposes InfluenceNetwork, a small neural network trained to estimate influence values. Its broader algorithm, NN-CIFT, applies these estimates to selecting subsets of data for instruction fine-tuning. The central idea is to learn an efficient estimator of influence so that data selection can benefit from influence information without repeatedly paying the full computational cost of the original methods.

Across the evaluated language models, ranging from 1.5 billion to 22 billion parameters, the influence estimators average just 0.0007% of the full models’ size. The authors report cost reductions of up to 99%. In comparisons involving four state-of-the-art influence functions, subset selection with NN-CIFT shows no performance compromise relative to the original functions despite substantial speedups. The paper also examines how hyperparameters affect the method.
summary.tldr: NN-CIFT learns influence estimates with tiny neural networks, reducing costs by up to 99% without sacrificing evaluated data-selection performance.

title: Neural Networks for Learnable and Scalable Influence Estimation of Instruction Fine-Tuning Data

abstract: Listwise reranking with large language models (LLMs) enhances top-ranked results in retrieval-based applications. Due to the limit in context size and high inference cost of long context, reranking is typically performed over a fixed size of small subsets, with the final ranking aggregated from these partial results. This fixed computation disregards query difficulty and document distribution, leading to inefficiencies. We propose AcuRank, an adaptive reranking framework that dynamically adjusts both the amount and target of computation based on uncertainty estimates over document relevance. Using a Bayesian TrueSkill model, we iteratively refine relevance estimates until reaching sufficient confidence levels, and our explicit modeling of ranking uncertainty enables principled control over reranking behavior and avoids unnecessary updates to confident predictions. Results on the TREC-DL and BEIR benchmarks show that our method consistently achieves a superior accuracy–efficiency trade-off and scales better with compute than fixed-computation baselines. These results highlight the effectiveness and generalizability of our method across diverse retrieval tasks and LLM-based reranking models.

paragraphs: LLM rerankers improve retrieval results by reconsidering which documents best answer a query. Because processing long lists is expensive and context space is limited, systems commonly rank small groups and combine the results. Giving every query and group a fixed amount of computation overlooks an important difference: some relevance decisions are already clear, while others remain ambiguous.

AcuRank uses uncertainty to decide both how much additional reranking to perform and which documents deserve that attention. A Bayesian TrueSkill model maintains relevance estimates together with their uncertainty. These estimates are refined iteratively until confidence is sufficient, allowing the system to avoid repeatedly updating predictions it already considers confident.

On TREC-DL and BEIR, the authors report a consistently better balance between ranking accuracy and computational cost than fixed-computation baselines. They also find better scaling as more computation becomes available across different retrieval tasks and LLM rerankers. The practical contribution is an explicit mechanism for directing computation toward unresolved relevance decisions.
summary.tldr: AcuRank directs reranking computation toward uncertain document relevance decisions, improving the measured accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

title: AcuRank: Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Computation for Listwise Reranking

abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that exhibit transferability across various models. Numerous approaches are proposed to enhance the transferability of adversarial examples, including advanced optimization, data augmentation, and model modifications. However, these methods still show limited transferability, partiovovocularly in cross-architecture scenarios, such as from CNN to ViT. To achieve high transferability, we propose a technique termed Spatial Adversarial Alignment (SAA), which employs an alignment loss and leverages a witness model to fine-tune the surrogate model. Specifically, SAA consists of two key parts: spatial-aware alignment and adversarial-aware alignment. First, we minimize the divergences of features between the two models in both global and local regions, facilitating spatial alignment. Second, we introduce a self-adversarial strategy that leverages adversarial examples to impose further constraints, aligning features from an adversarial perspective. Through this alignment, the surrogate model is trained to concentrate on the common features extracted by the witness model. This facilitates adversarial attacks on these shared features, thereby yielding perturbations that exhibit enhanced transferability. Extensive experiments on various architectures on ImageNet show that aligned surrogate models based on SAA can provide higher transferable adversarial examples, especially in cross-architecture attacks.

paragraphs: An adversarial example is an input modified to mislead a neural network. Some such examples also mislead other models, making their transferability an important property to study. This paper addresses the difficulty of transferring attacks between different architectures, including from convolutional networks to vision transformers, where existing enhancement methods still have limited success.

Spatial Adversarial Alignment fine-tunes the surrogate model used to construct attacks with guidance from a second, witness model. One component reduces differences between their features across both whole images and local regions. Another applies a self-adversarial strategy, using adversarial examples to impose additional constraints on how the models represent inputs.

Together, these components encourage the surrogate to concentrate on features shared with the witness model. Attacks directed at those features can then transfer more effectively. Experiments involving multiple architectures on ImageNet show increased transferability from aligned surrogates, especially across architecture families. The contribution is therefore a way to reshape the attack-generating model through feature alignment.
summary.tldr: Aligning a surrogate model’s spatial and adversarial features with a witness model improves attack transferability, especially across architectures.

title: Boosting Adversarial Transferability with Spatial Adversarial Alignment

abstract: Molecular Relational Learning (MRL) is a rapidly growing field that focuses on understanding the interaction dynamics between molecules, which is crucial for applications ranging from catalyst engineering to drug discovery. Despite recent progress, earlier MRL approaches are limited to using only the 2D topological structure of molecules, as obtaining the 3D interaction geometry remains prohibitively expensive. This paper introduces a novel 3D geometric pre-training strategy for MRL (3DMRL) that incorporates a 3D virtual interaction environment, overcoming the limitations of costly traditional quantum mechanical calculation methods. With the constructed 3D virtual interaction environment, 3DMRL trains 2D MRL model to learn the global and local 3D geometric information of molecular interaction. Extensive experiments on various tasks using real-world datasets, including out-of-distribution and extrapolation scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness of 3DMRL, showing up to a 24.93% improvement in performance across 40 tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Namkyeong/3DMRL.

paragraphs: Predicting how molecules interact requires more than describing each molecule separately. Earlier molecular relational learning methods primarily use two-dimensional molecular connectivity, while obtaining three-dimensional interaction geometry through traditional quantum mechanical calculations is prohibitively expensive. This paper introduces 3DMRL, a pre-training strategy intended to bring geometric information into models that work with two-dimensional molecular structures.

The central idea is to construct a virtual three-dimensional interaction environment and use it to train a two-dimensional model. Training exposes the model to both global geometry and local geometric details of molecular interactions. This makes the virtual environment a source of supervision: it provides spatial information that connectivity alone does not supply, without relying on the costly calculation route identified in the abstract.

Experiments cover 40 tasks using real-world datasets, including settings involving distribution shifts and extrapolation. The authors report performance improvements reaching 24.93%. That figure describes the largest stated improvement, rather than a uniform gain across every task. The findings support geometric pre-training as a useful way to strengthen molecular interaction learning.
summary.tldr: 3DMRL uses virtual three-dimensional molecular interactions to improve models built around two-dimensional molecular structures.

title: 3D Interaction Geometric Pre-training for Molecular Relational Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning enables agents to learn optimal behaviors through interactions with environments. However, real-world environments are typically non-stationary, requiring agents to continuously adapt to new tasks and changing conditions. Although Continual Reinforcement Learning facilitates learning across multiple tasks, existing methods often suffer from catastrophic forgetting and inefficient knowledge utilization. To address these challenges, we propose Continual Knowledge Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning (CKA-RL), which enables the accumulation and effective utilization of historical knowledge. Specifically, we introduce a Continual Knowledge Adaptation strategy, which involves maintaining a task-specific knowledge vector pool and dynamically using historical knowledge to adapt the agent to new tasks. This process mitigates catastrophic forgetting and enables efficient knowledge transfer across tasks by preserving and adapting critical model parameters. Additionally, we propose an Adaptive Knowledge Merging mechanism that combines similar knowledge vectors to address scalability challenges, reducing memory requirements while ensuring the retention of essential knowledge. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed CKA-RL outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an improvement of 4.20% in overall performance and 8.02% in forward transfer. The source code is available at https://github.com/Fhujinwu/CKA-RL.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent operating across changing tasks needs to reuse earlier experience while adapting its behavior. Continual learning can struggle with both sides of that requirement: new training may erase useful knowledge, and retained knowledge may not be used effectively. CKA-RL addresses how past task knowledge is stored, selected, and adapted.

The method maintains a pool of task-specific knowledge vectors. When a new task arrives, it dynamically uses this historical information while preserving and adapting critical model parameters. The goal is to reduce catastrophic forgetting and improve transfer between tasks. An additional merging mechanism combines similar vectors so that the memory cost of retaining knowledge is reduced while essential information is kept.

Across three benchmarks, the authors report improvements of 4.20% in overall performance and 8.02% in forward transfer over state-of-the-art methods. The transfer result concerns how earlier learning helps with later tasks, complementing the overall performance measurement. Together, the findings support managing reusable task knowledge as part of continual adaptation, including the practical need to control storage growth.
summary.tldr: CKA-RL stores, adapts, and merges task knowledge to improve continual reinforcement learning and transfer across tasks.

title: Continual Knowledge Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) play a central role in guiding inference-time scaling algorithms for large language models (LLMs). However, we observe that even state-of-the-art PRMs can be poorly calibrated. Specifically, they tend to overestimate the success probability that a partial reasoning step will lead to a correct final answer, particularly when smaller LLMs are used to complete the reasoning trajectory. To address this, we present a calibration approach—performed via quantile regression—that adjusts PRM outputs to better align with true success probabilities. Leveraging these calibrated success estimates and their associated confidence bounds, we introduce an instance-adaptive scaling (IAS) framework that dynamically adjusts the compute budget based on the estimated likelihood that a partial reasoning trajectory will yield a correct final answer. Unlike conventional methods that allocate a fixed number of reasoning trajectories per query, this approach adapts to each instance and reasoning step when using our calibrated PRMs. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that (i) our PRM calibration method achieves small calibration error, outperforming the baseline methods, (ii) calibration is crucial for enabling effective IAS, and (iii) the proposed IAS strategy reduces inference costs while maintaining final answer accuracy, utilizing less compute on more confident problems as desired.

paragraphs: Process reward models help guide language-model reasoning by evaluating partial reasoning trajectories. This paper finds that even strong models can overestimate the probability that a partial trajectory will end in a correct answer. The mismatch is especially pronounced when a smaller language model completes the remaining reasoning.

The authors use quantile regression to calibrate reward-model outputs so that they better reflect actual success probabilities. They then combine these estimates with confidence bounds in an instance-adaptive scaling framework. Instead of assigning every query a fixed number of reasoning trajectories, the framework adjusts computation according to the instance and its current reasoning step.

On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, calibration achieves small error and outperforms the compared calibration methods. The experiments also show that calibration is crucial to effective adaptive scaling. With calibrated estimates, the proposed strategy reduces inference costs while maintaining final-answer accuracy, allocating less computation to more confident problems. The findings link reliable probability estimates to a concrete decision: how much further reasoning to spend.
summary.tldr: Calibrating process reward models enables adaptive reasoning budgets that reduce inference costs while preserving accuracy on mathematical benchmarks.

title: Know What You Don't Know: Uncertainty Calibration of Process Reward Models

abstract: The effectiveness of domain translation in addressing image-based problems of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) depends on the quality of the translated images and the preservation of crucial discriminative features. However, achieving high-quality and stable translations typically requires paired data, which poses a challenge in scenarios with limited annotations in the target domain. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel method termed Stain-Guided Cycle Diffusion (SGCD), employing a dual diffusion model with bidirectional generative constraints to synthesize highly realistic data for downstream task fine-tuning. The bidirectional generative constraints ensure that the translated images retain the features critical to the downstream model in properly controlling the generation process. Additionally, a stain-guided consistency loss is introduced to enhance the denoising capability of the dual diffusion model, thereby improving the quality of images translated between different domains using latents from one domain and a diffusion model trained on another. Experiments conducted on four public datasets demonstrate that SGCD can effectively enhance the performance of downstream task models on the target domain.

paragraphs: Translating histopathology images between domains can help a classifier adapt, but the translated images must preserve features that distinguish the classes. Producing realistic images alone does not address that requirement. This paper develops Stain-Guided Cycle Diffusion for unsupervised domain adaptation, motivated by the difficulty of obtaining paired data when target-domain annotations are limited.

SGCD uses a dual diffusion model with constraints on generation in both directions. These constraints control translation so that features important to the downstream model are retained. A stain-guided consistency loss additionally improves denoising and translation quality when combining latent representations from one domain with a diffusion model trained on another.

The generated images are then used to fine-tune downstream task models. Experiments on four public datasets show that SGCD can improve their performance in the target domain. The method connects two requirements of useful adaptation: generating convincing target-domain imagery and preserving the discriminative information needed for classification. The reported gains concern the resulting downstream models, linking translation quality to task performance.
summary.tldr: SGCD combines bidirectional diffusion constraints with stain-guided consistency to improve histopathology image translation and target-domain classification.

title: SGCD: Stain-Guided CycleDiffusion for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation of Histopathology Image Classification

abstract: We introduce the first method for translating text embeddings from one vector space to another without any paired data, encoders, or predefined sets of matches. Our unsupervised approach translates any embedding to and from a universal latent representation (i.e., a universal semantic structure conjectured by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis). Our translations achieve high cosine similarity across model pairs with different architectures, parameter counts, and training datasets. The ability to translate unknown embeddings into a different space while preserving their geometry has serious implications for the security of vector databases. An adversary with access only to embedding vectors can extract sensitive information about the underlying documents, sufficient for classification and attribute inference.

paragraphs: Text embedding models map documents into vector spaces, but different models produce different coordinate systems. This paper introduces an unsupervised method for translating between those spaces without paired examples, access to the encoders, or predefined matches. The task is to relate representations using the available embedding vectors themselves.

The method translates embeddings through a universal latent representation associated with the semantic structure conjectured by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. It reports high cosine similarity for translations between models that differ in architecture, parameter count, and training data. These findings support the usefulness of shared geometric structure for translation across the tested model pairs.

The paper also demonstrates a security implication. An adversary with access only to embedding vectors can extract sensitive document information sufficient for classification and attribute inference. Preserving semantic geometry across spaces therefore has consequences beyond interoperability: the experiments show that vectors can expose meaningful properties of their source documents even without access to the original encoder.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised embedding translation reveals shared geometry across models and enables sensitive attribute inference from vectors alone.

title: Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings

abstract: Recent developments in DNN-based image watermarking techniques have achieved impressive results in protecting digital content. However, most existing methods are constrained to low-resolution images as they need to encode the entire image, leading to prohibitive memory and computational costs when applied to high-resolution images. Moreover, they lack robustness to distortions prevalent in large-image transmission, such as extreme scaling and random cropping. To address these issues, we propose a novel watermarking method based on implicit neural representations (INRs). Leveraging the properties of INRs, our method employs resolution-independent coordinate sampling mechanism to generate watermarks pixel-wise, achieving ultra-high resolution watermark generation with fixed and limited memory and computational resources. This design ensures strong robustness in watermark extraction, even under extreme cropping and scaling distortions. Additionally, we introduce a hierarchical multi-scale coordinate embedding and a low-rank watermark injection strategy to ensure high-quality watermark generation and robust decoding. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing schemes in terms of both robustness and computational efficiency while preserving high image quality. Our approach achieves an accuracy greater than 98\% in watermark extraction with only 0.4\% of the image area in 2K images. These results highlight the effectiveness of our method, making it a promising solution for large-scale and high-resolution image watermarking applications.

paragraphs: Neural image watermarking often processes an entire image, making very high resolutions costly in memory and computation. Large images also face cropping and scaling that can make embedded watermarks difficult to recover. This paper proposes an implicit neural representation approach to address both computational demands and robustness to these distortions.

The method generates watermark values pixel by pixel through resolution-independent coordinate sampling. The authors describe this as enabling ultra-high-resolution watermark generation with fixed, limited computational and memory resources. A hierarchical coordinate embedding at multiple scales and a low-rank watermark injection strategy further support image quality and reliable decoding.

Experiments report better robustness and computational efficiency than existing schemes while maintaining high image quality. In the stated 2K-image test, watermark extraction accuracy exceeds 98% when only 0.4% of the image area remains. That result demonstrates strong recovery under severe cropping in the evaluated setting, while the overall framework targets watermarking that remains practical as image resolution increases.
summary.tldr: Coordinate-based watermark generation supports high-resolution images and achieves over 98% extraction accuracy from 0.4% of image area in the reported 2K test.

title: Ultra-high Resolution Watermarking Framework Resistant to Extreme Cropping and Scaling

abstract: Current image generation and editing methods primarily process textual prompts as direct inputs without explicit reasoning about visual composition or operational steps. We present Generation Chain-of-Thought (GoT), a novel paradigm that empowers a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to first generate an explicit, structured reasoning chain in natural language—detailing semantic relationships, object attributes, and, crucially, precise spatial coordinates—before any image synthesis occurs. This intermediate reasoning output directly guides the subsequent visual generation or editing process. This approach transforms conventional text-to-image generation and editing into a reasoning-guided framework that analyzes semantic relationships and spatial arrangements. We define the formulation of GoT and construct large-scale GoT datasets containing over \textbf{9M} samples with detailed reasoning chains capturing semantic-spatial relationships. To leverage the advantages of GoT, we implement a unified framework that integrates Qwen2.5-VL for reasoning chain generation with an end-to-end diffusion model enhanced by our novel Semantic-Spatial Guidance Module. Experiments show our GoT framework achieves excellent performance on both generation and editing tasks, with significant improvements over baselines. Additionally, our approach enables interactive visual generation, allowing users to explicitly modify reasoning steps for precise image adjustments. GoT pioneers a new direction for reasoning-driven visual generation and editing, producing images that better align with human intent. We will release our datasets and models to facilitate future research.

paragraphs: An image prompt can specify objects and relationships without explicitly resolving their placement or the steps needed to edit them. Generation Chain-of-Thought, or GoT, introduces a structured natural-language planning stage before synthesis. This stage describes semantic relationships, object attributes, and precise spatial coordinates that directly guide image generation or editing.

The authors construct datasets containing more than nine million examples with detailed semantic and spatial reasoning chains. Their implementation pairs Qwen2.5-VL, which produces the chains, with a diffusion model. A Semantic-Spatial Guidance Module connects the intermediate reasoning to visual synthesis, giving the image-producing system an explicit description of the intended composition.

Experiments report significant improvements over baselines on both generation and editing tasks. The intermediate representation also supports interaction: users can change reasoning steps to request precise image adjustments. The contribution is therefore both a generation method and a controllable interface, where composition decisions are expressed in language before they influence the final visual output.
summary.tldr: GoT guides image generation and editing with explicit language-based plans describing object relationships, attributes, and spatial coordinates.

title: GoT: Unleashing Reasoning Capability of MLLM for Visual Generation and Editing

abstract: Few-shot node classification on hypergraphs requires models that generalize from scarce labels while capturing high-order structures. Existing hypergraph neural networks (HNNs) effectively encode such structures but often suffer from overfitting and scalability issues due to complex, black-box architectures. In this work, we propose ZEN (Zero-Parameter Hypergraph Neural Network), a fully linear and parameter-free model that achieves both expressiveness and efficiency. Built upon a unified formulation of linearized HNNs, ZEN introduces a tractable closed-form solution for the weight matrix and a redundancy-aware propagation scheme to avoid iterative training and to eliminate redundant self-information. On 11 real-world hypergraph benchmarks, ZEN consistently outperforms eight baseline models in classification accuracy while achieving up to 696x speedups over the fastest competitor. Moreover, the decision process of ZEN is fully interpretable, providing insights into the characteristic of a dataset. Our code and datasets are fully available at https://github.com/chaewoonbae/ZEN.

Existing hypergraph neural networks (HNNs) effectively encode such structures but often suffer from overfitting and scalability issues due to complex, black-box architectures. In this work, we propose ZEN (Zero-Parameter Hypergraph Neural Network), a fully linear and parameter-free model that achieves both expressiveness and efficiency. Built upon a unified formulation of linearized HNNs, ZEN introduces a tractable closed-form solution for the weight matrix and a redundancy-aware propagation scheme to avoid iterative training and to eliminate redundant self-information. On 11 real-world hypergraph benchmarks, ZEN consistently outperforms eight baseline models in classification accuracy while achieving up to 696x speedups over the fastest competitor. Moreover, the decision process of ZEN is fully interpretable, providing insights into the characteristic of a dataset. Our code and datasets are fully available at https://github.com/chaewoonbae/ZEN.
