Separating shape from appearance enables the model to be fine-tuned using only the single observed view.

The authors report that the fitted representation supports geometrically consistent novel views that faithfully represent the input object. They also demonstrate generalization beyond the training domain, including more realistic renderings and real photographs, and find that the scaffold accurately estimates three-dimensional shape. Experiments on synthetic and real images support the combined use of explicit shape guidance and a separately controlled appearance representation.
summary.tldr: Sharf separates shape and appearance to reconstruct an object from one image and render geometrically consistent new views.

title: Sharf: Shape-conditioned Radiance Fields from a Single View

abstract: Exploration in unknown environments is a fundamental problem in reinforcement learning and control. In this work, we study task-guided exploration and determine what precisely an agent must learn about their environment in order to complete a particular task. Formally, we study a broad class of decision-making problems in the setting of linear dynamical systems, a class that includes the linear quadratic regulator problem. We provide instance- and task-dependent lower bounds which explicitly quantify the difficulty of completing a task of interest. Motivated by our lower bound, we propose a computationally efficient experiment-design based exploration algorithm. We show that it optimally explores the environment, collecting precisely the information needed to complete the task, and provide finite-time bounds guaranteeing that it achieves the instance- and task-optimal sample complexity, up to constant factors. Through several examples of the linear quadratic regulator problem, we show that performing task-guided exploration provably improves on exploration schemes which do not take into account the task of interest. Along the way, we establish that certainty equivalence decision making is instance- and task-optimal, and obtain the first algorithm for the linear quadratic regulator problem which is instance-optimal. We conclude with several experiments illustrating the effectiveness of our approach in practice.

paragraphs: Exploration can collect information about an environment without prioritizing what matters for the eventual task. This paper asks precisely what an agent needs to learn for a particular decision problem. It studies a broad class of tasks in linear dynamical systems, including the linear quadratic regulator problem.

The authors derive lower bounds that depend on both the particular system and the task, quantifying the difficulty of gathering enough information. Those bounds motivate an efficient exploration algorithm based on experiment design. Finite-time guarantees show that its sample requirements match the instance- and task-dependent optimum up to constant factors within the studied setting.

Examples involving linear quadratic regulators establish provable improvements over exploration that ignores the task. The paper also proves instance- and task-optimality for certainty-equivalence decision making and presents the first instance-optimal algorithm for the regulator problem. Experiments illustrate practical effectiveness. Together, the results make task relevance a precise criterion for exploration, connecting what the agent measures to the decision it ultimately needs to make.
summary.tldr: Task-guided experiment design achieves instance- and task-optimal exploration sample complexity up to constant factors for the studied linear-system problems.

title: Task-Optimal Exploration in Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: In this paper, we propose a conceptually simple but very effective attention module for Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets). In contrast to existing channel-wise and spatial-wise attention modules, our module instead infers 3-D attention weights for the feature map in a layer without adding parameters to the original networks. Specifically, we base on some well-known neuroscience theories and propose to optimize an energy function to find the importance of each neuron. We further derive a fast closed-form solution for the energy function, and show that the solution can be implemented in less than ten lines of code. Another advantage of the module is that most of the operators are selected based on the solution to the defined energy function, avoiding too many efforts for structure tuning. Quantitative evaluations on various visual tasks demonstrate that the proposed module is flexible and effective to improve the representation ability of many ConvNets. Our code is available at Pytorch-SimAM.

paragraphs: Attention modules adjust the importance of features inside a convolutional network. SimAM assigns three-dimensional attention weights across a layer’s feature map without adding learned parameters to the original network. This allows importance to vary across the feature map rather than being expressed only as channel-wise or spatial-wise weights.

The authors draw on neuroscience theories to formulate an energy function for estimating each neuron’s importance. They derive a fast closed-form solution, so the importance calculation does not require an iterative optimization procedure at each use. The solution can be implemented in fewer than ten lines of code, making the proposed module compact.

Most of the module’s operators follow from the energy-function solution, reducing the amount of structural tuning involved in its design. Quantitative evaluations across several visual tasks show improved representation ability in many convolutional networks. The contribution is therefore an explicit importance criterion together with an efficient implementation, supported by empirical evidence that parameter-free attention can improve the evaluated networks.
summary.tldr: SimAM derives three-dimensional feature attention from an energy function without adding learned network parameters.

title: SimAM: A Simple, Parameter-Free Attention Module for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: No man is an island. Humans develop the ability to communicate with a large community by coordinating with different interlocutors within short conversations. This ability is largely understudied by the research on building neural language communicative agents. We study the task of few-shot language coordination: agents quickly adapting to their conversational partners’ language abilities. Different from current communicative agents trained with self-play, we in- investigate this more general paradigm by requiring the lead agent to coordinate with a population of agents each of whom has different linguistic abilities. This leads to a general agent able to quickly adapt to communicating with unseen agents in the population. Unlike prior work, success here requires the ability to model the partner’s beliefs, a vital component of human communication. Drawing inspiration from the study of theory-of-mind (ToM; Premack & Woodruff (1978)), we study the effect of the speaker explicitly modeling the listener’s mental state. Learning by communicating with a population, the speakers, as shown in our experiments, acquire the ability to learn to predict the reactions of their partner upon various messages on-the-fly. The speaker’s predictions for the future actions help it generate the best instructions in order to maximize communicative goal with message costs. To examine our hypothesis that the instructions generated with ToM modeling yield better communication per- performance, we employ our agents in both a referential game and a language navigation task. Positive results from our experiments also hint at the importance of explicitly modeling language acquisition as a socio-pragmatic progress.

The agents learn to predict partner reactions on the fly, helping them tailor communication during short interactions. The findings also suggest that studying language acquisition as a social, goal-directed process can be useful for building agents that coordinate across differences in language ability.
summary.tldr: Speakers that model their listeners' reactions learn to adapt communication quickly across partners with different language abilities.

title: Few-shot Language Coordination by Modeling Theory of Mind

abstract: In non-private stochastic convex optimization, stochastic gradient methods converge much faster on interpolation problems—namely, problems where there exists a solution that simultaneously minimizes all of the sample losses—than on non-interpolating ones; similar improvements are not known in the private setting. In this paper, we investigate differentially private stochastic optimization in the interpolation regime. First, we show that without additional assumptions, interpolation problems do not exhibit an improved convergence rates with differential privacy. However, when the functions exhibit quadratic growth around the optimum, we show (near) exponential improvements in the private sample complexity. In particular, we propose an adaptive algorithm that improves the sample complexity to achieve expected error $\alpha$ from $\frac{d}{\diffp \sqrt{\alpha}}$ to $\frac{1}{\alpha^\rho} + \frac{d}{\diffp} \log\paren{\frac{1}{\alpha}}$ for any fixed $\rho >0$, while retaining the standard minimax-optimal sample complexity for non-interpolation problems. We prove a lower bound that shows the dimension-dependent term in the expression above is tight. Furthermore, we provide a superefficiency result which demonstrates the necessity of the polynomial term for adaptive algorithms: any algorithm that has a polylogarithmic sample complexity for interpolation problems cannot achieve the minimax-optimal rates for the family of non-interpolation problems.

paragraphs: An interpolation problem has a solution that minimizes every sample loss simultaneously. Without privacy constraints, stochastic gradient methods can exploit this structure to converge much faster. This paper investigates whether differential privacy permits similar improvements and finds that interpolation alone is insufficient to improve convergence rates.

Additional structure changes the result. When the objective functions have quadratic growth around the optimum, the authors obtain near-exponential improvements in private sample complexity. Their adaptive algorithm makes the dimension-dependent contribution logarithmic in inverse target error, while retaining an additional polynomial contribution. It also preserves standard minimax-optimal sample complexity on problems that do not interpolate.

The paper pairs the algorithm with lower bounds explaining the limits of these gains. The dimension-dependent contribution is tight. A further result shows why an adaptive algorithm needs the polynomial contribution: achieving only polylogarithmic sample complexity on interpolation problems would prevent minimax-optimal performance across non-interpolation problems. The contribution therefore identifies both a sufficient condition for substantial private optimization gains and a tradeoff governing adaptation across the two problem families.
summary.tldr: Interpolation speeds private optimization under quadratic growth, but lower bounds constrain how far adaptive algorithms can exploit it.

title: Private optimization in the interpolation regime: faster rates and hardness results

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs), a class of distribution-learning methods based on a two-player game between a generator and a discriminator, can generally be formulated as a minmax problem based on the variational representation of a divergence between the unknown and the generated distributions. We introduce structure-preserving GANs as a data-efficient framework for learning distributions with additional structure such as group symmetry, by developing new variational representations for divergences. Our theory shows that we can reduce the discriminator space to its projection on the invariant discriminator space, using the conditional expectation with respect to the sigma-algebra associated to the underlying structure. In addition, we prove that the discriminator space reduction must be accompanied by a careful design of structured generators, as flawed designs may easily lead to a catastrophic “mode collapse” of the learned distribution. We contextualize our framework by building symmetry-preserving GANs for distributions with intrinsic group symmetry, and demonstrate that both players, namely the equivariant generator and invariant discriminator, play important but distinct roles in the learning process. Empirical experiments and ablation studies across a broad range of data sets, including real-world medical imaging, validate our theory, and show our proposed methods achieve significantly improved sample fidelity and diversity—almost an order of magnitude measured in Frechet Inception Distance—especially in the small data regime.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn distributions through competition between a generator and a discriminator. This paper develops a framework for distributions with additional structure, such as group symmetry. It introduces new variational representations of distribution divergences so that this structure can be incorporated into the learning problem.

The theory shows how to project the discriminator space onto an invariant space using conditional expectation associated with the structure. It also proves that reducing the discriminator space must be paired with careful generator design: flawed structured generators can lead to severe mode collapse. The two components therefore need coordinated treatment.

Experiments and ablations across datasets, including medical images, support the theory. Reported improvements in sample quality and diversity include nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement measured by Fréchet Inception Distance, especially with little data. The findings connect structural design choices to more effective learning in that regime.
summary.tldr: Structure-preserving GANs coordinate invariant discriminators and structured generators to improve sample quality and diversity, especially with limited data.

title: Structure-preserving GANs

abstract: Existing techniques for model inversion typically rely on hard-to-tune regularizers, such as total variation or feature regularization, which must be individually calibrated for each network in order to produce adequate images. In this work, we introduce Plug-In Inversion, which relies on a simple set of augmentations and does not require excessive hyper-parameter tuning. Under our proposed augmentation-based scheme, the same set of augmentation hyper-parameters can be used for inverting a wide range of image classification models, regardless of input dimensions or the architecture. We illustrate the practicality of our approach by inverting Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) trained on the ImageNet dataset, tasks which to the best of our knowledge have not been successfully accomplished by any previous works.

paragraphs: Model inversion for vision produces images from a trained model, but existing techniques often need carefully tuned regularizers to obtain adequate results. The paper highlights total variation and feature regularization as examples whose settings may need to be calibrated separately for each network. This creates practical friction when applying inversion across different image classifiers.

Plug-In Inversion uses a simple set of data augmentations and avoids excessive hyperparameter tuning. Under the proposed scheme, the same augmentation settings can be reused across a wide range of classifiers with different architectures and input dimensions. This reuse is the central practical benefit: the inversion procedure becomes easier to apply across model designs.

The authors demonstrate the approach by inverting Vision Transformers and multilayer perceptrons trained on ImageNet. They describe these demonstrations as previously unaccomplished to the best of their knowledge. The results support the method’s applicability to these architectures and its broader aim of reducing network-specific calibration, while preserving the qualified nature of the paper’s novelty claim.
summary.tldr: Plug-In Inversion uses reusable augmentation settings to invert diverse image classifiers with less model-specific tuning.

title: Plug-In Inversion: Model-Agnostic Inversion for Vision with Data Augmentations

abstract: Multi-agent policy gradient methods in centralized training with decentralized execution recently witnessed many progresses. During centralized training, multi-agent credit assignment is crucial, which can substantially promote learning performance. However, explicit multi-agent credit assignment in multi-agent policy gradient methods still receives less attention. In this paper, we investigate multi-agent credit assignment induced by reward shaping and provide a theoretical understanding in terms of its credit assignment and policy bias. Based on this, we propose an exponentially weighted advantage estimator, which is analogous to GAE, to enable multi-agent credit assignment while allowing the tradeoff with policy bias. Empirical results show that our approach can successfully perform effective multi-agent credit assignment, and thus substantially outperforms other advantage estimators.

paragraphs: The paper studies how cooperating agents can receive useful individual learning signals when training is centralized but execution is decentralized. A team outcome alone does not explicitly allocate credit among agents. The authors focus on this allocation within multi-agent policy-gradient methods, where explicit credit assignment has received comparatively less attention.

They first analyze how reward shaping induces credit assignment and what bias it introduces into policy learning. This connects the usefulness of a modified learning signal with its potential to alter the policy update. Building on that analysis, they propose an exponentially weighted advantage estimator analogous to generalized advantage estimation. The estimator supports credit assignment while allowing a tradeoff with policy bias.

Empirical results show effective multi-agent credit assignment and substantial improvements over other advantage estimators. The contribution is therefore both analytical and algorithmic: it explains an interaction between credit and bias, then incorporates that interaction into an estimator. Its stated benefit is improved learning in the reported experiments while retaining a way to balance the competing effects.
summary.tldr: An exponentially weighted advantage estimator improves multi-agent credit assignment while allowing a tradeoff with policy bias.

title: Difference Advantage Estimation for Multi-Agent Policy Gradients

abstract: Policy gradient (PG) estimation becomes a challenge when we are not allowed to sample with the target policy but only have access to a dataset generated by some unknown behavior policy. Conventional methods for off-policy PG estimation often suffer from either significant bias or exponentially large variance. In this paper, we propose the double Fitted PG estimation (FPG) algorithm. FPG can work with an arbitrary policy parameterization, assuming access to a Bellman-complete value function class. In the case of linear value function approximation, we provide a tight finite-sample upper bound on policy gradient estimation error, that is governed by the amount of distribution mismatch measured in feature space. We also establish the asymptotic normality of FPG estimation error with a precise covariance characterization, which is further shown to be statistically optimal with a matching Cramer-Rao lower bound. Empirically, we evaluate the performance of FPG on both policy gradient estimation and policy optimization, using either softmax tabular or ReLU policy networks. Under various metrics, our results show that FPG significantly outperforms existing off-policy PG estimation methods based on importance sampling and variance reduction techniques.

paragraphs: A policy gradient indicates how a decision policy should change to improve performance. Estimating it becomes difficult when the available data come from an unknown behavior policy and new samples from the target policy are unavailable. This paper addresses that offline estimation problem, where conventional approaches can have substantial bias or exponentially large variance.

The proposed double Fitted Policy Gradient algorithm supports arbitrary policy parameterizations, assuming access to a Bellman-complete value function class. For linear value approximation, the authors prove a tight finite-sample error bound controlled by distribution mismatch in feature space. This connects estimation accuracy to how the available data and target policy differ through the chosen features.

The authors also establish asymptotic normality with a precise covariance characterization and statistical optimality through a matching Cramer-Rao lower bound. Experiments examine both gradient estimation and policy optimization with softmax tabular policies and ReLU policy networks. Across the reported metrics, FPG substantially outperforms existing approaches based on importance sampling and variance reduction, complementing the theoretical analysis with empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: Double fitted iteration estimates policy gradients from offline data, with tight error analysis and statistical optimality results under the stated conditions.

title: Optimal Estimation of Policy Gradient via Double Fitted Iteration

abstract: Extreme classification (XC) involves predicting over large numbers of classes (thousands to millions), with real-world applications like news article classification and e-commerce product tagging. The zero-shot version of this task requires generalization to novel classes without additional supervision. In this paper, we develop SemSup-XC, a model that achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot and few-shot performance on three XC datasets derived from legal, e-commerce, and Wikipedia data. To develop SemSup-XC, we use automatically collected semantic class descriptions to represent classes and facilitate generalization through a novel hybrid matching module that matches input instances to class descriptions using a combination of semantic and lexical similarity. Trained with contrastive learning, SemSup-XC significantly outperforms baselines and establishes state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets considered, gaining up to 12 precision points on zero-shot and more than 10 precision points on one-shot tests, with similar gains for recall@10. Our ablation studies highlight the relative importance of our hybrid matching module and automatically collected class descriptions.

paragraphs: Extreme classification involves choosing labels from thousands or even millions of classes. In its zero-shot form, a model must handle new classes without additional supervision. SemSup-XC addresses this by representing classes through automatically collected descriptions, giving the model information about what a class means even when labeled examples for it are unavailable.

The model uses a hybrid matching module that compares an input with class descriptions through both semantic and lexical similarity. This combines matching by meaning with matching based on wording. Contrastive learning trains the model around these relationships. The approach makes the content of a class description a central part of classification, rather than treating each class only as an identifier.

Across three datasets drawn from legal, e-commerce, and Wikipedia data, SemSup-XC achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot and few-shot performance. Reported gains reach 12 precision points in zero-shot tests and exceed 10 points in one-shot tests, with similar improvements in recall@10. Ablations highlight the contributions of the hybrid matching module and collected descriptions, supporting both components' importance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SemSup-XC combines class descriptions with semantic and lexical matching to improve zero-shot and few-shot extreme classification.

title: SemSup-XC: Semantic Supervision for Zero and Few-shot Extreme Classification

abstract: Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and its variants are the most popular optimization algorithms in federated learning (FL). Previous convergence analyses of FedAvg either assume full client participation or partial client participation where the clients can be uniformly sampled. However, in practical cross-device FL systems, only a subset of clients that satisfy local criteria such as battery status, network connectivity, and maximum participation frequency requirements (to ensure privacy) are available for training at a given time. As a result, client availability follows a natural cyclic pattern . We provide (to our knowledge) the first theoretical framework to analyze the convergence of FedAvg with cyclic client participation with several different client optimizers such as GD, SGD, and shuffled SGD. Our analysis discovers that cyclic client participation can achieve a faster asymptotic convergence rate than vanilla FedAvg with uniform client participation under suitable conditions, providing valuable insights into the design of client sampling protocols.
originalAbstract: Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and its variants are the most popular optimization algorithms in federated learning (FL). Previous convergence analyses of FedAvg either assume full client participation or partial client participation where the clients can be uniformly sampled. However, in practical cross-device FL systems, only a subset of clients that satisfy local criteria such as battery status, network connectivity, and maximum participation frequency requirements (to ensure privacy) are available for training at a given time. As a result, client availability follows a natural cyclic pattern . We provide (to our knowledge) the first theoretical framework to analyze the convergence of FedAvg with cyclic client participation with several different client optimizers such as GD, SGD, and shuffled SGD. Our analysis discovers that cyclic client participation can achieve a faster asymptotic convergence rate than vanilla FedAvg with uniform client participation under suitable conditions, providing valuable insights into the design of client sampling protocols.

paragraphs: Federated Averaging trains a shared model through participating clients. Many earlier convergence analyses assume that every client participates or that participating clients can be sampled uniformly. Practical device availability depends on battery levels, connectivity, and participation-frequency requirements, which can instead create recurring patterns in who is available.

This paper develops a theoretical framework for analyzing FedAvg when client participation is cyclic. It covers several ways clients perform local optimization, including gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, and shuffled stochastic gradient descent. The framework brings the participation pattern into the convergence analysis rather than treating uniform sampling as the default.

The analysis shows that cyclic participation can achieve a faster asymptotic convergence rate than vanilla FedAvg with uniform participation under suitable conditions. This is a conditional rate comparison, so it does not imply that every cyclic schedule improves training. Its significance is that recurring availability need not be treated only as a practical obstacle: the resulting structure can offer advantages that inform client-sampling protocol design.
summary.tldr: A convergence framework shows that cyclic client participation can accelerate FedAvg asymptotically under suitable conditions.

title: On the Convergence of Federated Averaging with Cyclic Client Participation

abstract: Advancements in deep learning are often associated with increasing model sizes. Training and deploying large models require sophisticated hardware and incur significantly higher costs. Thus, model compression is a widely explored approach to solving the problem. However, SOTA techniques fall short in one or more desirable aspects of compression - for instance, pruning does not reduce memory for training, quantization can only provide up to 32$\times$ compression, HashedNet is cache-inefficient, etc. This paper proposes a model-agnostic, cache-friendly, and hardware-aware model compression approach: Random Operation Access Specific Tile (ROAST) hashing. ROAST collapses the parameters by clubbing them through a lightweight mapping. While clubbing these parameters, ROAST utilizes cache hierarchies by aligning the memory access pattern with the parameter access pattern. ROAST is up to ${\sim}25\times$ faster to train and ${\sim}50\times$ faster to infer than the popular parameter sharing method HashedNet. Additionally, ROAST introduces global weight sharing, which is empirically and theoretically superior to local weight sharing in HashedNet, and can be of independent interest. With ROAST, we can efficiently train and deploy the model using a much smaller memory footprint ($\sim 10 - 100\times$ lesser) in text and image classification tasks. ROAST-MM kernel implementation is open-source (https://github.com/apd10/RzLinear/tree/stable)

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network saves memory, but the way compressed parameters are accessed also affects execution speed. This paper introduces ROAST hashing, a model-agnostic compression method that explicitly accounts for hardware memory access. It targets the costs of both training and deploying large models.

ROAST uses a lightweight mapping to group parameters so they share stored values. Its mapping aligns memory access with the order in which operations need parameters, making use of cache hierarchies. The method also introduces global weight sharing, which the authors support theoretically and empirically as superior to the local sharing used by HashedNet.

Compared with HashedNet, the reported speedups reach approximately 25 times for training and 50 times for inference. On text and image classification tasks, ROAST enables training and deployment with memory footprints approximately 10 to 100 times smaller. These are reported results rather than fixed speedups for every workload. The broader contribution is to connect parameter sharing with efficient hardware access, so reducing stored weights can also translate into practical computational benefits.
summary.tldr: ROAST combines global parameter sharing with cache-aware access to reduce model memory and accelerate execution relative to HashedNet.

title: Hardware-Aware Compression with Random Operation Access Specific Tile (ROAST) Hashing

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently become the standard approach for learning with graph-structured data. Prior work has shed light into their potential, but also their limitations. Unfortunately, it was shown that standard GNNs are limited in their expressive power. These models are no more powerful than the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) algorithm in terms of distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. In this paper, we propose Path Neural Networks (PathNNs), a model that updates node representations by aggregating paths emanating from nodes. We derive three different variants of the PathNN model that aggregate single shortest paths, all shortest paths and all simple paths of length up to K. We prove that two of these variants are strictly more powerful than the 1-WL algorithm, and we experimentally validate our theoretical results. We find that PathNNs can distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs that are indistinguishable by 1-WL, while our most expressive PathNN variant can even distinguish between 3-WL indistinguishable graphs. The different PathNN variants are also evaluated on graph classification and graph regression datasets, where in most cases, they outperform the baseline methods.

paragraphs: Standard graph neural networks can fail to distinguish graphs with different structures. Their distinguishing power is bounded by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test, or 1-WL. Path Neural Networks address this limitation by updating each node's representation using paths that start at that node.

The paper develops three variants: one aggregates single shortest paths, another all shortest paths, and another all simple paths up to length K. The authors prove that two variants are strictly more expressive than 1-WL. Experiments confirm that PathNNs can separate pairs of non-isomorphic graphs that 1-WL cannot distinguish.

The most expressive variant also distinguishes some graphs that 3-WL cannot separate. This is a statement about those graph distinctions, rather than a claim of universal dominance over 3-WL. Evaluations on graph classification and regression datasets find that the variants outperform baselines in most cases. Together, the results connect path-based aggregation to both stronger structural discrimination and improved performance on the evaluated prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: PathNNs aggregate paths to increase graph-distinguishing power and outperform baselines on most evaluated classification and regression datasets.

title: Path Neural Networks: Expressive and Accurate Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Budget management strategies in repeated auctions have received growing attention in online advertising markets. However, previous work on budget management in online bidding mainly focused on second-price auctions. The rapid shift from second-price auctions to first-price auctions for online ads in recent years has motivated the challenging question of how to bid in repeated first-price auctions while controlling budgets. In this work, we study the problem of learning in repeated first-price auctions with budgets. We design a dual-based algorithm that can achieve a near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret with full information feedback where the maximum competing bid is always revealed after each auction. We further consider the setting with one-sided information feedback where only the winning bid is revealed after each auction. We show that our modified algorithm can still achieve an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret with mild assumptions on the bidder’s value distribution. Finally, we complement the theoretical results with numerical experiments to confirm the effectiveness of our budget management policy.

paragraphs: Repeated auction bidding requires balancing opportunities to win against a limited spending budget. This paper studies that problem for first-price auctions, motivated by changes in online advertising markets. The learning challenge depends partly on what a bidder can observe after each auction, since feedback determines what can be learned about competing bids.

The authors develop a dual-based algorithm for full-information feedback, where the maximum competing bid is revealed after every auction. They prove a near-optimal regret bound of roughly the square root of the number of auctions, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Regret measures the performance gap to the comparison benchmark, so this bound controls how that gap grows across repeated decisions.

They then modify the algorithm for one-sided feedback, where only the winning bid is disclosed. The same regret order remains achievable under mild assumptions on the bidder’s value distribution. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the budget policy. The results connect budget management with learning under two feedback regimes, while retaining an explicit distributional condition for the less informative setting.
summary.tldr: A dual-based bidding algorithm achieves near-optimal regret under full feedback and the same regret order under one-sided feedback with mild value-distribution assumptions.

title: Learning to Bid in Repeated First-Price Auctions with Budgets

abstract: This paper demonstrates that language models are strong structure-based protein designers. We present LM-Design, a generic approach to reprogramming sequence-based protein language models (pLMs), that have learned massive sequential evolutionary knowledge from the universe of natural protein sequences, to acquire an immediate capability to design preferable protein sequences for given folds. We conduct a structural surgery on pLMs, where a lightweight structural adapter is implanted into pLMs and endows it with structural awareness. During inference, iterative refinement is performed to effectively optimize the generated protein sequences. Experiments show that LM-Design improves the state-of-the-art results by a large margin, leading to 4% to 12% accuracy gains in sequence recovery (e.g., 55.65%/56.63% on CATH 4.2/4.3 single-chain benchmarks, and $>$60% when designing protein complexes). We provide extensive and in-depth analyses, which verify that LM-Design can (1) indeed leverage both structural and sequential knowledge to accurately handle structurally non-deterministic regions, (2) benefit from scaling data and model size, and (3) generalize to other proteins (e.g., antibodies and de novo proteins).

paragraphs: Protein language models acquire information from large collections of natural protein sequences. LM-Design adapts that sequence knowledge to a structural design task: proposing protein sequences for a given fold. The paper’s central idea is to add structural awareness to an existing sequence model so that both sources of information guide generation.

The method inserts a lightweight structural adapter into the protein language model. During inference, iterative refinement further optimizes the proposed sequences. This provides a generic way to reprogram sequence-based models for structure-conditioned design while drawing on the evolutionary information already learned from natural sequences.

Experiments report sequence-recovery accuracy gains of 4% to 12%, including 55.65% and 56.63% on the CATH 4.2 and 4.3 single-chain benchmarks and above 60% for protein complexes. Additional analyses show that the approach uses structural and sequential knowledge in structurally non-deterministic regions, benefits from larger datasets and models, and generalizes to examples including antibodies and de novo proteins. The reported findings establish stronger sequence design and recovery performance across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: LM-Design adds a structural adapter and iterative refinement to protein language models, improving sequence design for specified folds.

title: Structure-informed Language Models Are Protein Designers

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) drive current AI breakthroughs despite very little being known about their internal representations. In this work, we propose to shed the light on LLMs inner mechanisms through the lens of geometry. In particular, we develop in closed form $(i)$ the intrinsic dimension in which the Multi-Head Attention embeddings are constrained to exist and $(ii)$ the partition and per-region affine mappings of the feedforward (MLP) network of LLMs’ layers. Our theoretical findings further enable the design of novel principled solutions applicable to state-of-the-art LLMs. First, we show that, through our geometric understanding, we can bypass LLMs’ RLHF protection by controlling the embedding’s intrinsic dimension through informed prompt manipulation. Second, we derive interpretable geometrical features that can be extracted from any (pre-trained) LLM, providing a rich abstract representation of their inputs. We observe that these features are sufficient to help solve toxicity detection, and even allow the identification of various types of toxicity. Our results demonstrate how, even in large-scale regimes, exact theoretical results can answer practical questions in LLMs. Code: https://github.com/RandallBalestriero/SplineLLM

paragraphs: The paper investigates language-model internals through geometry. It derives closed-form descriptions of the intrinsic dimension available to multi-head attention embeddings and of the regions and affine mappings formed by feedforward layers. These descriptions turn aspects of internal representations into mathematical objects that can be analyzed directly.

The authors use this analysis in two applications. First, they show that informed prompt manipulation can control embedding dimension and bypass protection from reinforcement learning with human feedback. Second, they construct interpretable geometric features that can be extracted from pretrained language models and used to represent properties of their inputs.

The extracted features help detect toxicity and distinguish different types of toxic content. Together, these findings connect exact structural analysis with both a model vulnerability and a detection task. The contribution is therefore more than a description of representation geometry: it demonstrates that geometric quantities can guide practical interventions and provide useful signals for understanding language-model inputs.
summary.tldr: Exact descriptions of language-model geometry support interpretable toxicity detection and reveal a way to bypass RLHF protection through prompt manipulation.

title: Characterizing Large Language Model Geometry Helps Solve Toxicity Detection and Generation

abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable performance on many generative tasks. Despite recent success, most diffusion models are restricted in that they only allow linear transformation of the data distribution. In contrast, broader family of transformations can help train generative distributions more efficiently, simplifying the reverse process and closing the gap between the true negative log-likelihood and the variational approximation. In this paper, we present Neural Diffusion Models (NDMs), a generalization of conventional diffusion models that enables defining and learning time-dependent non-linear transformations of data. We show how to optimise NDMs using a variational bound in a simulation-free setting. Moreover, we derive a time-continuous formulation of NDMs, which allows fast and reliable inference using off-the-shelf numerical ODE and SDE solvers. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of NDMs through experiments on many image generation benchmarks, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, downsampled versions of ImageNet and CelebA-HQ. NDMs outperform conventional diffusion models in terms of likelihood, achieving state-of-the-art results on ImageNet and CelebA-HQ, and produces high-quality samples.

paragraphs: Conventional diffusion models commonly restrict how they transform the data distribution to linear transformations. Neural Diffusion Models expand this design space by learning nonlinear transformations that vary with time. The motivation is that a more flexible transformation family can make the reverse generation process easier and tighten the variational approximation used to assess likelihood.

The paper develops a way to optimize these models through a variational bound without simulation during that optimization. It also derives a continuous-time formulation. This allows inference to use existing numerical solvers for ordinary and stochastic differential equations, connecting the generalized model to established tools for carrying out the generation process.

Experiments cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, downsampled ImageNet, and CelebA-HQ. The authors report better likelihoods than conventional diffusion models, including state-of-the-art likelihood results on ImageNet and CelebA-HQ, along with high-quality samples. The contribution is therefore both a broader mathematical model and an implementable training and inference framework, with the evaluated likelihood gains supporting the value of learning more flexible transformations.
summary.tldr: Neural Diffusion Models learn time-dependent nonlinear transformations and improve likelihoods across image-generation benchmarks.

title: Neural Diffusion Models

abstract: Macro placement is a crucial step in modern chip design, and reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising technique for improving the placement quality. However, existing RL-based techniques are hindered by their low sample efficiency, requiring numerous online rollouts or substantial offline expert data to achieve bootstrap, which are often impractical in industrial scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose a novel sample-efficient framework, namely EfficientPlace, for fast macro placement. EfficientPlace integrates a global tree search algorithm to strategically direct the optimization process, as well as a RL agent for local policy learning to advance the tree search. Experiments on commonly used benchmarks demonstrate that EfficientPlace achieves remarkable placement quality within a short timeframe, outperforming recent state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Macro placement is an important optimization step in chip design. Reinforcement learning has shown promise for improving placement quality, but existing approaches can require many online rollouts or substantial offline expert data to get started. Those demands motivate a method that uses its learning experience more efficiently.

EfficientPlace combines a global tree search with an agent that learns local policies. The search directs the overall optimization process, while the reinforcement learning component helps advance the search through local policy learning. This division gives the method a global mechanism for organizing exploration and a learned mechanism for making progress within that organization.

The authors evaluate the framework on commonly used benchmarks and report strong placement quality within a short time, outperforming recent leading approaches. The findings support integrating search and reinforcement learning as a route to faster, more sample-efficient macro placement. The paper's central contribution is the interaction between the global search procedure and the locally trained agent, aimed at reducing the experience burden of placement optimization.
summary.tldr: EfficientPlace combines global tree search with local reinforcement learning to achieve strong macro placement quality in a short time.

title: Reinforcement Learning within Tree Search for Fast Macro Placement

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited impressive capabilities in comprehending complex instructions. However, their blind adherence to provided instructions has led to concerns regarding risks of malicious use. Existing defence mechanisms, such as model fine-tuning or output censorship methods have proven to be fallible at ensuring that LLMs do not return semantically impermissible responses. We present fundamental limitations of verifying the semantic properties of LLM outputs and identifying compositional threats, illustrating inherent challenges of current approaches to censoring LLM outputs. Specifically, we demonstrate that semantic censorship can be perceived as an undecidable problem, and semantic properties of LLM outputs can become impossible to verify when the LLM is capable of providing "encrypted" outputs. We further show challenges of censorship can extend beyond just semantic censorship, as attackers can reconstruct impermissible outputs from a collection of permissible ones. Consequently, we call for a re-evaluation of the problem of censorship and its goals, stressing the need for new definitions and approaches to censorship. In addition, we provide an initial attempt toward achieving this goal through syntactic censorship, drawing from a security perspective to design censorship methods that can provide guarantees.

paragraphs: This position paper examines whether language-model defenses can reliably prevent responses with impermissible meaning. It focuses on fundamental verification problems behind fine-tuning and output censorship. The authors argue that failures of existing defenses motivate reconsidering what censorship should guarantee and how those guarantees should be defined.

They show that semantic censorship can be framed as an undecidable problem. They also identify conditions under which verifying an output's semantic properties can become impossible, including when a model can produce encrypted outputs. Another difficulty arises across multiple responses: individually permissible outputs can be combined to reconstruct an impermissible result.

These arguments challenge guarantees based only on judging the meaning of isolated responses. The paper calls for revised definitions and approaches, and offers an initial direction through syntactic censorship informed by security principles. Its position is that explicit restrictions on output form may support guarantees that semantic screening cannot generally provide, while the proposed direction is presented as an initial attempt.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies fundamental obstacles to semantic output censorship and proposes exploring security-based syntactic guarantees.

title: Position: Fundamental Limitations of LLM Censorship Necessitate New Approaches

abstract: Collaboration between different data centers is often challenged by heterogeneity across sites. To account for the heterogeneity, the state-of-the-art method is to re-weight the covariate distributions in each site to match the distribution of the target population. Nevertheless, this method still relies on the concept of traditional meta-analysis after adjusting for the distribution shift. This work proposes a collaborative inverse propensity score weighting estimator for causal inference with heterogeneous data. Instead of adjusting the distribution shift separately, we use weighted propensity score models to collaboratively adjust for the distribution shift. Our method shows significant improvements over the methods based on meta-analysis when heterogeneity increases. By incorporating outcome regression models, we prove the asymptotic normality when the covariates have dimension $d<8$. Our methods preserve privacy at individual sites by implementing federated learning protocols.

paragraphs: Combining causal evidence from multiple data centers becomes difficult when the populations at those centers differ. A common strategy first reweights each site's observed characteristics to resemble a target population, then combines results through meta-analysis. This paper proposes handling the population differences collaboratively within the causal estimator.

The method uses inverse propensity score weighting with weighted propensity models that jointly account for distribution shifts. Instead of making population adjustment a separate site-by-site preprocessing step, it incorporates that adjustment into the collaboration. Federated learning protocols allow the approach to preserve individual-site privacy while enabling the shared estimation procedure.

The authors report significant improvements over meta-analysis-based methods as heterogeneity increases. They also incorporate outcome regression models and prove asymptotic normality when the covariate dimension is below eight. That dimensional condition belongs to the stated theoretical result. Together, the findings support collaborative adjustment as a useful approach to combining heterogeneous evidence, with a distributional guarantee under the specified setting.
summary.tldr: Collaboratively weighted propensity models improve causal estimation across heterogeneous sites, with a stated asymptotic guarantee for covariate dimension below eight.

title: Collaborative Heterogeneous Causal Inference Beyond Meta-analysis

abstract: Minimum-norm interpolators have recently gained attention primarily as an analyzable model to shed light on the double descent phenomenon observed for neural networks. The majority of the work has focused on analyzing interpolators in Hilbert spaces, where typically an effectively low-rank structure of the feature covariance prevents a large bias. More recently, tight vanishing bounds have also been shown for isotropic high-dimensional data for $\ell_p$-spaces with $p\in[1,2)$, leveraging sparse structure of the ground truth. However, these proofs are tailored to specific settings and hard to generalize. This paper takes a first step towards establishing a general framework that connects generalization properties of the interpolators to well-known concepts from high-dimensional geometry, specifically, from the local theory of Banach spaces. In particular, we show that under $2$-uniform convexity, the bias of the minimal norm solution is bounded by the Gaussian complexity of the class. We then prove a “reverse” Efron-Stein lower bound on the expected conditional variance of the minimal norm solution under cotype $2$. Finally, we prove that this bound is sharp for $\ell_p$-linear regression under sub-Gaussian covariates.

paragraphs: Minimum-norm interpolation selects a smallest-norm solution among those that fit the training data exactly. Such models help researchers study double descent, but existing explanations often rely on particular feature structures or sparsity assumptions. This paper takes a step toward a more general account based on the geometry of the underlying function space.

The authors connect generalization to concepts from the local theory of Banach spaces. Under 2-uniform convexity, they bound the bias of the minimum-norm solution using the Gaussian complexity of the function class. This links one component of prediction error to a measure of class complexity, with the geometric assumption supplying the condition for the result.

For Lp linear regression with sub-Gaussian covariates, they prove that this variance bound is sharp. These results address bias and variance through different geometric conditions, providing a framework for understanding interpolation that reaches beyond proofs tailored to individual settings.
summary.tldr: The paper connects minimum-norm interpolation to Banach-space geometry through conditional bias bounds and sharp variance lower bounds.

title: Minimum Norm Interpolation Meets The Local Theory of Banach Spaces

abstract: Graph Neural Network (GNN) resembles the diffusion process, leading to the over-smoothing of learned representations when stacking many layers. Hence, the reverse process of message passing can produce the distinguishable node representations by inverting the forward message propagation. The distinguishable representations can help us to better classify neighboring nodes with different labels, such as in heterophilic graphs. In this work, we apply the design principle of the reverse process to the three variants of the GNNs. Additional analysis reveals that the reverse mechanism can mitigate the over-smoothing over hundreds of layers. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml-postech/reverse-gnn.

The empirical claim remains qualified: the reported improvements occur in many cases, rather than every graph setting.
summary.tldr: Reversing message propagation helps graph neural networks preserve node differences, improving many heterophilic-graph results and mitigating oversmoothing over hundreds of layers.

title: Mitigating Oversmoothing Through Reverse Process of GNNs for Heterophilic Graphs

abstract: We investigate the out-of-domain generalization of random feature (RF) models and Transformers. We first prove that in the ‘generalization on the unseen (GOTU)’ setting, where training data is fully seen in some part of the domain but testing is made on another part, and for RF models in the small feature regime, the convergence takes place to interpolators of minimal degree as in the Boolean case (Abbe et al., 2023). We then consider the sparse target regime and explain how this regime relates to the small feature regime, but with a different regularization term that can alter the picture in the non-Boolean case. We show two different outcomes for the sparse regime with q-ary data tokens: (1) if the data is embedded with roots of unities, then a min-degree interpolator is learned like in the Boolean case for RF models, (2) if the data is not embedded as such, e.g., simply as integers, then RF models and Transformers may not learn minimal degree interpolators. This shows that the Boolean setting and its roots of unities generalization are special cases where the minimal degree interpolator offers a rare characterization of how learning takes place. For more general integer and real-valued settings, a more nuanced picture remains to be fully characterized.

This paper studies whether random-feature models and Transformers prefer interpolating functions of minimal degree, extending a question previously examined for Boolean inputs.

For random-feature models in a small-feature regime, the authors prove convergence to minimal-degree interpolators. They then examine sparse targets, connecting that setting to the small-feature regime while identifying a different regularization term. For non-Boolean data, that difference can change which interpolating function learning selects.

The findings identify Boolean and roots-of-unity representations as special cases where this bias characterizes learning. General integer and real-valued settings require a more nuanced account that remains incompletely characterized.
summary.tldr: Minimal-degree generalization depends on the learning regime and token representation, and can fail beyond special non-Boolean embeddings.

title: On the Minimal Degree Bias in Generalization on the Unseen for non-Boolean Functions

abstract: Deep learning solvers for partial differential equations typically have limited accuracy. We propose to overcome this problem by using them as preconditioners. More specifically, we apply discretization-invariant neural operators to learn preconditioners for the flexible conjugate gradient method (FCG). Architecture paired with novel loss function and training scheme allows for learning efficient preconditioners that can be used across different resolutions. On the theoretical side, FCG theory allows us to safely use nonlinear preconditioners that can be applied in $O(N)$ operations without constraining the form of the preconditioners matrix. To justify learning scheme components (the loss function and the way training data is collected) we perform several ablation studies. Numerical results indicate that our approach favorably compares with classical preconditioners and allows to reuse of preconditioners learned for lower resolution to the higher resolution data.

paragraphs: Neural networks used directly as partial differential equation solvers often have limited accuracy. This paper gives them a different role: learning preconditioners that help an iterative numerical solver work efficiently. The resulting FCG-NO method pairs neural operators with flexible conjugate gradients, combining learned assistance with an established equation-solving procedure.

The neural operators are designed to work across discretizations, so their use is not tied to a single resolution. Architecture, loss function, and training-data collection are developed together to learn effective preconditioners. Flexible conjugate gradient theory permits nonlinear preconditioners in this setting, and the learned preconditioners can be applied in O(N) operations without imposing a restricted preconditioner-matrix form.

Ablation studies investigate the contributions of the loss and training-data collection scheme. Numerical results compare favorably with classical preconditioners and demonstrate reuse of preconditioners trained at lower resolution on higher-resolution data. The findings support using neural operators to accelerate numerical solving while addressing the accuracy problem that motivates moving away from standalone learned solvers.
summary.tldr: FCG-NO learns neural-operator preconditioners for flexible conjugate gradients, with favorable numerical results and transfer across resolutions.

title: Neural operators meet conjugate gradients: The FCG-NO method for efficient PDE solving

abstract: We study online learning in episodic constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where the learner aims at collecting as much reward as possible over the episodes, while satisfying some long-term constraints during the learning process. Rewards and constraints can be selected either stochastically or adversarially, and the transition function is not known to the learner. While online learning in classical (unconstrained) MDPs has received considerable attention over the last years, the setting of CMDPs is still largely unexplored. This is surprising, since in real-world applications, such as, e.g., autonomous driving, automated bidding, and recommender systems, there are usually additional constraints and specifications that an agent has to obey during the learning process. In this paper, we provide the first best-of-both-worlds algorithm for CMDPs with long-term constraints, in the flavor of Balseiro et al. (2023). Our algorithm is capable of handling settings in which rewards and constraints are selected either stochastically or adversarially, without requiring any knowledge of the underling process. Moreover, our algorithm matches state-of-the-art regret and constraint violation bounds for settings in which constraints are selected stochastically, while it is the first to provide guarantees in the case in which they are chosen adversarially.

paragraphs: A learning agent often must maximize reward while meeting requirements accumulated over time, such as a spending or resource constraint. This paper studies episodic constrained Markov decision processes with unknown transitions. Both rewards and constraints may be generated stochastically or chosen adversarially, making the learning environment especially flexible.

The proposed algorithm handles these regimes without knowing which process generated the observations. Its best-of-both-worlds design aims to retain strong behavior under benign stochastic conditions while providing guarantees when constraints or rewards are adversarial. Long-term constraint control is part of the learning objective, rather than a requirement checked only after a policy has been trained.

For stochastic constraints, the method matches existing regret and constraint-violation bounds. The authors also provide the first guarantees in the studied adversarial-constraint setting. The contribution is theoretical coverage across these environments; long-term violation bounds should not be mistaken for a statement that every individual action satisfies every possible safety constraint.
summary.tldr: A best-of-both-worlds CMDP algorithm controls regret and long-term violations under stochastic or adversarial rewards and constraints.

title: Online Learning in CMDPs: Handling Stochastic and Adversarial Constraints

abstract: Video encompasses both visual and auditory data, creating a perceptually rich experience where these two modalities complement each other. As such, videos are a valuable type of media for the investigation of the interplay between audio and visual elements. Previous studies of audio-visual modalities primarily focused on either audio-visual representation learning or generative modeling of a modality conditioned on the other, creating a disconnect between these two branches. A unified framework that learns representation and generates modalities has not been developed yet. In this work, we introduce a novel framework called Vision to Audio and Beyond (VAB) to bridge the gap between audio-visual representation learning and vision-to-audio generation. The key approach of VAB is that rather than working with raw video frames and audio data, VAB performs representation learning and generative modeling within latent spaces. In particular, VAB uses a pre-trained audio tokenizer and an image encoder to obtain audio tokens and visual features, respectively. It then performs the pre-training task of visual-conditioned masked audio token prediction. This training strategy enables the model to engage in contextual learning and simultaneous video-to-audio generation. After the pre-training phase, VAB employs the iterative-decoding approach to rapidly generate audio tokens conditioned on visual features. Since VAB is a unified model, its backbone can be fine-tuned for various audio-visual downstream tasks. Our experiments showcase the efficiency of VAB in producing high-quality audio from video, and its capability to acquire semantic audio-visual features, leading to competitive results in audio-visual retrieval and classification.

This task supports contextual representation learning alongside video-to-audio generation, making a single training setup serve both purposes.

summary.tldr: VAB unifies video-to-audio generation and audio-visual representation learning through visually conditioned prediction of masked audio tokens.

title: From Vision to Audio and Beyond: A Unified Model for Audio-Visual Representation and Generation

abstract: The study of machine learning under limited resources has gathered increasing attention, considering improving the learning efficiency and effectiveness with budgeted resources. However, previous efforts mainly focus on single learning task, and a common resource-limited scenario is less explored: to handle multiple time-constrained learning tasks concurrently with budgeted computational resources. In this paper, we point out that this is a very challenging task because it demands the learner to be concerned about not only the progress of the learning tasks but also the coordinative allocation of computational resources. We present the Learning with Adaptive Resource Allocation (LARA) approach, which comprises an efficient online estimator for learning progress prediction, an adaptive search method for computational resource allocation, and a balancing strategy for alleviating prediction-allocation compounding errors. Empirical studies validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Learning under a limited computing budget becomes more complicated when several tasks must run concurrently and each faces time constraints. The system must track how training is progressing while deciding how to divide resources among tasks. This paper focuses on that joint problem, which receives less attention than resource-limited learning for an individual task.

The proposed Learning with Adaptive Resource Allocation approach, LARA, has three components. An efficient online estimator predicts learning progress. An adaptive search method uses progress information to allocate computational resources. A balancing strategy addresses compounding errors between prediction and allocation, recognizing that these two parts of the process can affect one another.

Empirical studies support the effectiveness of the combined approach. The contribution is a coordinated way to manage learning progress and resource assignment across concurrent tasks. By including an explicit mechanism for prediction-allocation errors, LARA addresses the reliability of the allocation process as well as the immediate question of where the available computation should go.
summary.tldr: LARA combines progress prediction, adaptive resource allocation, and error balancing to manage multiple time-constrained learning tasks under a shared computing budget.

title: Learning with Adaptive Resource Allocation

abstract: Benign overfitting is the phenomenon wherein none of the predictors in the hypothesis class can achieve perfect accuracy (i.e., non-realizable or noisy setting), but a model that interpolates the training data still achieves good generalization. A series of recent works aim to understand this phenomenon for regression and classification tasks using linear predictors as well as two-layer neural networks. In this paper, we study such a benign overfitting phenomenon in an adversarial setting. We show that under a distributional assumption, interpolating neural networks found using adversarial training generalize well despite inference-time attacks. Specifically, we provide convergence and generalization guarantees for adversarial training of two-layer networks (with smooth as well as non-smooth activation functions) showing that under moderate $\ell_2$ norm perturbation budget, the trained model has near-zero robust training loss and near-optimal robust generalization error. We support our theoretical findings with an empirical study on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting occurs when a model fits its training data exactly yet still generalizes well, even though noise or other obstacles prevent perfect prediction across the underlying problem. This paper asks whether that phenomenon can also occur under adversarial training, where performance must remain good when inputs are deliberately perturbed at inference time.

The authors establish convergence and generalization guarantees for adversarially trained two-layer neural networks, considering both smooth and non-smooth activation functions. Their conclusions depend on a distributional assumption and a moderate perturbation budget measured by the l2 norm. Under these conditions, training yields near-zero robust training loss together with near-optimal robust generalization error.

The findings show that fitting the training data closely can coexist with robust generalization in the analyzed setting. They extend the discussion of benign overfitting from ordinary prediction to prediction under attacks, while retaining explicit conditions on the data and perturbations. An empirical study using synthetic and real-world data supports the theoretical conclusions.
summary.tldr: Under stated distributional and perturbation conditions, adversarially trained two-layer networks can fit training data closely while retaining near-optimal robust generalization.

title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarial Training of Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-objective alignment of foundation models with human preferences, which is a critical step towards helpful and harmless AI systems. However, it is generally costly and unstable to fine-tune large foundation models using reinforcement learning (RL), and the multi-dimensionality, heterogeneity, and conflicting nature of human preferences further complicate the alignment process. In this paper, we introduce Rewards-in-Context (RiC), which conditions the response of a foundation model on multiple rewards in its prompt context and applies supervised fine-tuning for alignment. The salient features of RiC are simplicity and adaptivity, as it only requires supervised fine-tuning of a single foundation model and supports dynamic adjustment for user preferences during inference time. Inspired by the analytical solution of an abstracted convex optimization problem, our dynamic inference-time adjustment method approaches the Pareto-optimal solution for multiple objectives. Empirical evidence demonstrates the efficacy of our method in aligning both Large Language Models (LLMs) and diffusion models to accommodate diverse rewards with only around 10% GPU hours compared with multi-objective RL baseline.

Reinforcement learning can make this process costly and unstable for large models. Rewards-in-Context, or RiC, addresses the problem by conditioning model responses on multiple rewards supplied in the prompt context.

RiC uses supervised fine-tuning of a single foundation model and allows preferences to be adjusted during inference. The contribution combines a relatively simple training procedure with control over preference trade-offs at inference time. Its findings support flexible multi-objective alignment without requiring a separately fine-tuned model for each preference adjustment.
summary.tldr: RiC uses reward-conditioned supervised fine-tuning to support inference-time preference adjustment, with reported GPU usage around 10% of a multi-objective RL baseline.

title: Rewards-in-Context: Multi-objective Alignment of Foundation Models with Dynamic Preference Adjustment

abstract: We investigate the phenomenon of grokking – delayed generalization accompanied by non-monotonic test loss behavior – in a simple binary logistic classification task, for which "memorizing" and "generalizing" solutions can be strictly defined. Surprisingly, we find that grokking arises naturally even in this minimal model when the parameters of the problem are close to a critical point, and provide both empirical and analytical insights into its mechanism. Concretely, by appealing to the implicit bias of gradient descent, we show that logistic regression can exhibit grokking when the training dataset is nearly linearly separable from the origin and there is strong noise in the perpendicular directions. The underlying reason is that near the critical point, "flat" directions in the loss landscape with nearly zero gradient cause training dynamics to linger for arbitrarily long times near quasi-stable solutions before eventually reaching the global minimum. Finally, we highlight similarities between our findings and the recent literature, strengthening the conjecture that grokking generally occurs in proximity to the interpolation threshold, reminiscent of critical phenomena often observed in physical systems.

paragraphs: Grokking describes delayed generalization accompanied by test loss that changes non-monotonically during training. This paper studies the phenomenon in binary logistic classification, a minimal setting where memorizing and generalizing solutions can be defined precisely. The authors find that even this simple model can exhibit grokking near a critical configuration of the problem.

Their analysis uses the implicit bias of gradient descent. Grokking can occur when training data are nearly linearly separable from the origin and noise is strong in perpendicular directions. Near this boundary, some directions in the loss landscape have almost no gradient. Training can consequently spend arbitrarily long periods near quasi-stable solutions before eventually reaching the global minimum.

Empirical observations and analytical results support this mechanism within the studied setting. The authors also connect it to related findings and strengthen the conjecture that grokking generally occurs near the interpolation threshold. That broader connection remains a conjecture. The concrete contribution is an explanation of how very slow movement through nearly flat regions can produce delayed generalization in a simple classification model.
summary.tldr: Logistic regression can exhibit grokking near a separability boundary, where nearly flat loss directions cause long delays before generalization.

title: Grokking at the Edge of Linear Separability

abstract: The classical static Schrödinger Bridge (SSB) problem, which seeks the most likely stochastic evolution between two marginal probability measures, has been studied extensively in the optimal transport and statistical physics communities, and more recently in machine learning communities in the surge of generative models. The standard approach to solve SSB is to first identify its Kantorovich dual and use Sinkhorn’s algorithm to find the optimal potential functions. While the original SSB is only a strictly convex minimization problem, this approach is known to warrant linear convergence under mild assumptions. In this work, we consider a generalized SSB allowing any strictly increasing divergence functional, far generalizing the entropy functional $x\log x$ in the standard SSB. This problem naturally arises in a wide range of seemingly unrelated problems in entropic optimal transport, random graphs/matrices, and combinatorics. We establish Kantorovich duality and linear convergence of Sinkhorn’s algorithm for the generalized SSB problem under mild conditions. Our results provide a new rigorous foundation for understanding Sinkhorn-type iterative methods in the context of large-scale generalized Schrödinger bridges.

paragraphs: The static Schrödinger bridge problem seeks the most likely stochastic evolution connecting two prescribed probability distributions. A standard solution strategy moves to a dual formulation and applies Sinkhorn’s algorithm to find optimal potential functions. For the classical problem, this iterative procedure is known to converge linearly under mild assumptions.

This paper extends that foundation to a generalized bridge problem allowing any strictly increasing divergence functional, substantially broadening the role played by the usual entropy expression. Such generalized problems arise across entropic optimal transport, random graphs and matrices, and combinatorics. The question is whether the dual formulation and convergence guarantees survive this broader choice of functional.

The authors establish Kantorovich duality and linear convergence of Sinkhorn’s algorithm for the generalized problem under mild conditions. Linear convergence describes geometric reduction of the relevant error as iterations proceed. These results give a rigorous basis for Sinkhorn-type methods across a wider family of bridge problems, with the stated conditions remaining part of the guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes duality and conditional linear convergence for Sinkhorn’s algorithm across a broad generalization of the static Schrödinger bridge problem.

title: Linear convergence of Sinkhorn’s algorithm for generalized static Schrödinger bridge

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness is a desired property of computer vision models. Improving model robustness requires high-quality signals from robustness benchmarks to quantify progress. While various benchmark datasets such as ImageNet-C were proposed in the ImageNet era, most ImageNet-C corruption types are no longer OOD relative to today’s large, web-scraped datasets, which already contain common corruptions such as blur or JPEG compression artifacts. Consequently, these benchmarks are no longer well-suited for evaluating OOD robustness in the era of web-scale datasets. Indeed, recent models show saturating scores on ImageNet-era OOD benchmarks, indicating that it is unclear whether models trained on web-scale datasets truly become better at OOD generalization or whether they have simply been exposed to the test distortions during training. To address this, we introduce LAION-C as a benchmark alternative for ImageNet-C. LAION-C consists of six novel distortion types specifically designed to be OOD, even for web-scale datasets such as LAION. In a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models, we find that the LAION-C dataset poses significant challenges to contemporary models, including MLLMs such as Gemini and GPT-4o. We additionally conducted a psychophysical experiment to evaluate the difficulty of our corruptions for human observers, enabling a comparison of models to lab-quality human robustness data. We observe a paradigm shift in OOD generalization: from humans outperforming models, to the best models now matching or outperforming the best human observers.
