paragraphs: A robustness benchmark becomes harder to interpret when its supposedly unfamiliar distortions already occur in training data. The paper argues that this affects older image benchmarks: web-scale datasets contain common effects such as blur and compression artifacts. Strong benchmark scores may therefore reflect exposure to those distortions as well as an ability to generalize.

LAION-C introduces six new distortion types designed to remain out of distribution even for web-scale datasets such as LAION. The authors evaluate contemporary vision models, including multimodal language models such as Gemini and GPT-4o, and find that these distortions present substantial challenges. The benchmark aims to provide a more informative test under this changed training regime.

The study also includes a psychophysical experiment measuring human performance on the corruptions under laboratory conditions. In these comparisons, the best models match or outperform the best human observers. That result concerns the evaluated distortions and tasks; it shows that challenging new robustness tests can coexist with model performance reaching or exceeding the measured human level.
summary.tldr: LAION-C tests web-scale vision models with six new distortions and finds substantial challenges alongside top models matching or exceeding measured human performance.

title: LAION-C: An Out-of-Distribution Benchmark for Web-Scale Vision Models

abstract: Binary Spiking Neural Networks (BSNNs) offer promising efficiency advantages for resource-constrained computing. However, their training algorithms often require substantial memory overhead due to latent weights storage and temporal processing requirements. To address this issue, we propose Binary Spiking Online (BSO) optimization algorithm, a novel online training algorithm that significantly reduces training memory. BSO directly updates weights through flip signals under the online training framework. These signals are triggered when the product of gradient momentum and weights exceeds a threshold, eliminating the need for latent weights during training. To enhance performance, we propose T-BSO, a temporal-aware variant that leverages the inherent temporal dynamics of BSNNs by capturing gradient information across time steps for adaptive threshold adjustment. Theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees for both BSO and T-BSO, with formal regret bounds characterizing their convergence rates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that both BSO and T-BSO achieve superior optimization performance compared to existing training methods for BSNNs. The codes are available at https://github.com/hamingsi/BSO.

Binary Spiking Online optimization, or BSO, targets this training cost through an online procedure that updates binary weights directly.

The temporal-aware extension, T-BSO, uses gradient information across time steps to adjust thresholds adaptively, incorporating the temporal dynamics that are intrinsic to spiking networks.

The paper establishes convergence guarantees for both variants and gives formal regret bounds characterizing their convergence rates. Experiments report better optimization performance than existing training methods for binary spiking networks, alongside the framework’s reduced training-memory requirements. The contribution links an explicit binary update mechanism with temporal adaptation, addressing the cost of training these networks as well as their optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: BSO reduces binary spiking network training memory through direct weight flips, while T-BSO adapts those updates using temporal gradients.

title: BSO: Binary Spiking Online Optimization Algorithm

abstract: Asynchronous Stochastic Gradient Descent (Asynchronous SGD) is a cornerstone method for parallelizing learning in distributed machine learning. However, its performance suffers under arbitrarily heterogeneous computation times across workers, leading to suboptimal time complexity and inefficiency as the number of workers scales. While several Asynchronous SGD variants have been proposed, recent findings by Tyurin & Richtárik (NeurIPS 2023) reveal that none achieve optimal time complexity, leaving a significant gap in the literature. In this paper, we propose Ringmaster ASGD, a novel Asynchronous SGD method designed to address these limitations and tame the inherent challenges of Asynchronous SGD. We establish, through rigorous theoretical analysis, that Ringmaster ASGD achieves optimal time complexity under arbitrarily heterogeneous and dynamically fluctuating worker computation times. This makes it the first Asynchronous SGD method to meet the theoretical lower bounds for time complexity in such scenarios.

paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent distributes learning across workers without requiring their computations to finish together. However, workers can differ greatly in speed, and those speeds can change over time. The paper identifies these variations as a source of suboptimal training time and inefficient scaling in existing asynchronous methods.

Ringmaster ASGD is a new asynchronous method designed for this setting. Its central result is a theoretical guarantee of optimal time complexity even with arbitrarily heterogeneous and dynamically fluctuating worker computation times. The guarantee addresses both persistent differences among workers and changes in their timing during execution.

Optimality here means that the method meets the theoretical lower bounds for time complexity in the analyzed scenarios. The authors present it as the first asynchronous SGD method to achieve that result, closing the gap left by previously proposed variants. This matters because distributing more computation across workers does not by itself establish that training finishes as quickly as theoretically possible. The contribution supplies that time-based guarantee for a demanding worker-timing setting.
summary.tldr: Ringmaster ASGD achieves theoretically optimal time complexity despite arbitrary differences and fluctuations in worker computation times.

title: Ringmaster ASGD: The First Asynchronous SGD with Optimal Time Complexity

abstract: In Machine learning, separating data into classes is a very fundamental problem. A mathematical framework around the classes is presented in this work to deepen the understanding of classes. The classes are defined as vectors in a Vector Space, where addition corresponds to the union of classes, and scalar multiplication resembles set complement of classes. The Zero-Vector in the vector space corresponds to a class referred to as the Metta-Class. This discovery enables numerous applications. One such application, termed ’clear learning’ in this work, focuses on learning the true nature (manifold) of the data instead of merely learning a boundary sufficient for classification. Another application, called ’unary class learning’, involves learning a single class in isolation rather than learning by comparing two or more classes. Additionally, ’set operations on classes’ is another application highlighted in this work. Furthermore, Continual Learning of classes is facilitated by smaller networks. The Metta-Class enables neural networks to learn only the data manifold; therefore, it can also be used for generation of new data. Results for the key applications are shown using the MNIST dataset. To further strengthen the claims, some results are also produced using the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k embeddings. The code supporting these applications is publicly available at: github.com/hm-4/Metta-Class.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a mathematical framework that represents data classes as vectors. Within this construction, vector addition corresponds to class union, while scalar multiplication resembles taking class complements. The authors identify the zero vector with a particular class they call the Metta-Class and use it to develop several learning applications.

One application, called clear learning, aims to learn the data manifold—the structure occupied by the data—rather than only a boundary sufficient for classification. Another, unary class learning, learns a class in isolation instead of through comparison with other classes. The framework also supports set operations on classes and is presented as facilitating continual learning with smaller networks.

The authors connect learning the manifold through the Metta-Class to generating new data. They show results for the main applications on MNIST and provide additional results using CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k embeddings. The contribution combines a proposed algebraic view of classes with demonstrations of the learning behaviors it enables in these settings.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a vector-space framework for classes whose Metta-Class supports manifold learning, isolated class learning, and other demonstrated applications.

title: Discovering a Zero (Zero-Vector Class of Machine Learning)

abstract: Fine-grained hashing has become a powerful solution for rapid and efficient image retrieval, particularly in scenarios requiring high discrimination between visually similar categories. To enable each hash bit to correspond to specific visual attributes, we propose a novel method that harnesses learnable queries for attribute-aware hash code learning. This method deploys a tailored set of queries to capture and represent nuanced attribute-level information within the hashing process, thereby enhancing both the interpretability and relevance of each hash bit. Building on this query-based optimization framework, we incorporate an auxiliary branch to help alleviate the challenges of complex landscape optimization often encountered with low-bit hash codes. This auxiliary branch models high-order attribute interactions, reinforcing the robustness and specificity of the generated hash codes. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method generates attribute-aware hash codes and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in retrieval accuracy and robustness, especially for low-bit hash codes, underscoring its potential in fine-grained image hashing tasks.

paragraphs: Fine-grained image retrieval must distinguish categories that can look almost identical while searching efficiently. Hashing addresses efficiency by representing images with short binary codes. This paper aims to make those codes more informative and interpretable by connecting individual bits to specific visual attributes rather than leaving their meaning implicit.

The method uses learnable queries to capture subtle attribute-level information during hash-code learning. It also adds an auxiliary branch that models higher-order interactions among attributes. That branch helps with the difficult optimization associated with short codes, where a limited number of bits must preserve the distinctions needed for accurate retrieval.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report attribute-aware codes and consistently better retrieval accuracy and robustness than state-of-the-art alternatives, particularly when codes contain few bits. The findings suggest that explicitly organizing the representation around attributes can improve both its usefulness and its interpretability. The auxiliary interaction modeling further supports compact codes by helping represent relationships among visual attributes within the constrained binary representation.
summary.tldr: Learnable attribute queries and an auxiliary interaction model improve compact image-retrieval hash codes, especially at low bit counts.

title: Learning Attribute-Aware Hash Codes for Fine-Grained Image Retrieval via Query Optimization

abstract: Significant achievements in personalization of diffusion models have been witnessed. Conventional tuning-free methods mostly encode multiple reference images by averaging or concatenating their image embeddings as the injection condition, but such an image-independent operation cannot perform interaction among images to capture consistent visual elements within multiple references. Although tuning-based approaches can effectively extract consistent elements within multiple images through the training process, it necessitates test-time finetuning for each distinct image group. This paper introduces EasyRef, a plug-and-play adaption method that empowers diffusion models to condition consistent visual elements (e.g., style and human facial identity, etc.) across multiple reference images under instruction controls. To effectively exploit consistent visual elements within multiple images, we leverage the multi-image comprehension and instruction-following capabilities of the multimodal large language model (MLLM), prompting it to capture consistent visual elements based on the instruction. Besides, injecting the MLLM’s representations into the diffusion process through adapters can easily generalize to unseen domains. To mitigate computational costs and enhance fine-grained detail preservation, we introduce an efficient reference aggregation strategy and a progressive training scheme. Finally, we introduce MRBench, a new multi-reference image generation benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate EasyRef surpasses both tuning-free and tuning-based methods, achieving superior aesthetic quality and robust zero-shot generalization across diverse domains.

paragraphs: EasyRef aims to make diffusion models use the visual elements shared across several reference images. Simply averaging or concatenating independently encoded images does not let the references interact to identify what they have in common. Methods that learn from each image group can capture these elements, but require additional fine-tuning for every new group.

The proposed method uses a multimodal language model to examine the references together and follow instructions about which consistent elements matter, such as visual style or facial identity. Adapters transfer its representations into the diffusion process. An efficient reference-aggregation strategy and progressive training scheme are designed to reduce computation while preserving fine details.

The paper also introduces MRBench for evaluating generation from multiple reference images. Experiments report that EasyRef outperforms both tuning-free and tuning-based alternatives, with stronger aesthetic quality and zero-shot generalization across diverse domains. The central result is that instruction-guided understanding of an image group can provide useful conditioning for generation without requiring separate test-time fine-tuning for each group.
summary.tldr: EasyRef uses a multimodal language model to extract instruction-selected visual elements shared across reference images and guide diffusion generation.

title: EasyRef: Omni-Generalized Group Image Reference for Diffusion Models via Multimodal LLM

abstract: Recent work shows that flow-matching networks can be effective for value function estimation in reinforcement learning, but it remains unclear why they work well or whether flow-matching Q-functions differ fundamentally from standard critics. We show that their success is not explained by distributional RL: explicitly modeling return distributions often degrades performance. Instead, we argue that flow-matching Q-functions are effective because they couple a learned velocity field with an integration procedure that is used both during training and to read out Q-values at inference time. This coupling enables robust value prediction through test-time recovery from imperfect intermediate estimates where errors dampen out as more integration steps are performed. This mechanism is absent in monolithic critics. Beyond test-time recovery, training with the integration procedure induces more plastic representations, allowing critics to represent non-stationary future TD targets without overwriting previous features. We formalize these effects and validate them empirically, showing that flow-matching critics outperform monolithic critics by over $2\times$ in performance and achieve $5$–$10\times$ higher sample efficiency in high-UTD regimes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why flow-matching critics work well for value estimation in reinforcement learning. The authors find that explicitly representing return distributions does not explain their success and often reduces performance. They instead attribute the benefits to combining a learned velocity field with an integration procedure used both in training and when producing Q-values.

That combination supports test-time recovery: imperfect intermediate estimates can improve as further integration steps dampen their errors. The authors identify this mechanism as absent from monolithic critics. The paper formalizes these mechanisms and tests them empirically. In high-UTD regimes, the authors report more than twice the performance of monolithic critics and five to ten times higher sample efficiency. The findings point to the interaction between learned dynamics and iterative value readout as a source of the gains, with representational adaptability providing an additional benefit during learning.
summary.tldr: The paper attributes flow-matching critics’ gains to iterative error recovery and adaptable representations, with strong reported benefits in high-UTD regimes.

title: What Does Flow-Matching Bring to TD-Learning?

abstract: Evaluating LLM agents for scientific tasks has focused on token costs while ignoring tool-use costs like simulation time and experimental resources. As a result, metrics like pass@k become impractical under realistic budget constraints. To address this gap, we introduce SimulCost, the first benchmark targeting cost-sensitive parameter tuning in physics simulations. SimulCost compares LLM tuning cost-sensitive parameters against traditional scanning approach in both accuracy and computational cost, spanning 2,643 single-round (initial guess) and 2,304 multi-round (adjustment by trial-and-error) tasks across 11 simulators from fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and plasma physics, whose costs are analytically defined and platform-independent. A twelfth simulator, a production plasma code measurable only by wall clock, is reported separately. Frontier LLMs achieve 45–62% success rates in single-round mode, dropping to 34–50% under high accuracy requirements, rendering their initial guesses unreliable especially for high accuracy tasks. Multi-round mode improves rates to 66–81%, but LLMs are 1.5–2.7$\times$ slower than traditional scanning, making them uneconomical choices. We also investigate parameter group correlations for knowledge transfer potential, and the impact of in-context examples and reasoning effort, providing practical implications for deployment and fine-tuning. We open-source SimulCost as a static benchmark and extensible toolkit to facilitate research on improving cost-aware agentic designs for physics simulations, and for expanding new simulation environments. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/SimulCost-Bench

abstract: Test-time strategies have shown remarkable success in improving large language models, but their application to next-token prediction (NTP) autoregressive (AR) image generation remains largely underexplored. Existing test-time scaling (TTS) methods for visual autoregressive models (VAR) rely on frequent partial decoding and external reward models, which are inefficient and often ineffective for NTP-based image generation due to the inherent instability of intermediate decoding results. To address these limitations, we propose ScalingAR, a novel test-time scaling framework tailored for NTP-based AR image generation. ScalingAR introduces token entropy as a confidence signal and operates at two complementary levels: (i) Profile Level, integrates intrinsic uncertainty and conditional utilization into a unified confidence state, and (ii) Policy Level, leverages this state for adaptive trajectory pruning and dynamic guidance scheduling. Without requiring early decoding or auxiliary rewards, ScalingAR achieves significant improvements across diverse benchmarks. Experiments show that ScalingAR (I) improves base models by 12.5% on GenEval and 15.2% on TIIF-Bench, (II) reduces visual token consumption by 62.0% while outperforming baselines, and (III) enhances robustness, mitigating performance degradation by 26.0% in challenging scenarios. These results establish ScalingAR as a robust and efficient test-time scaling solution for autoregressive image generation.

paragraphs: ScalingAR improves next-token autoregressive image generation by adapting computation at inference time. Existing approaches often inspect partially decoded images and rely on external reward models. The paper argues that unstable intermediate images make those strategies inefficient and often ineffective for this particular generation process, motivating confidence signals available directly from token prediction.

The framework uses token entropy to assess confidence. At its profile level, it combines the model’s intrinsic uncertainty with how it uses conditioning information. At its policy level, that combined state controls which generation trajectories are pruned and how guidance changes over time. ScalingAR also reduces visual-token consumption by 62.0% while outperforming baselines and mitigates performance degradation by 26.0% in challenging scenarios. The results support confidence-guided allocation of generation effort as a way to improve quality, efficiency, and robustness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ScalingAR uses token-level confidence to adapt image-generation trajectories and guidance, improving quality while reducing token consumption.

title: ScalingAR: Scaling Confidence for Autoregressive Image Generation

abstract: Positional encodings (PEs) enhance the power of graph neural networks (GNNs), both theoretically and empirically. Two of the most popular families of PEs—spectral (e.g., Laplacian eigenspaces, effective resistance) and random walk (polynomials of the adjacency matrix)—are theoretically equivalent in expressive power, and both are known to lie between the 1-WL and 3-WL tests in terms of expressivity. However, this equivalence assumes the GNN uses the "complete” version of these PEs, which requires $O(n^3)$ time and space complexity. Practitioners therefore commonly use truncated variants of these encodings (e.g., the first $k$ eigenspaces or powers of adjacency matrix). However, the theoretical properties of these truncated PEs are unknown. In this work, we initiate the study of these truncated PEs. Theoretically, we show that, under truncation, several families of PEs are fundamentally different in expressive power. As a corollary, we show that truncated spectral PEs are no longer stronger than the 1-WL test. We also study a family of spectral PEs, the $k$-harmonic distances, to highlight the differences in expressive power of even closely related truncated PEs. Finally, we experimentally show that a mix of truncated PEs is preferable to any single family on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Positional encodings give graph neural networks additional information about graph structure. Complete spectral and random-walk encodings have equivalent theoretical expressive power, but the complete versions require cubic time and space in the number of nodes. Practical systems therefore retain only a subset, such as the first few eigenspaces or adjacency-matrix powers.

This paper investigates what truncation does to those expressivity guarantees. It shows that several encoding families become fundamentally different once truncated, so equivalence of their complete forms does not transfer automatically to practical versions. In particular, truncated spectral encodings are no longer stronger than the 1-WL test. The analysis of k-harmonic distances also reveals differences among closely related spectral encodings.

Experiments on real-world datasets find that mixing truncated encoding families is preferable to using a single family. The theoretical and empirical findings point in the same practical direction: the retained portion of an encoding matters, and families that look interchangeable in their complete mathematical form can supply different structural information after truncation.
summary.tldr: Truncation breaks expressivity equivalences between graph positional encodings, and experiments favor combining truncated families.

title: Understanding Truncated Positional Encodings for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of unsupervised skill segmentation and hierarchical structure discovery in reinforcement learning. While recent approaches have sought to segment trajectories into reusable skills or options, most rely on action labels, rewards, or handcrafted annotations, limiting their applicability. We propose a method that segments unlabelled trajectories into skills and induces a hierarchical structure over them using a grammar-based approach. The resulting hierarchy captures both low-level behaviours and their composition into higher-level skills. We evaluate our approach in high-dimensional, pixel-based environments, including Craftax and the full, unmodified version of Minecraft. Using metrics for skill segmentation, reuse, and hierarchy quality, we find that our method consistently produces more structured and semantically meaningful hierarchies than existing baselines. Furthermore, as a proof of concept, we demonstrate that these discovered hierarchies accelerate and stabilise learning on downstream reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: An agent's experience contains recurring behaviors that could become reusable skills, but identifying them often requires action labels, rewards, or handcrafted annotations. This paper studies how to discover skills and their organization from unlabelled trajectories. Its goal includes both locating behavioral segments and understanding how simpler behaviors compose into more complex ones.

The proposed method uses a grammar-based approach to segment trajectories and induce a hierarchy over the resulting skills. The hierarchy represents low-level behaviors together with their combinations into higher-level skills. Discovering both levels makes the output a structured account of behavior, rather than just a set of independently recurring trajectory fragments.

Evaluations use high-dimensional environments observed through pixels, including Craftax and full, unmodified Minecraft. Metrics for segmentation, reuse, and hierarchy quality show consistently more structured and semantically meaningful hierarchies than existing baselines. A further proof of concept shows faster and more stable learning on downstream reinforcement-learning tasks. This demonstrates potential practical value for the discovered structure while preserving the limited, proof-of-concept scope of that downstream result.
summary.tldr: A grammar-based method discovers reusable skill hierarchies from unlabelled trajectories and shows proof-of-concept benefits for downstream reinforcement learning.

title: Unsupervised Hierarchical Skill Discovery

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) refine tokens iteratively but commit them irreversibly, leading to a "stability lag" where early decisions remain fragile even after being written. We reveal that Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) error easily flips these borderline decisions at the write frontier, which are then permanently locked in and amplified. To address this, we propose Frontier-Aware Instability-Reweighted Calibration (FAIR-Calib), a two-stage PTQ framework for dLLMs. Stage I probes a full-precision teacher to estimate a position prior that combines frontier hits and masked-stage reliability. Stage II performs off-policy, layer-wise calibration by minimizing a reweighted hidden-state MSE, effectively prioritizing the protection of fragile frontier states without requiring expensive end-to-end diffusion rollouts. We further theoretically justify our weighted objective as a surrogate for output KL divergence. Empirically, FAIR-Calib consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on LLaDA and Dream (W4A4), significantly reducing frontier decision flips and suppressing post-commit mismatches across diverse benchmarks.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models refine tokens over several steps, but written tokens can become irreversible before their underlying decisions are stable. The paper identifies this stability lag as a particular vulnerability during post-training quantization. Small numerical errors can flip borderline choices at the write frontier, after which the mistaken choices remain fixed and their effects can grow.

FAIR-Calib directs calibration effort toward these fragile states. First, it probes a full-precision teacher to estimate which token positions deserve protection, combining how often they encounter the frontier with their reliability during masked stages. It then calibrates individual layers using a weighted hidden-state reconstruction loss. This avoids expensive end-to-end diffusion rollouts while emphasizing errors that matter most near commitment.

They also report fewer frontier decision flips and fewer mismatches after commitment, connecting the performance gains to the failure mechanism the method targets.
summary.tldr: FAIR-Calib protects fragile token decisions during diffusion-language-model quantization by giving their hidden states greater calibration weight.

title: FAIR-Calib: Frontier-Aware Instability-Reweighted Calibration for Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Large Language Models

abstract: We study the multi-task linear regression problem in the presence of contaminated tasks. We address the setting where the unknown parameters of a majority of tasks are close in the $\ell_2$-norm, while a fraction of tasks are arbitrary outliers. Existing theoretical frameworks for this problem rely heavily on the assumption that the empirical second moment of each task has a minimum eigenvalue bounded away from zero (order $\Omega(1)$). Crucially, this assumption fails in many high-dimensional scenarios, rendering prior guarantees vacuous. To overcome this limitation, we propose an estimator based on matrix-weighted norm regularization. We also introduce a relative balancedness condition, quantified by a balancedness constant, that compares each task’s second moment with the average inlier geometry and relaxes the need for taskwise second-moment lower bounds. In favorable regimes with moderate balancedness, our prediction MSE bounds match the rate of Duan and Wang (2023) under substantially weaker spectral assumptions; the resulting task-overall MSE is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our estimator enjoys a safety guarantee: when the relevant balancedness constant is large or infinite, or when tasks are unrelated, the method performs no worse than independent task learning.

paragraphs: Learning related regression tasks together can help when most tasks have similar parameters, even if some are arbitrary outliers. Existing guarantees often require each task's empirical second-moment matrix to have a smallest eigenvalue bounded away from zero. That requirement can fail in high-dimensional settings, leaving the guarantees uninformative.

This paper proposes matrix-weighted norm regularization and a relative balancedness condition. Instead of requiring every task to have strong information in every direction, balancedness compares each task's second-moment structure with the average geometry of the inlier tasks. The analysis still assumes that a majority of task parameters are close in Euclidean distance, while allowing a fraction of tasks to be contaminated.

With moderate balancedness in favorable regimes, prediction-error bounds match an earlier rate under weaker spectral assumptions, and aggregate error is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. The estimator also has a safety guarantee: when balancedness is unfavorable or tasks are unrelated, it performs no worse than learning tasks independently. This links useful sharing to the available task geometry while providing protection when sharing offers no advantage.
summary.tldr: A matrix-weighted estimator provides robust multi-task regression guarantees under weaker spectral assumptions and safeguards against harmful task sharing.

title: Multi-task Linear Regression without Eigenvalue Lower Bounds: Adaptivity, Robustness, and Safety

abstract: Hyper-relational knowledge graphs (HKGs) effectively represent complex facts. While inferring new knowledge in HKGs is a critical problem, current methods cast it as a simple link prediction, assuming that nearly all entities and relations within a fact are known, leaving only a single blank to be filled. However, this restricted assumption may not hold in real-world scenarios in which multiple, or even all, constituent components of a fact may be missing simultaneously. To bridge this gap, we introduce a task called fact generation: generating a valid hyper-relational fact from an arbitrarily masked query, i.e., completing a partially observed fact or generating a fact from scratch. We propose KREPE, the first generative representation learning method for HKGs that learns to model the probability distributions of missing components conditioned on the local fact components and global structure of HKGs via a masked discrete diffusion. KREPE models both the intra-fact dependencies by contextual message passing and inter-fact correlations by aggregating stochastically sampled contexts. KREPE seamlessly unifies link prediction and fact generation within a single training framework, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard HKG link prediction benchmarks and outperforming LLM-based baselines in generating novel and correct facts.

paragraphs: Hyper-relational knowledge graphs represent facts with multiple connected components. Standard link prediction typically assumes almost all of a fact is already known and asks the model to fill one blank. This paper broadens that setting to fact generation, where any number of components may be missing, including every component.

The proposed method, KREPE, learns distributions over missing components through masked discrete diffusion. Its predictions use both the available pieces of the current fact and the surrounding graph structure. Contextual message passing models dependencies within a fact, while aggregation of randomly sampled contexts captures relationships between facts. These two sources of information help the model handle incomplete queries with different amounts of observed evidence.

KREPE trains link prediction and fact generation within one framework. The authors report state-of-the-art results on standard hyper-relational link prediction benchmarks and better generation of novel, correct facts than the compared language-model baselines. The contribution therefore extends the range of questions a knowledge-graph model can answer while also improving performance on the conventional single-blank task.
summary.tldr: KREPE uses masked discrete diffusion to complete arbitrarily missing fact components or generate whole facts in hyper-relational knowledge graphs.

title: Generative Representation Learning on Hyper-relational Knowledge Graphs via Masked Discrete Diffusion

abstract: Recent advances in tool-integrated language agents have significantly improved their ability to solve complex reasoning tasks. However, existing alignment methods predominantly focus on maximizing task accuracy, while overlooking auxiliary objectives such as tool-use efficiency, which are essential for practical deployment. To address this gap, we introduce ParetoPO, a two-stage multi-objective optimization framework for aligning tool-using large language models (LLMs) under competing objectives. In the first stage, ParetoPO leverages hypervolume-guided dynamic scalarization to adapt reward weights based on global Pareto frontier progress. In the second stage, it replaces scalarized learning signals with Pareto-ranking-based advantage computation, promoting nondominated trajectories through dominance-aware credit assignment. This design enables fine-grained, action-level optimization across multiple conflicting objectives. Experimental results on mathematic reasoning and multi-hop QA tasks show that ParetoPO consistently discovers policies with superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to static and heuristic baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/ICML2026_ParetoPO.

paragraphs: Tool-using language agents need to solve tasks accurately while using tools efficiently. Optimizing accuracy alone overlooks this practical trade-off. ParetoPO treats alignment as a multi-objective problem, aiming to discover policies that balance competing goals rather than committing throughout training to a fixed weighting of them.

Its first stage dynamically adjusts reward weights using progress along the global Pareto frontier, guided by hypervolume. The second stage replaces combined scalar rewards as the learning signal with advantages based on Pareto ranking. This favors nondominated trajectories: alternatives for which another trajectory does not improve one objective without sacrificing another. Dominance-aware credit assignment supports optimization at individual actions.

On mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question-answering tasks, ParetoPO consistently discovers policies with better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs than static and heuristic baselines. The results show the value of changing how competing objectives guide learning over time. The framework combines broad progress toward better trade-offs with finer action-level signals that preserve distinctions a single weighted reward can obscure.
summary.tldr: ParetoPO trains tool-using agents with adaptive reward weighting and Pareto-based ranking to improve accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

title: Towards Pareto-Optimal Tool-Integrated Agents with Pareto Ranking Policy Optimization

abstract: Evaluating agentic AI on open-ended professional tasks faces a fundamental dilemma between rigor and flexibility. Static rubrics provide rigorous, reproducible assessment but fail to accommodate diverse valid response strategies, while LLM-as-a-judge approaches adapt to individual responses yet suffer from instability and bias. Human experts address this dilemma by combining domain-grounded principles with dynamic, claim-level assessment. Inspired by this process, we propose JADE, a two-layer evaluation framework. Layer 1 encodes expert knowledge as a predefined set of evaluation skills, providing stable evaluation criteria. Layer 2 performs report-specific, claim-level evaluation to flexibly assess diverse reasoning strategies, with evidence-dependency gating to invalidate conclusions built on refuted claims. Experiments on BizBench show that JADE improves evaluation stability and reveals critical agent failure modes missed by holistic LLM-based evaluators. We further demonstrate strong alignment with expert-authored rubrics and effective transfer to HealthBench and DR.BENCH, covering medical and 10-domain professional evaluation settings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/smiling-world/JADE.

paragraphs: Open-ended professional tasks can have multiple valid solutions, making evaluation difficult. Fixed rubrics offer consistency but can miss legitimate alternative approaches. Language-model judges can adapt to individual responses, yet their judgments may be unstable or biased. JADE combines stable expert criteria with assessment that adapts to the claims in each report.

Its first layer encodes expert knowledge as predefined evaluation skills. Its second layer examines report-specific claims and how they depend on one another. Evidence-dependency gating invalidates conclusions that rely on refuted claims. This allows evaluation to consider the structure of an argument instead of treating a polished final conclusion as independently supported.

On BizBench, JADE improves evaluation stability and detects important agent failures missed by holistic language-model evaluators. The authors also report strong agreement with expert-authored rubrics and effective transfer to HealthBench and DR.BENCH. These findings support an evaluation approach that keeps professional standards stable while allowing different reasoning strategies to be judged on their own evidence.
summary.tldr: JADE combines expert-defined evaluation criteria with claim-level dependency checks to assess open-ended professional work more reliably.

title: JADE: Expert-Grounded Dynamic Evaluation for Open-Ended Professional Tasks

abstract: We present WorldMirror, a unified feed-forward model for comprehensive 3D geometric prediction tasks. Unlike existing methods constrained to image-only inputs or customized for a specific task, our framework flexibly integrates diverse geometric priors, including camera poses, intrinsics, and depth maps, while simultaneously generating multiple 3D representations: dense point clouds, multi-view depth maps, camera parameters, surface normals, and 3D Gaussians. Remarkably, prior injection yields universal gains across all tasks, suggesting that input flexibility and multi-task prediction are mutually reinforcing. WorldMirror achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks from camera, point map, depth, and surface normal estimation to novel view synthesis, while maintaining the efficiency of feed-forward inference. Code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/HunyuanWorld-Mirror.

paragraphs: WorldMirror unifies several forms of three-dimensional reconstruction in a single feed-forward model. It can accept geometric information such as camera poses, camera intrinsics, and depth maps alongside its inputs. This flexibility allows available prior knowledge to contribute to reconstruction instead of restricting the framework to image-only input or one specialized task.

The model jointly produces dense point clouds, depth maps across views, camera parameters, surface normals, and 3D Gaussians. These outputs represent complementary aspects of scene geometry and appearance. Producing them within one framework connects flexible geometric inputs with multiple prediction targets, allowing the same reconstruction system to support a broad collection of tasks.

The authors report gains from prior injection across all evaluated tasks, suggesting that input flexibility and joint prediction reinforce one another. WorldMirror achieves state-of-the-art results across benchmarks for cameras, point maps, depth, surface normals, and novel-view synthesis while retaining feed-forward inference efficiency. The findings support a unified approach in which available geometric knowledge improves several reconstruction outputs together, rather than helping only one narrowly defined prediction.
summary.tldr: WorldMirror uses flexible geometric priors to improve multiple 3D reconstruction outputs within one efficient feed-forward model.

title: WorldMirror: Universal 3D World Reconstruction with Any-Prior Prompting

abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides a statistical framework for uncertainty quantification that constructs prediction sets with coverage guarantees. While CP yields uncontrolled prediction set sizes, Backward Conformal Prediction (BCP) inverts this paradigm by enforcing a predefined upper bound on set size and estimating the resulting coverage guarantee. However, the looseness induced by Markov’s inequality within the BCP framework causes a significant gap between the estimated coverage bound and the empirical coverage. In this work, we introduce ST-BCP, a novel method that introduces a data-dependent transformation of nonconformity scores to narrow the coverage gap. In particular, we develop a computable transformation and prove that it outperforms the baseline identity transformation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, reducing the average coverage gap from 4.20% to 1.12% on common benchmarks.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs sets of possible answers with coverage guarantees, but does not control how large those sets become. Backward Conformal Prediction reverses this arrangement: it imposes an upper limit on set size and estimates the coverage that can be guaranteed. This is useful when the number of returned possibilities is itself constrained.

The paper targets a gap between that estimated coverage bound and the coverage observed empirically. In the existing framework, using Markov's inequality introduces looseness into the bound. ST-BCP addresses this by applying a data-dependent transformation to nonconformity scores, the quantities used to assess how well candidate answers fit the prediction process.

The authors construct a computable transformation and prove that it improves on leaving the scores unchanged. Experiments on common benchmarks reduce the average coverage gap from 4.20% to 1.12%. The reported improvement concerns how tightly the guarantee reflects observed coverage. It strengthens the usefulness of the size-constrained framework by making its coverage assessment less conservative in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ST-BCP transforms nonconformity scores to tighten coverage bounds for prediction sets with a predefined size limit.

title: Improving Backward Conformal Prediction via Non-Conformity Score Transformation

abstract: Diffusion models transform noise into data by injecting information that was captured in their neural network during the training phase. In this paper we ask: what is this information? We find that, in pixel-space diffusion models, (1) a large fraction of the total information in the neural network is committed to reconstructing small-scale perceptual details of the image, and (2) the correlations between images and their class labels are informed by the semantic content of the images, and are largely agnostic to the low-level details. We argue that these properties are intrinsically tied to the manifold structure of the data itself. Finally, we show that these facts explain the efficacy of classifier-free guidance: the guidance vector amplifies the mutual information between images and conditioning signals early in the generative process, influencing semantic structure, but tapers out as perceptual details are filled in.

paragraphs: A diffusion model turns noise into an image using information stored in its network during training. This paper asks how that information divides between semantic content and fine perceptual detail. In pixel-space diffusion models, the authors find that a large fraction of the network’s information is devoted to reconstructing small-scale image details.

The relationship between an image and its class label behaves differently. It depends mainly on semantic content and is largely insensitive to low-level details. The authors argue that this separation reflects the manifold structure of the data itself: the organization of images and their variation. This connects the division of learned information to properties of the data being modeled.

The paper uses these findings to explain classifier-free guidance. Early in generation, the guidance vector strengthens the mutual information between images and conditioning signals, influencing semantic structure. Its contribution then tapers as the model fills in perceptual detail. This account explains how guidance can exert substantial control over image meaning even though much of the network’s information serves finer visual reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Separating semantic information from perceptual detail helps explain when and how classifier-free guidance shapes diffusion-generated images.

title: On the Separability of Information in Diffusion Models

abstract: Subgoal-based policy tree search, which uses a policy to guide search, is effective for complex single-agent deterministic problems but often relies on explicit subgoal generation that can incur substantial overhead and hinders scalability. In this paper, we overcome these limitations by using a learned “rerooter” through the recently-introduced $\sqrt{\text{LTS}}$ algorithm. A rerooter implicitly decomposes the problem into soft subtasks. While previous work focused on the formal guarantees for given or handcrafted rerooters, in this work we propose three rerooter designs: (i) a clustering-based rerooter that exploits global state-space structure, (ii) a heuristic-based rerooter that leverages learned cost-to-go estimates, and (iii) a hybrid that combines both signals. Our framework avoids having to explicitly reconstruct and reason over generated subgoals, thereby enabling scalable allocation of search effort with significantly lower computational overhead. Empirically, our rerooting-based methods scale to complex environments where subgoal-based policy tree search fails, and achieve state-of-the-art online training efficiency on the domains tested.

paragraphs: Policy-guided tree search can tackle difficult deterministic single-agent problems by breaking them into subgoals. Explicitly generating and reasoning over those subgoals, however, can become costly. This paper uses a learned rerooter within the √LTS algorithm to create an implicit decomposition into soft subtasks and direct search effort without reconstructing explicit intermediate goals.

The authors propose three rerooter designs. One uses clustering to capture global structure in the state space. Another uses learned estimates of the remaining cost to reach a goal. A hybrid combines the two sources of information, bringing together the organization of possible states and estimates of progress toward a solution.

Earlier work emphasized formal guarantees for given or handcrafted rerooters; this paper focuses on learning useful designs. Empirically, its methods scale to complex environments where subgoal-based policy tree search fails and achieve state-of-the-art online training efficiency on the tested domains. These results support implicit decomposition as a practical way to allocate search computation while reducing the overhead associated with explicit subgoal management.
summary.tldr: Learned rerooters use state-space structure and cost estimates to guide scalable tree search without explicitly generating subgoals.

title: Structure-Induced Information for Rerooting Levin Tree Search

abstract: Engineering construction automation aims to transform natural language specifications into physically viable structures, requiring complex integrated reasoning under strict physical constraints. While modern LLMs possess broad knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities that make them promising candidates for this domain, their construction competencies remain largely unevaluated. To address this gap, we introduce BuildArena, the first physics-aligned interactive benchmark designed for language-driven engineering construction. Technically, it contributes to the community in two aspects: (1) an extendable task design strategy spanning static and dynamic mechanics across multiple difficulty tiers; (2) a 3D Spatial Geometric Computation Library for supporting construction based on language instructions. On nine frontier LLMs and three additional open-weight models, BuildArena comprehensively evaluates their capabilities for language-driven and physics-grounded construction automation. We release the code at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/BuildArena to benefit construction automation in engineering applications.

paragraphs: Turning a written construction request into a viable structure requires language understanding, spatial reasoning, and compliance with physical constraints. BuildArena creates an interactive benchmark for assessing these capabilities together. It addresses a gap between language models’ broad reasoning abilities and the limited evaluation of their ability to perform engineering construction.

The benchmark contributes an extendable strategy for designing tasks across multiple difficulty levels. Those tasks cover both static and dynamic mechanics, bringing different physical requirements into the evaluation. A second contribution is a library for geometric computation in three-dimensional space, which supports construction from language instructions. Together, the task design and computation library provide infrastructure for studying language-driven construction under physical constraints.

The authors evaluate nine frontier language models and three additional open-weight models using this framework. The abstract establishes the scope of that evaluation without reporting a model ranking or numerical outcome. The paper’s stated contribution is therefore chiefly an evaluation resource: a way to examine integrated construction competence in an interactive, physics-grounded setting, with released code supporting further work.
summary.tldr: BuildArena evaluates whether language models can turn written construction instructions into structures that satisfy physical requirements.

title: BuildArena: A Physics-Aligned Interactive Benchmark of LLMs for Engineering Construction

abstract: When reliable target structures are unavailable at scale or phenotypes arise from dysregulated pathways, transcriptomic perturbations provide a system-level functional readout for drug action. In this work, we formalize Transcriptome-based Drug Design (TBDD) as a generative inverse problem: designing drug molecules conditioned on desired transcriptomic state transitions. We analyze the inherently ill-posed nature of this task, which is further complicated by the profound domain gap between biology and chemistry and by the sparsity of transcriptomic signals. To address these challenges, we propose CURE (A CellUlar Response Engine), a multi-resolution transcriptome-guided diffusion framework. CURE features a specialized Transcriptome Perturbation Functional Feature Extractor (TFE) that (1) distills function-oriented perturbation embeddings from pre/post states, (2) aligns these signatures to dual chemical views to bridge the cross-modal gap, and (3) performs heterogeneity-aware aggregation to extract robust state-specific signals from noisy transcriptomic data. Extensive evaluations on both standard benchmarks and rigorous out-of-distribution protocols demonstrate that CURE consistently outperforms strong baselines in structural quality and functional consistency. Furthermore, we validate its practical utility via a zero-shot gene-inhibitor design task, highlighting the potential of phenotype-driven generative discovery.
originalAbstract: When reliable target structures are unavailable at scale or phenotypes arise from dysregulated pathways, transcriptomic perturbations provide a system-level functional readout for drug action. In this work, we formalize Transcriptome-based Drug Design (TBDD) as a generative inverse problem: designing drug molecules conditioned on desired transcriptomic state transitions. We analyze the inherently ill-posed nature of this task, which is further complicated by the profound domain gap between biology and chemistry and by the sparsity of transcriptomic signals. To address these challenges, we propose CURE (A CellUlar Response Engine), a multi-resolution transcriptome-guided diffusion framework. CURE features a specialized Transcriptome Perturbation Functional Feature Extractor (TFE) that (1) distills function-oriented perturbation embeddings from pre/post states, (2) aligns these signatures to dual chemical views to bridge the cross-modal gap, and (3) performs heterogeneity-aware aggregation to extract robust state-specific signals from noisy transcriptomic data. Extensive evaluations on both standard benchmarks and rigorous out-of-distribution protocols demonstrate that CURE consistently outperforms strong baselines in structural quality and functional consistency. Furthermore, we validate its practical utility via a zero-shot gene-inhibitor design task, highlighting the potential of phenotype-driven generative discovery.

paragraphs: CURE approaches molecular design through desired changes in cellular gene expression. This functional perspective is useful when reliable target structures are unavailable at scale or when disrupted pathways shape a phenotype. The paper formulates the task as an inverse problem: given a desired transition between transcriptomic states, generate molecules consistent with that transition.

The authors identify the problem as inherently ill-posed, with an additional gap between biological and chemical representations and sparse transcriptomic signals. Their diffusion framework uses a specialized feature extractor to summarize functional changes between pre- and post-perturbation states. It aligns those summaries with two chemical views and aggregates heterogeneous observations to extract more robust state-specific information from noisy data.

On standard benchmarks and out-of-distribution evaluations, CURE consistently outperforms strong baselines in molecular structural quality and functional consistency. A zero-shot gene-inhibitor design task provides further evidence of practical utility. These results support transcriptomic conditioning as a promising route for function-oriented molecular generation, connecting the desired cellular response to the design process.
summary.tldr: CURE generates molecules conditioned on desired gene-expression changes, improving structural quality and functional consistency in the reported evaluations.

title: Reading the Cell, Designing the Cure: Perturbation-Conditioned Molecular Diffusion for Function-Oriented Drug Design

abstract: Vector quantization is a fundamental tool for compressing high-dimensional embeddings, yet existing multi-codebook methods rely on static codebooks that limit expressiveness under heterogeneous data geometry. While recent dynamic quantizers like QINCo adapt codebooks to individual inputs and improve expressiveness, their strict sequential dependencies create decoding bottlenecks. We propose Residual Quantization via Mixture of Experts (RQ-MoE), a framework combining a two-level MoE with dual-stream quantization to enable input-dependent codebook adaptation for efficient vector quantization. RQ-MoE enables dynamic codebook construction and decouples instruction from quantization, facilitating parallel decoding. Theoretically, we show that standard Residual Quantization and QINCo can be recovered as constrained special cases of RQ-MoE, and derive a guideline for setting expert dimensionality in RQ-MoE. Extensive experiments show that RQ-MoE achieves state-of-the-art or on-par performance in reconstruction and retrieval, while it can provide 6$\times$–14$\times$ faster decoding than prior vector quantization methods. The implementation is available at https://github.com/KDEGroup/RQ-MoE.

paragraphs: Vector quantization compresses high-dimensional embeddings using codebooks. Static codebooks can struggle when the data have varied geometric structure. Input-adaptive methods such as QINCo improve expressiveness, but their sequential dependencies make decoding a bottleneck. The paper targets this tension between adapting the compressed representation and reconstructing it efficiently.

RQ-MoE combines a two-level mixture of experts with dual-stream quantization. It constructs codebooks dynamically for individual inputs while separating instruction from quantization, enabling parallel decoding. This organization aims to preserve the benefits of input-dependent codebooks without requiring the same strict sequence of decoding operations.

Experiments report state-of-the-art or comparable reconstruction and retrieval quality, alongside decoding that can be 6–14 times faster than prior vector-quantization methods. The findings connect a more general quantization architecture to both competitive representation quality and substantial reported decoding gains.
summary.tldr: RQ-MoE adapts compression codebooks to each input while enabling parallel decoding, reporting competitive quality and potential decoding speedups of 6–14 times.

title: RQ-MoE: Residual Quantization via Mixture of Experts for Efficient Input-Dependent Vector Compression

abstract: Automated proving of polynomial inequalities is a fundamental challenge in automated mathematical reasoning, where rich algebraic structure and a rapidly growing certificate search space hinder scalability. Purely symbolic approaches provide strong guarantees but often scale poorly as the number of variables or the degree increases. In parallel, LLM-guided methods have made notable progress, particularly on competition-style inequalities with a small number of variables. To address the remaining scalability challenges, we propose NSPI, a neuro-symbolic framework that combines the complementary strengths of LLMs and symbolic computation for polynomial-inequality proving. Concretely, an LLM proposes a conjecture in the form of an approximate polynomial Sum-Of-Squares (SOS) decomposition; we refine it via symbolic computation to obtain an exact polynomial SOS representation, which directly proves the target inequality, and we further certify the proof in Lean, yielding an end-to-end pipeline from heuristic discovery to machine-checked proof. Experiments on challenging benchmarks involving polynomials with up to 10 variables demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed method. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruobingzuo66/NSPI.

paragraphs: Proving polynomial inequalities becomes difficult as the number of variables and polynomial degree increase. Symbolic methods offer strong guarantees, but searching for a suitable proof certificate can become expensive. NSPI combines language-model suggestions with symbolic computation to address this search problem while retaining a path to exact, machine-checked mathematical proofs.

The language model first proposes an approximate decomposition of a polynomial into a sum of squares. Symbolic computation then refines that proposal into an exact representation, which proves the target inequality. The resulting proof is certified in Lean. Each stage serves a distinct purpose: heuristic discovery proposes structure, exact algebra establishes the certificate, and formal checking verifies the proof.

Experiments on challenging benchmarks containing polynomials with up to ten variables support the method’s effectiveness and scalability. The result concerns this certificate-based pipeline and the evaluated problems. Its significance is that approximate model-generated mathematical ideas can become useful starting points for a process whose final output is an exact, formally certified proof.
summary.tldr: NSPI turns language-model proposals for polynomial sum-of-squares decompositions into exact certificates and Lean-checked inequality proofs.

title: From LLM-Generated Conjectures to Lean Formalizations: Automated Polynomial Inequality Proving via Sum-of-Squares Certificates

abstract: We study the label complexity of pool-based active learning in the agnostic PAC model. Specifically, we derive general bounds on the number of label requests made by the A2 algorithm proposed by Balcan, Beygelzimer & Langford (Balcan et al., 2006). This represents the first nontrivial general-purpose upper bound on label complexity in the agnostic PAC model.
originalAbstract: We study the label complexity of pool-based active learning in the agnostic PAC model. Specifically, we derive general bounds on the number of label requests made by the A2 algorithm proposed by Balcan, Beygelzimer & Langford (Balcan et al., 2006). This represents the first nontrivial general-purpose upper bound on label complexity in the agnostic PAC model.

paragraphs: Active learning studies how a learner can choose which examples to have labeled. In the pool-based setting considered here, the learner selects its requests from a collection of available examples. The paper asks how many label requests a particular algorithm needs, making the cost of obtaining labels the central object of analysis.

The authors study the A2 algorithm in the agnostic PAC framework. Agnostic learning allows for the possibility that the available prediction models cannot perfectly explain the labels. A label-complexity guarantee therefore has to address learning without assuming that some candidate model makes no errors. The contribution is a general upper bound on the algorithm’s label requests in this setting.

The abstract identifies this as the first nontrivial, general-purpose upper bound for agnostic PAC active learning. Its significance is a theoretical guarantee about label requirements for an existing algorithm. An upper bound limits the requests needed under the framework; it does not establish that every problem needs that many labels or that the bound is the smallest possible.
summary.tldr: The paper derives the first nontrivial general-purpose upper bound on label requests for A2 in agnostic PAC active learning.

title: A bound on the label complexity of agnostic active learning

abstract: Graph transduction methods label input data by learning a classification function that is regularized to exhibit smoothness along a graph over labeled and unlabeled samples. In practice, these algorithms are sensitive to the initial set of labels provided by the user. For instance, classification accuracy drops if the training set contains weak labels, if imbalances exist across label classes or if the labeled portion of the data is not chosen at random. This paper introduces a propagation algorithm that more reliably minimizes a cost function over both a function on the graph and a binary label matrix. The cost function generalizes prior work in graph transduction and also introduces node normalization terms for resilience to label imbalances. We demonstrate that global minimization of the function is intractable but instead provide an alternating minimization scheme that incrementally adjusts the function and the labels towards a reliable local minimum. Unlike prior methods, the resulting propagation of labels does not prematurely commit to an erroneous labeling and obtains more consistent labels. Experiments are shown for synthetic and real classification tasks including digit and text recognition. A substantial improvement in accuracy compared to state of the art semi-supervised methods is achieved. The advantage are even more dramatic when labeled instances are limited.

paragraphs: Graph transduction labels data using a graph connecting labeled and unlabeled examples, encouraging predictions to vary smoothly along that graph. Existing methods can be sensitive to the initial labels, particularly when labels are weak, classes are imbalanced, or labeled examples are not selected randomly. Early labeling mistakes can affect later propagation.

The paper introduces an objective that jointly involves a prediction function on the graph and a binary label matrix. It generalizes earlier objectives and adds node normalization terms intended to improve resilience to class imbalance. Because globally minimizing the objective is intractable, the authors use alternating minimization to adjust the function and labels incrementally toward a reliable local minimum.

This procedure avoids prematurely committing to erroneous labels and produces more consistent labeling in the reported work. Experiments include synthetic tasks and real digit and text recognition problems. The authors report substantial accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, with especially pronounced advantages when few labeled examples are available. These are empirical gains from an approach explicitly targeting local optimization.
summary.tldr: Alternately updating graph predictions and labels improves reported transduction accuracy, especially with few labeled examples.

title: Graph transduction via alternating minimization

abstract: We present a novel technique for automated problem decomposition to address the problem of scalability in Reinforcement Learning. Our technique makes use of a set of near-optimal trajectories to discover {\it options} and incorporates them into the learning process, dramatically reducing the time it takes to solve the underlying problem. We run a series of experiments in two different domains and show that our method offers up to 30 fold speedup over the baseline.
originalAbstract: We present a novel technique for automated problem decomposition to address the problem of scalability in Reinforcement Learning. Our technique makes use of a set of near-optimal trajectories to discover {\it options} and incorporates them into the learning process, dramatically reducing the time it takes to solve the underlying problem. We run a series of experiments in two different domains and show that our method offers up to 30 fold speedup over the baseline.

paragraphs: The paper addresses scalability in reinforcement learning by automatically decomposing a problem using example trajectories. Its starting point is a set of trajectories that are already near optimal. These examples supply information about successful behavior that the method uses to discover options and then incorporate them into subsequent learning.

The central idea is to let examples inform the decomposition of the learning problem. Rather than requiring the decomposition to be specified separately, the technique extracts it from the supplied trajectories. The role of those trajectories is therefore substantive: the method depends on access to near-optimal examples, and its reported benefit concerns learning with options discovered from that source.

Experiments in two domains show substantial reductions in the time required to solve the underlying problems, with speedups reaching thirtyfold over the baseline. That figure is the largest reported improvement, rather than a promise for every task. The findings support using successful example behavior to discover useful options and make reinforcement learning faster in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: The method discovers options from near-optimal trajectories and achieves up to thirtyfold faster reinforcement learning in two evaluated domains.

title: Discovering options from example trajectories

abstract: We present and derive a new stick-breaking construction of the beta process. The construction is closely related to a special case of the stick-breaking construction of the Dirichlet process (Sethuraman, 1994) applied to the beta distribution. We derive an inference procedure that relies on Monte Carlo integration to reduce the number of parameters to be inferred, and present results on synthetic data, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and a time-evolving gene expression data set.
originalAbstract: We present and derive a new stick-breaking construction of the beta process. The construction is closely related to a special case of the stick-breaking construction of the Dirichlet process (Sethuraman, 1994) applied to the beta distribution. We derive an inference procedure that relies on Monte Carlo integration to reduce the number of parameters to be inferred, and present results on synthetic data, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and a time-evolving gene expression data set.

paragraphs: The paper introduces and derives a new stick-breaking construction of the beta process. A construction provides an explicit way to build the mathematical object used by a model, making its structure available for further algorithmic development. Here, the authors connect their construction to a special case of the Dirichlet process stick-breaking construction applied to the beta distribution.

That connection is central to the contribution: the proposed construction develops a relationship between two probabilistic constructions rather than simply presenting an unrelated recipe. The paper also moves from the construction to inference, deriving a procedure for working with the resulting model. This procedure uses Monte Carlo integration to reduce the number of parameters that must be inferred.

Reducing the inference burden gives the mathematical construction a practical role. The authors present results on synthetic data, handwritten digits from MNIST, and gene expression data that evolve over time. These applications illustrate the method across different data settings. The stated contribution combines a new representation, its derivation, and an inference procedure supported by application results.
summary.tldr: A new stick-breaking construction of the beta process leads to an inference procedure that uses Monte Carlo integration to reduce the number of inferred parameters.

title: A Stick-Breaking Construction of the Beta Process

abstract: Cointegration is an important topic for time-series, and describes a relationship between two series in which a linear combination is stationary. Classically, the test for cointegration is based on a two stage process in which first the linear relation between the series is estimated by Ordinary Least Squares. Subsequently a unit root test is performed on the residuals. A well-known deficiency of this classical approach is that is can lead to erroneous conclusions about the presence of cointegration. As an alternative, we present a coherent framework for estimating whether cointegration exists using Bayesian inference which is empirically superior to the classical approach. Finally, we apply our technique to model segmented cointegration in which cointegration may exist only for limited time. In contrast to previous approaches our model makes no restriction on the number of possible cointegration segments.

paragraphs: Two time series are cointegrated when a linear combination of them is stationary, meaning that the combination has stable statistical behavior over time. The conventional test first estimates a linear relationship using ordinary least squares and then tests its residuals for a unit root. The paper identifies erroneous conclusions about cointegration as a known weakness of this two-stage procedure.

The authors replace that workflow with a coherent Bayesian framework for estimating whether cointegration exists. The relationship between the series and the assessment of cointegration are handled within this framework. Their empirical comparison finds the Bayesian approach superior to the classical procedure, supporting it as an alternative for assessing this particular kind of relationship between time series.

The framework is also applied to segmented cointegration, where the relationship may hold only during limited periods. This extends the question from whether cointegration exists to how its presence can vary over time. Unlike previous approaches discussed in the abstract, the model places no restriction on the number of possible cointegration segments.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework improves empirical cointegration assessment and models relationships that hold across an unrestricted number of time segments.

title: Bayesian Conditional Cointegration

abstract: We consider two active binary-classification problems with atypical objectives. In the first, active search, our goal is to actively uncover as many members of a given class as possible. In the second, active surveying, our goal is to actively query points to ultimately predict the class proportion of a given class. Numerous real-world problems can be framed in these terms, and in either case typical model-based concerns such as generalization error are only of secondary importance. We approach these problems via Bayesian decision theory; after choosing natural utility functions, we derive the optimal policies. We provide three contributions. In addition to introducing the active surveying problem, we extend previous work on active search in two ways. First, we prove a novel theoretical result, that less-myopic approximations to the optimal policy can outperform more-myopic approximations by any arbitrary degree. We then derive bounds that for certain models allow us to reduce (in practice dramatically) the exponential search space required by a naïve implementation of the optimal policy, enabling further lookahead while still ensuring the optimal decisions are always made.

In the second, active surveying, our goal is to actively query points to ultimately predict the class proportion of a given class. Numerous real-world problems can be framed in these terms, and in either case typical model-based concerns such as generalization error are only of secondary importance. We approach these problems via Bayesian decision theory; after choosing natural utility functions, we derive the optimal policies. We provide three contributions. First, we prove a novel theoretical result, that less-myopic approximations to the optimal policy can outperform more-myopic approximations by any arbitrary degree. paragraphs: The paper distinguishes two goals for actively choosing which points to label. Active search seeks to find as many members of a target class as possible. Active surveying seeks to estimate the proportion belonging to that class. In both cases, accurate general-purpose classification is secondary to the specific information the queries should deliver.

Using Bayesian decision theory, the authors choose utility functions for these objectives and derive optimal querying policies. They also prove that looking further ahead can matter enormously: less-myopic approximations can outperform more-myopic ones by an arbitrarily large amount. This establishes the possibility of a large advantage, rather than saying that additional lookahead always yields such gains.

Computing an optimal policy naively requires exploring an exponential search space. For certain models, the paper derives bounds that reduce this search while preserving optimal decisions. These reductions can be dramatic in practice and allow deeper lookahead. The work therefore connects a clear statement of the querying objective with both optimal decision rules and a way to make some of those rules more computationally accessible.
summary.tldr: Bayesian decision rules align active queries with finding target examples or estimating their prevalence, with bounds that enable deeper optimal lookahead for certain models.

title: Bayesian Optimal Active Search and Surveying
